content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine an
application for a new Premises Licence, in respect of Blacktree
Stores Ltd, for 11 Station Parade, Virigina Water, GU25 4AB.
 
The applicants attended in person but were not
represented.  All parties were
introduced.
 
The Council’s Senior Licensing Officer
presented their report which it was noted was unchanged since
publication.  The application was for
off sales only of alcohol, from 06:00 – 23:00 Monday –
Sunday, with the opening hours mirroring those of the proposed
licensable activity.
 
Members noted the proposed location of the
convenience store, and were advised that a site meeting had taken
place involving the applicants, Police Alcohol Licensing Officer,
and the Council’s Senior Licensing Officer.  A number of issues had been discussed, including
the proposed conditions to promote the licensing objectives, that
were included with the application, which would be enforceable, if
the licence was granted.  These were set
out in full in the agenda papers.
 
It was confirmed that none of the Responsible
Authorities had made any objections to the application for a
premises licence being granted.  However
three residents had made relevant representations, which were
summarised and appended in full.
 
The Sub-Committee was directed to the relevant
sections of the Council’s Statement of Licensing Policy and
the guidance issued under Section 182 of the Licensing Act
2003.
 
There being no questions for the Senior
Licensing Officer, the applicants were then invited to state their
case.
 
The applicants addressed each of the
Objector’s concerns; confirming their intention to provide
litter bins outside the premises to deter littering, and clarifying
that Station Parade and Station Approach contained three other
convenience stores, two of which with identical hours to those
sought.  The applicants had 22 years of
experience in the trade, with a number of outlets they had
successfully managed over the years. 
They would be taking a ‘hands on’ interest in the
business, and demonstrated a clear knowledge of retail in alcohol
and an appreciation of the licensing objectives; including how to
prevent, as far as reasonable possible, under age sales, and
shoplifting (by for example in one store they only allowed up to 3
children in the shop at any one time between the hours of 15:00 and
17:00 hours).  They utilised an
e-software package to log incidents and till prompts for age
verification which produced instant reports, in which all staff
would be trained.  This was considered
more robust than a paper register.
 
The applicants were well versed in operating
retail outlets, and doing local research to identify that Station
Parade was likely to be successful, with footfall from the railway
station nearby.
 
In response to questions from the
Sub-Committee, the applicants confirmed staffing arrangements,
training, and the importance of building a positive rapport and
good ties with the community in which they wished to
operate.  The store’s design was
also reviewed, it being established that spirits would only be
accessible by staff behind the counter, which re-assured the
Sub-Committee.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer emphasised the
importance of logging any criminal activity with the Police, which
the applicants readily agreed with.
 
In their closing statement the applicants
re-iterated that as independent operators they could provide an
excellent and responsive level of service to the community, and the
proposed conditions would help promote the licensing
objectives.
 
The Sub-Committee retired to determine the
application at 17:25 and re-convened at 17:40.
 
Members had regard to the evidence presented
orally and in the agenda papers, taking into account the relevant
representations, and in turn the Council’s Statement of
Licensing Policy and revised guidance under Section 182 of the
Licensing Act 2003. 
 
Members were impressed by the
applicants’ thorough knowledge, experience, and awareness of
their responsibilities, and jurisdiction.  Members also considered the applicants had taken
appropriate and proportionate steps to promote the licensing
objectives, address concerns raised by the objectors, and also took
into account that no responsible authorities had made any
representations. 
 
The Sub-Committee was content to grant the
application for a new premises licence, subject to the conditions
which had been offered by the applicants in their Operating
Schedule of the application.
 
The Sub-Committee wished the applicants well,
noting that should there be issues in the future, the option to
review the licence if called to do so remained, as was standard
practice if the licensing objectives were being undermined.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the application for
a premises licence in respect of Blacktree Stores Limited, 11
Station Parade, Virginia Water, GU25 4AB, be granted, subject to
the conditions as set out in the agenda
topline: The Council has decided to grant a new premises licence for off sales of alcohol at a convenience store in Virginia Water.

content:
The Committee received for information what
was agreed to be a detailed and positive summary of the
Council’s work in Health and Safety for 2025/26.
 
The Committee recalled that the Health and
Safety Governance structure was introduced in 2024, and continued
to provide a clear model to manage workforce health and safety.
 
Officers highlighted the achievements made
during the year as part of the workforce health and safety action
plan.  These included the introduction
of a health and safety channel in Teams to promote
cross-departmental working and collaboration, and a review of
several health and wellbeing related policies and procedures to
bring these up to date with changing legislation and promote
consistency of application across the organisation.
 
Members noted that there had been an increase
in aggressive incidents towards staff. 
As a result, reporting concerns as well as ‘near
misses’ was widely promoted and facilitated by Teams, GPS,
and use of QR codes.
 
The Committee was informed about
‘Belong@Runnymede’, and the
Equality Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) and wellbeing annual
programme.  These were introduced to
raise awareness of staff wellbeing. 
Since their launch, the Council had participated in a full calendar
of events; more than one or two events every month.  Officers clarified that ‘Blue Monday’
had been translated into ‘Brew Monday’ where free tea
and coffee was available for staff, proving an opportunity to make
time to talk informally, thus combating the effects of the third
Monday in January, which was widely recognised to be the
‘saddest day of the year’.
 
Tackling stress continued to be a priority for
the Safety Committee and departmental Leads; understanding the
causes, and the relation between personal stress and how work
pressures could exacerbate the situation.
 
Officers advised that the Action Plan for
2026/27 included a review of data, monitoring training and
refreshers, and continuing to embed good practice in health and
safety.  Members were assured that Local
Government Re-organisation would not affect the programme nor the
Council’s commitment to health and safety.
 
The Committee agreed that the health, safety
and wellbeing of the Council’s workforce was integral to how
well the Council performed.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has approved recommendations to enhance health and safety for its workforce in 2025/26.

content:
The Committee was presented with the annual
ombudsman’s letter and an anonymised summary of cases to meet
the Council’s statutory duty under the Local Govt and Housing
Act.
 
The report included the Ombudsman’s data
and where possible crossmatched with the Council’s own
records.
 
Officers reported that the Ombudsman had dealt
with 11 cases during the year, 6 of which were investigated and
closed, four cases that were either not for them or were not ready
to be considered, and one case that was upheld.  This compared with 8 cases recorded in the
previous year.  Members recalled that
this was a Housing received last year but the outcome was not
received until May this year, so the Ombudsman counted it in the
2025/26 data.
 
At the same time as receiving the annual
letter, the Ombudsman had sent a spreadsheet which contained 14
referrals, 7 of which Officers were aware and pleased to report
that none were upheld.
 
Officers explained that the number of cases on
the Ombudsman’s website and the spreadsheet differed because
not all cases were formally notified to the Council.  There were three cases the Ombudsman had resolved
without needing to check anything with the Council, and none were
upheld.
 
Officers confirmed that they were awaiting the
outcome of another Housing case which had been with the Ombudsman
since December last year.
 
Members reviewed comparative data with the
other Surrey authorities followed by a series of service
improvements from a selection of authorities in Surrey.  The Committee found this information useful to
share learning and promote improvements.
 
Following the issue of the annual letter, the
Ombudsman then wrote to those public authorities where they had
particular concerns about their complaint handling or wanted to
highlight exceptional practice.  Members
were pleased to learn that Runnymede was not amongst those
authorities.
 
Officers further confirmed that Runnymede had
not been the subject of any public interest reports giving the
authority a clean bill of health for the 13th year since
the Ombudsman started doing these reports which publicises where an
authority had handled a case very badly and the Ombudsman felt it
was is in the public interest for everyone to know about it and
learn from it.
 
At the time of writing the report Officers had
not yet received the Ombudsman’s full annual
report.  However, it had that day been
published, and a link to it was sent to the Chair and Vice-Chair of
the Committee. 
 
Officers summarised the report, which gave
details of  trends and common issues
that had arisen during the year by complaint and authority
type.  The Ombudsman reported that
nationally the number of complaints they received had risen sharply
by 33%, and was consistent across all areas.   The number of cases relating to benefits and
council tax grew by 67%, followed by Housing at 46%. The lowest
increase was in Planning at 9%.
 
Officers drew the Committee’s attention
to narrative in the report where the Ombudsman welcomed local
government re-organisation, stating that ‘Devolution is a
once in a generation chance to fix public services and local
leaders must not waste it’. 
 
In preparation for LGR Officers had recently
completed a data sheet for the Customer Services workstream which
included complaints and the Ombudsman.
 
Officers considered that Runnymede’s
systems, policies and procedures reflected good practice which it
was hoped would be adopted going forward into West Surrey, being
compliant with the Ombudsman’s complaint handling code.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations following the review of the annual ombudsman's letter and cases.

content:
The Committee received for information an
update on procurement activity for 2025/26.
 
Officers reported another active year in which
the small team in Procurement had reviewed and revised all of the
Council’s template documents.  In
addition, a new Procurement Toolkit had been published alongside a
new user guide for the Council’s e-tendering system which had
received positive feedback from colleagues.
 
Members recalled that the updated Procurement
Strategy had been recently approved by full Council.  As part of the Social Value Policy update, the
Social Value Portal’s Open Access TOM system was
adopted.  Officers confirmed that this
had been trialled in two projects and provided a total of
£483,270 social value commitments were made by the successful
contractors.  It was agreed that the
tool would be used in procurement projects with a total contract
value above £100,000.
 
Officers had monitored the Procurement related
key performance indicators.  These
showed good performance levels in terms of percentage of spend on
the Contracts Register, and no legal challenges. 
 
In addition, the number of local suppliers had
been analysed.  This revealed 2% within
Runnymede, and 15% across Surrey. 
Officers advised that since the disapplication of Section 17 of the
Local Government Act 1988, Local Authorities could reserve
contracts below a specific value to companies in or bordering the
borough, or within the UK.
 
The Committee noted that 78 requests for
waivers, sourcing plans, and modifications had been reviewed by the
Council’s Procurement Board in 2025/26.  These had all been carefully scrutinised,
resulting in 18 being granted, compared with 15 in 2024/25,
reflecting this was a last resort option.
 
Members recognised the support which the
Council’s Procurement team was giving to Spelthorne Borough
Council.  This included training to 60
Officers in basic procurement and contract management.  In addition, preparatory work for the transition
into West Surrey was acknowledged.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for updating procurement processes for the upcoming year.

The Committee received the report.
   
 
The principal issue for Engineering was the
departure of the Team Manager who had been replaced by a
contractor. 
 
Green Spaces had reviewed the allotments
waiting list following the Overview & Scrutiny Review in 2025
and there were now 150 active applicants.
 
The 24% targets for recycling related to the
proportion of waste arisings that were diverted from being
incinerated. 
 
Officers apologised for any instances where
responses to customer service issues had been delayed and agreed to
discuss member concerns about the responsiveness of the Council at
a forthcoming senior leadership meeting.

The Committee received an exempt report
setting out proposals for four additional staff (3 loaders, 1
driver) and a refuse freighter to support the refuse
service’s response to increased and increasing number of
households served.  The property count
had increased from 36,733 in 2020 to 39,460 in 2026.  The current headcount was 176 drivers and
loaders.  The service was regularly
hiring agency staff which was resulting in agency overspends - of
over 50% 2025/26. 
 
It was regularly hiring a 26-tonne freighter
to support the fleet of 11 such vehicles.  The preferred and best value option was to
purchase a used diesel vehicle. 
 
The recommendations required a capital
estimate of £75,000 for the vehicle and a supplementary
revenue estimate of £157,144 which would be off-set by agency savings and would be recommended
to 9 July Corporate Management Committee.  The scope and scale of the proposals were
understood to require the consent of the West Surrey Shadow
Authority and this was included in the recommendations. 
 
Recommended:
 
The Corporate Management
Committee be requested to approve a supplementary Revenue Estimate
in the sum of £157,144 to create 3 new Loader posts and 1 new
Driver post in order to meet the current
operational requirements of the collection service.
 
The Corporate Management
Committee be requested to approve a supplementary Capital Estimate
in the sum of £75,000 for the purchase of a used or
refurbished 26-tonne refuse collection vehicle to support the
increased property count in the Borough.

The Committee received a report setting out
Food Service Plan for 2026/27 for approval.  The plan was drawn up in line with Food Standards
Agency guidance.  Around 700 local
premises were covered and the service continued to focus on those
premises assessed as high risk on a scale A-E.
 
It was noted there were 364 interventions by
the service, which predominantly resulted in written warnings which
could include improvement recommendations and advice.
 
Members drew attention to recent central
guidance being phased in in coming years.  Officers advised that this was outside of the
scope of the 2026/27 plan and that any  requirements of the guidance would be picked-up via the shadow authority / unitary
authority. It was agreed that further information about this would
be provided via a written briefing.
 
RESOLVED that the Food Service Plan 2026/27 be
approved.

In accordance with the procedure for the
conduct of business, Councillor E Gill was elected as Chair of the
meeting.  The Chair ensured that all
present understood the procedure to be followed.

content:
The Committee was asked to determine whether
an applicant was fit and proper within the meaning of the Local
Government (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1976 to be granted an
application for a Hackney Carriage/Private Hire Driver’s
Licence.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer was invited to
present their report.  This set out the
details of the application, and highlighted the fact that before
the applicant’s licence had expired in February 2025, he
applied for it to be renewed in January 2025, but had failed to
disclose three driving offences of exceeding the speed
limit.  Each amounted to 3 points,
totalling 9 points.  This had come to
light when Officers checked the DVLA licence records as a normal
part of the renewal procedure. 
Applicants are required to provide a unique number in order to
undertake the check which the applicant had duly provided on the
form.
 
When interviewed by Officers in February 2025,
the applicant admitted to a further motoring offence from October
2024.
 
With regard to the applicant’s previous
record, Officers advised that since being first licensed in 2014,
there had been one record of previous non-compliance.  This occurred in 2019, for which a warning was
issued at the time.  Again, this was a
motoring offence from November 2018. 
Officers confirmed that no other complaints had been received in
the 11 years that the applicant had been licensed.
 
The applicant’s renewal application was
refused in February 2025.  Subsequently,
following a further 3 points being placed on the DVLA licence, the
applicant, was disqualified in September 2025, for a period of six
months, and reinstated in March 2026. 
The applicant then submitted an application for a new Hackney
Carriage/Private Hire Driver’s licence in April 2026, which
Officers considered merited determination by the Committee.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer explained that as
a result of this case, and following an internal review, it was
deemed appropriate to amend the application form to make the
declaration of criminal or motoring offences clearer; specifically,
to break the original question down to ask applicants to declare
yes or no the answer to 5 sub questions regarding criminal or
motoring offences.
 
It was confirmed that the applicant’s
current DVLA licence contained a TT99 endorsement code
(disqualification under totting up) which would not be removed
until April 2029.  However, the 12
endorsement points that led to the disqualification had been
removed.
 
The Committee was directed to the
Council’s Hackney Carriage and Private Hire Licensing Policy,
which stated that normally if a person had lost their DVLA licence
due to ‘totting up’, 3 years should elapse (after the
restoration of the DVLA Driving licence) before an applicant would
be granted a Hackney Carriage or Private Hire Driver’s
licence.  In addition, Members were
signposted to the Institute of Licensing ‘Suitability
Guidance’, and the paramount consideration of public
safety.
 
There being no questions for the Senior
Licensing Officer, the applicant was invited to state their
case.
 
The applicant had submitted a written
statement and other supporting documentation which was included in
the bundle before the Committee.
 
The applicant stated that he had been a
professional driver for over 20 years, and a Hackney Carriage
driver since 2014.  He readily took full
responsibility for his mistake, and deeply regretted that his
behaviour had fallen short of what was expected.  He took a pride in his work and agreed that public
safety was a priority.  When he was
disqualified from driving for 6 months, this had given him an
opportunity to reflect, and make changes.  When his licence was re-instated he had taken
proactive steps to make improvements and had taken a defensive
driving course and was now working towards achieving advanced
driver status with the Institute of Advanced Motorists
Ltd.  The applicant stated that he was
determined to regain the trust of the licensing authority.
 
The applicant was asked if anything had
precipitated the short series of motoring offences which followed a
long history of good conduct.
 
The applicant provided the Committee with some
of his driving history.  He had founded
a taxi firm in Egham with a colleague, and was very
successful.  He referred to having a
life event which had affected his judgement and that had taught him
a big life lesson.  He considered that
his mistake on the application form was genuine, that he
didn’t intend to deceive anyone, and did not recall the
previous warning from 2019.  He said
that he was not proud of his actions, it was not really
dignified.
 
The Committee said to the applicant that
Members could only depart from the Licensing Authority’s
policy in exceptional circumstances, and had to feel they could
trust the applicant to put public safety first.
 
The applicant readily agreed and said that he
now had a different mind set, and that
driving legally, as a professional was his number one
priority.  As a family man, ne
appreciated the need for safety of the travelling public.
 
The applicant provided more details of what
was shortly afterwards established as 5 motoring offences; all for
exceeding the speed limit in various locations including central
London, the motorway, and flyover.  One
Member commented that the speeding offences were relatively
minor.  However, the applicant said that
it was still exceeding, and that he should have paid
attention.  The applicant felt that it
was good that he had been caught as it gave him a chance to reflect
and try different opportunities, including to become a Private Hire
Operator.  He instilled in his drivers
the absolute necessity to drive safely, and pay attention because
it affected everyone’s lives.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer drew the
Committee’s attention to the team’s decision to amend
the wording on the application form, because they agreed it could
have been more clear.  Officers agreed
that the applicant had not been deliberately deceptive and that he
had made a genuine mistake.  The
Committee was also asked to consider the applicant’s
character, which was an important assessment of whether someone was
‘fit a proper’ to hold a hackney carriage and/or
private hire driver’s licence.
 
The meeting was adjourned at 11.33 am, and
reconvened at 11.45 am to allow the Committee to clarify with the
Senior Licensing Officer whether it was reasonable to add a
condition if granting the licence to pass an Advanced Driver course
and attain membership of the Institute of Advanced Motorists (IAM
‘road smart’).  The Senior
Licensing Officer considered it was a specific, measurable, and
enforceable condition.
 
There was a short discussion about the
practicalities of attaining membership through undergoing a series
of courses, and how long that might take.  Drivers could choose to take between 6 and 12
modules as 1:1 sessions, then take the final test to attain
Advanced Driver certification and membership when they felt ready
to do so.
 
The meeting was adjourned again at 11.55 am to
allow the Senior Licensing Officer to make some checks about the
IAM process.
 
The meeting was reconvened at 12:05
pm.  The Senior Licensing Officer
confirmed the process of attaining Advanced Driver certification
and membership of the IAM, and that it would be reasonable to allow
the applicant up to a year to fulfil the condition, if the
application was granted.
 
The applicant re-asserted his desire and need
to do the course, that he had reformed in character, and his
behaviours, to be fully responsible and trustworthy.
 
The meeting was adjourned at 12:11 pm and
reconvened at 12:17 pm.
 
The decision of the Committee conveyed
verbally to the applicant was that his application would be
granted, subject to the condition that he undertook the IAM courses
and attained membership thereof by 25 June 2027, and submitted the
proof of this to the Licensing Authority, by which time would be
the new West Surrey Council.
 
The applicant was advised that if he was
unable to meet this condition, his licence would be revoked by the
new Licensing Authority.
 
The rationale for departing from the Licensing
Authority’s policy was that the Committee considered that the
applicant had demonstrated that he took his responsibilities
seriously, had changed his behaviour, and that Advanced driver
certification and membership of the IAM would be sufficient and
independent evidence of his high standard of driving skills,
abilities and behaviours, which would exceed those of other
drivers.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the applicant is a
fit and proper person within the meaning of the Act.  Therefore, to grant the applicant a Hackney
Carriage/Private Hire Driver’s licence subject to the
following condition:
 
that by no later
than 25 June 2027, the applicant shall submit proof to the
Licensing Authority that they have undertaken the IAM Road Smart
Advanced Driver course, and achieved membership of the IAM by
passing an advanced driving test administered by the IAM.
topline: The Council has decided to grant an applicant a Hackney Carriage/Private Hire Driver's licence with a condition to undertake an Advanced Driver course and achieve membership of the Institute of Advanced Motorists.

The Committee received a report which
summarised activities relating to Englefield Green.  The report also provided Members with an update on
expenditure previously approved, together with further proposals
for the use of the Englefield Green Ringfenced funds.
 
Officers reported that in June 2025 Officers
were asked to explore options for spending the Englefield Green
ringfenced funds prior to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) on
31 March 2027.  Taking into account all
previously committed expenditure the balance of the fund on 31
March 2027 would be £214,625.
 
The Committee was presented with various
options for consideration in order to utilise the funds prior to
LGR.
 
Litter bins –
removal of old concrete and posts
 
The new litter bins were approved in October
2025 and had now been procured,, following receipt of Crown Estate
approval, they would be installed during summer 2026. In accordance
with the specification set out by the Crown Estate, the concrete
bases and anchors of the old bins must be removed and the ground
made good. Officers were therefore seeking approval for this new
expenditure to be funded from the Ringfenced Fund at an additional
cost of £3,515.00 (which will be added to the existing sum of
£950 set aside for this purpose).
 
 
Refurbishment and
vandal-proof sanitary ware
 
The public toilets located on Englefield Green
close to the cricket pavilion were of mixed sanitary ware. The
urinals were constructed of metal, with the ladies, disabled
toilets and basins constructed of porcelain. Metal sanitary ware
was considerably more robust and more resistant to vandalism.
Therefore, Green Spaces Officers suggested that £3,700 of the
Englefield Green Ringfenced Fund should be allocated to replacing
the two basins and two toilets currently constructed of
porcelain.
 
Three-year Grass
Maintenance Programme
 
A three-year grass maintenance programme had
been proposed by Complete Weed Control at a total cost of
£28,330. The maintenance programme was outlined in Appendix
A.   If Members decided to approve
this programme, it would be funded from the Englefield Green
Ringfenced Fund. Officers recommended that an agreement regarding
grass cutting on the cricket outfield be reached with the
Englefield Green Cricket Club prior to commencement of the revised
grass maintenance routine, noting that a range of options had been
discussed with the Chair on the Cricket Club on 10th
June 2026. 
 
 
Members would note that a considerable balance
would be remaining on vesting day of the new West Surrey Unitary
Authority. (1st April 2027).  The
exclusive use of the Englefield Green Earmarked Reserve Maintenance
fund for maintenance management and enhancement projects in the
existing leasehold demise could not be guaranteed beyond this
point.  Officers therefore proposed that
this Committee considered and approved a variation to the
restrictions placed on the expenditure of the Ringfenced Fund
monies in 2015 to permit them to also be used to support
recreational and leisure projects, refurbishment of allotments,
play areas, community groups and sports facilities in the wider
Englefield Green locality i.e. within the boundaries of the West
Englefield Green and East Englefield Green Wards at the date of
this report.
 
It was important to note that the Englefield
Green Committee would continue to have access to the Ringfenced
Fund to deliver works relating to maintenance of Englefield Green
whilst the budget remained. All approvals relating to expenditure
from the Ringfenced Fund outside the Green (i.e. on recreational
and leisure projects, play areas, community groups, sports
facilities and refurbishment of allotments in the West Englefield
Green and East Englefield Green Wards) would be outside the remit
of the Englefield Green Committee. Decisions on such expenditure
would therefore be made through the Community Services
Committee.
 
 
There was potential for the calls on the
Ringfenced Funds to be greater than the funds held. Decisions as to
any conflicts on the allocation of monies in the Ringfenced Fund
between the Englefield Green and the Community Services Committee
should be made by the Corporate Management Committee.
 
Officers advised the Committee that whilst the
Crown Estate had been heavily involved with negotiations between
the Council and the developers the Crown Estate now had no legal
interest in the funds. 
 
Members recalled they had previously approved
an excellently written Woodland Management Plan.  Officers were asked to bring a budget proposal for
the use of ringfenced funds for its continued implementation going
forwards to the next meeting. 
 
Resolved that:
 

a)   
The Englefield Green Committee approves the release of
£28,330 from the Englefield Green Ringfenced Fund to deliver
the grass maintenance programme outlined in Appendix A

b)   
The grass maintenance programme is approved, conditional on an
agreement being reached with the Englefield Green Cricket Club
regarding future grass-cutting arrangements for the cricket square
and outfield

c)    
The Englefield Green Committee approves improvements to the public
toilets, as identified in the report, at an approximate cost of
£3,700 to be funded from the Englefield Green Ringfenced
fund

d)   
The Englefield Green Committee approves a budget of £3,515
from the Englefield Green Ringfenced fund to cover the Crown Estate
requirement that all bin concrete bases and posts be removed prior
to installation of the new bins

e)   
The Englefield Green Committee approve the variation of the
restriction on the use of the Ringfenced fund to permit the
Ringfenced fund to also be used for recreational and leisure
projects, refurbishment of allotments, play areas, community groups
and sports facilities in the East and West Englefield Green wards,
as follows:
 
1)   
Decisions as to the expenditure of the Ringfenced Fund on the
Englefield Green be made by the Englefield Green Committee: and
2)   
Decisions as to expenditure of the Ringfenced Fund on recreational
and leisure projects, refurbishment of allotments, play areas,
community groups and sports facilities in the East and West
Englefield Green wards, to be made by the Community Services
Committee; and
3)   
Decisions as to any conflicts as to the allocation of monies in the
Ringfenced fund between the Englefield Green and the Community
Services Committee to be made by the Corporate Management
Committee.
topline: The Englefield Green Committee has decided to allocate funds from the Ringfenced Fund for various projects including litter bin removal, public toilet refurbishment, and a grass maintenance program.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
commence a procurement exercise in the sum of £35,000 to
appoint a supplier to install sensory and neurodivergent friendly
play panels across the borough, and to make specific enhancements
at Victory Park.
 
In addition, the Committee was asked to make a
series of recommendations to Corporate Management Committee to
facilitate this, and the development of facilities at Victory
Park.
 
Officers proposed to build on previous
projects to improve accessibility, inclusivity, and overall user
experience for residents in the Council’s parks
facilities. 
 
Victory Park, in Addlestone, had been
identified as one on which to concentrate efforts to help it
achieve the status of a ‘destination’ park.  Additional funding could make it possible to
install additional equipment such as a zipline or a larger more
adventurous multi-use unit to better serve older
children.  This park, and other sites in
the borough would also benefit from the installation of
approximately 35 or more sensory panels.
 
A sum of £80,000 had already been
secured from NHS funding for Victory Park, and £20,000 for
sensory board provision, both approved by the Community Services
Committee.  Officers had identified a
further £35,000 of additional funding which would assist both
the above projects to be split as set out in the
recommendations.
 
Members were asked to note that future
maintenance costs would not increase as a result, beyond those
already budgeted for.
 
The Committee was very pleased to support the
proposals to enhance the Council’s parks, particularly for
children who had been identified by the County Council as requiring
an Education Health and Care Plan, of whom the majority were
diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder.
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
Corporate Management Committee be requested to approve a capital
estimate in the sum of £20,000 to enhance the Victory Park
play area, in addition to the £80,000 previously secured
through NHS funding to be funded from the existing parks play area
improvement provision in the current Capital Programme to support
its development as a destination park;

 

ii)        
Corporate Management Committee be requested to approve a capital
estimate in the sum of £15,000 for the installation of
sensory and neurodivergent-friendly play panels across the Borough,
building on the existing £20,000 funding allocation from the
Youth Development Fund to be funded from the existing parks play
area improvement provision in the current Capital Programme;

 

iii)        Corporate
Management Committee be requested to approve the commencement of a
procurement exercise to the value of £100,000 to appoint a
supplier for i); and

 

iv)       
the commencement of a procurement exercise for £35,000 to
appoint a supplier for (ii) be approved
topline: The Council has decided to approve funding for the installation of sensory panels and enhancements at Victory Park to improve accessibility and inclusivity in parks.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
continue with a pilot started over the winter of 2025 which was to
leave the borough’s five formal parks open after dusk to
achieve savings on the cost of locking and unlocking.  The proposal arose from a staff suggestion made as
part of the savings and efficiencies programme.  In 2025/26 savings of £19,230 had been
delivered on the cost of locking and unlocking the park gates and
key holding services.  The total cost of
opening and closing the parks in 2024/25 was £65,160.
 
Members reviewed the current opening and
closing times, the existing facilities and security measures at
each site.  The Committee was also
advised of an e-petition opened on the Council’s website
regarding the opening times at Victory Park, one of the five formal
parks affected by the proposals.
 
The Committee was directed to a document
entitled ‘Risks and mitigation measures for keeping parks
open at night.  Key risks in the summer
months were anti-social behaviour, personal safety and crime,
environmental and wildlife impact, fire, accidents and injuries,
overcrowding and public nuisance, infrastructure wear and tear and
public health and hygiene.  In the
winter months the risks included public safety, Health risks,
Liability, and Security concerns.  This
document set out recommended actions in the summer and winter
months; these had been included where Officers considered them
practical and financially viable.
 
Members discussed whether the risk of
vandalism, anti-social behaviour, unauthorised incursions, or other
incidents of criminal behaviour would be increased by leaving the
parks open all hours, although the evidence gathered by Officers so
far suggested that the risk was low. 
Officers advised that although the parks would be left open, the
toilets would still be closed overnight.  New metal toilets were being installed at
Heathervale Recreation Ground and
Victory Park.
 
Officers proposed that additional CCTV could
be installed in those parks where there was none at the
moment.  These were Chertsey Recreation
Ground and the Grounds Maintenance compound at Abbeyfields.  The
estimated cost in Year 1 was approximately £23,400 falling to
£3,400 in Year 2.  It was noted
that firmer figures would be available later in the year, when the
pilot was reviewed.  This would include
full financial implications that would fall on West Surrey Council
in the future.  In addition, where
height barriers were in place these would remain.
 
Some Members considered that more consultation
was needed before making a definite decision and that it would be
sensible to review the situation after the summer when more
incidents were likely to occur.  Members
referred to concerns raised by residents local to Victory Park, and
the Committee agreed that wider consultation, including with
residents nearby the formal parks would be beneficial.  It was noted that service users at Chertsey
Recreation Ground would be consulted about the installation of
CCTV.
 
It was also noted that there was a desire from
residents in Parkside to have a separate access gate to
Heathervale Recreation Ground, and
there were no plans to re-open the gate from the park onto the
towpath.
 
It was suggested that Officers could consider
utilising the Citizens Engagement Panel and wider use of on-line
platforms to gather feedback and evidence to support the review and
report back to the Committee in November 2026 and going forward
into West Surrey Council.  At the same
time residents with concerns were encouraged to use existing
channels to report anti-social behaviour, data for which was
collated by Community Safety.
 
Officers were asked to record in the Minutes a
request made by an attending Member of the Council that a review of
park lighting in parks and open spaces being ‘on and
maintained’ (as per para 8.4 of the Officer’s report)
be considered as part of the wider review.  [This was not an agreed action, it was an
instruction to Minute the request]
 
The Committee looked forward to receiving an
update on the pilot at its meeting in November 2026.
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
the extension of the winter opening arrangements at Heathervale Recreation Ground, The Orchard and
Abbeyfields, Truss’s Island and
Ottershaw Memorial Fields and proposed changes to opening and
closing arrangements at Victory Park and Chertsey Recreation Ground
for the summer 2026 period be approved;

 

ii)         Members
note the arrangements will operate on a dynamic and evidence led
basis, and that the Corporate Head of Environmental Services in
consultation with the Runnymede Neighbourhood Police Team and
Community Safety colleagues, may amend or reinstate security
measures at individual sites;

 

iii)        Members note
that security costs in 2025/2026 were approximately

£45,936 which is £19,230 less than the cost in
2024/2025;

 

iv)       
a proportion of savings which would be delivered in 2026/2027, are
reinvested in targeted mitigation measures as follows.  An estimated installation cost of £20,000
plus maintenance, transmission and electricity costs estimated to
be £3,400 per year for both cameras.
 
Installation of CCTV at
Chertsey Recreation Ground
 
Installation of CCTV at
Abbeyfields/The Orchard; and
 

v)         a report
is presented to the Community Services Committee in November 2026
with:

 
·        
an evaluation of outcomes of changed security
arrangements,
·        
analysis of available CCTV incident and police data,
·        
financial impacts including predicted savings for
2026/2027,
·        
evidence-based recommendations on longer term park opening and
security arrangements
topline: The Council has decided to extend the pilot project of leaving formal parks open after dusk to save costs, despite concerns about potential risks and the need for more consultation with local residents.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought for
a revised Home Improvement Agency (HIA), Assistance
Policy.  Members were also appraised of
service delivery for 2025/26.
 
For 2025/26, the HIA received 145 referrals,
with an upward trend in Quarter 4.  The
number of completed cases totalled 72, with the fewest completed in
Quarter 4.  This indicated a capacity
issue and increased demand.  The types
of adaptations showed that showers/wet rooms were the common,
followed by stairlifts.  Local authority
tenants had the highest number of referrals followed by owner
occupiers and social landlord tenants, 
The HIA dealt with the mandatory Disabled Facilities Grants (DFG)
and discretionary grants to assist vulnerable disabled and elderly
residents.
 
Officers had reviewed the policy to ensure it
remained responsive, transparent and aligned with current demand,
financial pressures and residents’ needs.  The proposed changes included a table outlining
the types of grant available, a new section under the DFG for
applicants with degenerative, progressive or life limiting
conditions, notably Motor Neurone Disease (MND), a reduction in the
savings threshold from £23,500 to £16,000 to align with
means tested benefit rules, an increase in the clearance grant
amount from £5,000 to £7,500, a table outlining the
changes to the approval process, an overview of the application
process, and a means testing scored checklist.
 
Members agreed that the revised policy
provided clearer guidance and improved transparency for
applicants.  Members welcomed the option
to fast-track applications under the DFG for conditions such as MND
and supported the other changes which promoted consistency and
fairness, as well as creating a more flexible, responsive and user
focussed system.
 
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
the performance and increasing demand on the Home Improvement
Agency service during 2025–2026 be noted; and

 

ii)         the
revised Home Improvement Agency Assistance Policy, as set out
within the Officer’s report and Appendix A be approved, to
ensure the continued effective, transparent and legally compliant
delivery of Disabled Facilities Grants and discretionary housing
assistance across all tenures.
topline: The council has decided to approve a revised Home Improvement Agency Assistance Policy to address increasing demand and capacity issues for disabled and elderly residents.

content:
The Committee was presented with a detailed
report regarding a pilot in Surrey in which Runnymede had
participated to address gambling harms, and the increased risks
associated with them for particular sectors of the community.
 
Members noted with concern the broader picture
of gambling harms, the specific effects in Surrey, and how the most
socio-economically deprived and disadvantaged groups in England had
the lowest gambling participation rates but the highest levels of
harmful gambling.
 
The first Whole System Approach (WSA) to
Gambling harms brought a range of partners together including the
health authority, licensing authorities, GambleAware, Voluntary,
community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector.  The aim was to prioritise the strategy,
development and testing the prototype and its priorities in the WSA
model in Runnymede.
 
Members were advised of the launch event for
the WSA, training that had taken place and future plans, including
the addition of Gambling Harms training for the Licensing &
Regulatory Committees, the licensing regime, and how preventing
gambling harms impacted on advertising. 
In addition, the new Surrey wide draft strategy 2026-2031 set out 8
priorities based on the outcome of the pilot in
Runnymede.  These included raising
awareness, working with criminal justice partners, further
research, and having a responsive frontline with clear referral
pathways.
 
Officers were asked to clarify the definitions
of ‘blue’ and ‘orange’ on the map at
section 2.16 of the report, and ‘Addlestone North and
South’ as indicative Areas of Deprivation.
 
The Committee was pleased that
Runnymede’s significant contribution would inform the WSA
going forward, its adoption as a priority workstream, and the work
to continue through the Runnymede Healthy Communities
Partnership.
 
Officers were thanked for their thoroughly
researched report, which was duly noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations to address gambling harms in Surrey, focusing on the most vulnerable communities.

content:
The Committee received an exempt report in
which approval was sought to take action to undertake works at
Runnymede Pleasure Ground (RPG) to demolish two derelict
properties.  This required authority to
allocate funding in the sum reported from the RPG Trust reserves to
fund the works, and undertake a procurement exercise to appoint a
suitable contractor with the maximum contract value.
 
Officers referred to a previous approval given
in 2013 to demolish two properties on land adjacent to RPG, but
which had not been actioned.  Over time
the two properties had become uninhabitable, and required extensive
refurbishment and remedial works if they were to be brought back
into use.  Officers considered this was
not an option.  Members noted that
consideration was given in the past to alternative use for the
properties and the land on which they sat, but these had all proved
unviable.
 
Members were asked to note the detailed legal
implications in the report, setting out the various restrictions on
the land, and to what purpose it could be used, as well as a number
of enforceable restrictive covenants with regard to
buildings. 
 
Members also noted the environmental, risk,
and financial implications; and the steps therein which had to be
undertaken prior to any works commencing.  These included ecological and biodiversity
reports, including a bat survey, the results of which would
determine when and if the works could take place safely.
 
The Committee agreed there was no option but
to demolish the two properties in question, as they were beyond
economical refurbishment, although some concern was raised about
the use of a significant amount of money from the Trust’s
reserves to fund the works.
 
Officers were asked to confirm when the
properties in question fell vacant, and when Council Tax ceased to
be paid thereon.
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
the demolition of the two dilapidated cottages be
approved;
 

ii)         the
allocation of up to the sum as reported from the RPG reserves to
fund the works be approved; and

 
iii)        undertaking a
procurement exercise to appoint a suitable contractor with the
maximum contract value as reported be approved
topline: The Committee has decided to demolish two derelict properties at Runnymede Pleasure Ground and allocate funding from the RPG Trust reserves for the works.

content:
The Committee’s approval
was sought for a funding application made through the Runnymede
Healthy Communities Partnership by ‘Your Sanctuary’ to
deliver the “Wanna Talk?” programme in the
borough.
 
Members recalled that at the
meeting of the Committee in January 2026, approval had been given
to how Place-Based funding in the sum of £50,000 from the
former North West Surrey Health and Care Alliance would be
allocated to support health and wellbeing projects.
 
The Committee noted that
applications for funding up to £5,000 were delegated to the
Corporate Head of Community Services, in consultation with the
Chair of the Community Services Committee and the Chair of the
Health and Wellbeing Partnerships. 
Funding over £5,000 would be determined by the Community
Services Committee.
 
Officers confirmed that 11
funding applications, totalling £82,206 had been received.
Successful projects included Home Start Runnymede, and
International Music Making.  Other
partners with whom the panel were keen to work included Holme Farm,
Citizens Advice Runnymede and Spelthorne, Luminus Insight and Mind Warriors.
 
Members were advised that one
application exceeded the £5,000 threshold.  The amount requested was £10,000 to deliver
the “Wanna Talk?” project in primarily state secondary
schools in the borough.  Those listed in
the application were Philip Southcote, Salesians, St George’s
College, Chertsey High, Jubilee High, and Magna Carta.  Officers were asked to consider whether additional
secondary schools and educational establishments could be included
in the project such as Strode’s College and Sir William
Perkins’s School.  Officers
advised that the primary focus was on state funded
schools.
 
The programme was designed to
help young people recognise healthy and unhealthy/abusive
relationships, understand consent, respect and personal boundaries,
build confidence, resilience, self-esteem, emotional wellbeing and
relationship building skills.  The
Committee agreed these were all crucial for future life choices and
the prevention of abusive patterns.
 
The Committee was supportive of
the application, noting its alignment with the Health and Wellbeing
Strategy, and the Runnymede Community Safety Partnership priority;
Preventing Violence Against Women and Girls. 
 
Officers advised that the
funding, if approved, was a one-off grant.  Therefore, sustainability of the project had been
taken into account.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the
funding application to deliver the Your Sanctuary “Wanna
Talk?” programme across Runnymede borough be
approved
topline: The Committee has decided to approve funding for the 'Wanna Talk?' programme in Runnymede borough

content:
The Committee’s approval
was sought to pursue an opportunity to extend Community Transport
services to Spelthorne Borough Council.
 
Members recalled that the Council
already delivered the co-ordination of Community Transport services
across Runnymede and Surrey Heath, through its own transport
coordination team. 
 
Officers advised that an
opportunity had arisen for the Council to deliver
Spelthorne’s Community Transport co-ordination services,
following the forthcoming expiry of its existing arrangements with
Elmbridge Borough Council in September 2026.
 
Approval of the changes to the
Community Services staff establishment, also approved at the
meeting, would facilitate Spelthorne Borough Council’s
request that the Council delivered this function on their behalf,
from October 2025 until March 2027, and thereafter as part of the
West Surrey Council.
 
Members agreed this was a timely opportunity
to collaborate with a neighbouring borough council.  The opportunity to harmonise a service between
boroughs would help the transition from two authorities into
one.
 
Members were pleased to learn that the
Council’s ability to deliver this opportunity within its
existing staff resources, software, office accommodation etc
allowed for a modest income to be realised that would reduce the
level of subsidy against the service.
 
In terms of financial arrangements, the
Committee approved the intended charges to Spelthorne, which
included the set up period, and noted the proposed charges for
2027/28, as set out in the report.
 
With regard to risk, the main one identified
was any unforeseen, additional requirements, which would become
apparent when the full specification was realised.  Therefore, with this in mind, the Committee was
also content to give delegated authority to the Assistant Chief
Executive (Place) should the need arise for more flexibility,
including whether to proceed with the proposed arrangements.
 
Members concurred that this presented an
opportunity to demonstrate, again, the ability and willingness of
Community Services, and the Council more widely, to be lean and
flexible in its approach to service delivery, was timely and
reflective of the approach that might be required post vesting day
by West Surrey Council.
 
The Committee approved the recommendations
accordingly.
 
Resolved that
–
 

i)         
entering a contract with Spelthorne Borough Council, for a period
of eighteen months, for the delivery of Community Transport
co-ordination services be approved; and

 

ii)        
delegated authority be granted to the Assistant Chief Executive
(Place), in consultation with the Chair and Vice Chair of Community
Services Committee to not proceed with the contract should further
discussions disclose that it is not practical for operational
reasons to proceed
topline: The Council has decided to extend Community Transport services to Spelthorne Borough Council.

content:
The Committee’s authority
was sought to undertake a compliant procurement exercise for the
provision of frozen meals to support the Meals at Home service
across Runnymede and Surrey Heath. 
 
Officers advised that following
the decoupling of the vehicle lease from the food supply contract,
the Council had to procure its food provision independently in line
with Contract Standing Orders.  Officers
considered that the proposed procurement route as identified in the
report ensured service continuity, value for money and ongoing
support to vulnerable residents.
 
Officers explained what the current
contractual obligations were prior to the waiver approved in
January 2026, where the vehicle lease was transferred from the food
supplier the vehicles supplier, and that the Council was bound to
procuring its food through the food supplier, via the sub agreement
to lease the vehicles through.
 
Officers confirmed that procurement was
required following the separation of the vehicle lease from the
food supply arrangement, which necessitated an independent,
competitive process in accordance with the Council’s Contract
Standing Orders.
 
Officers had reviewed the available options,
as set out in the Officer’s report.  Members noted that each option presented different
implications in terms of compliance, value for money, service
continuity and timing, particularly in the context of Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR).
 
The Committee concurred with the
Officer’s recommendation, recognising that the
Council’s Meals at Home service was a critical frontline
service supporting some of the most vulnerable residents.
 
It was agreed that the proposed approach
ensured legal compliance, value for money and service quality and
continuity.  The Committee was content
for Officers to proceed with the procurement and secure a
sustainable long-term food supply arrangement.
 
Resolved that
–
 

i)         
the commencement of a competitive procurement process for the
supply of meals to the Meals at Home service with an estimated
value of up to the sum reported per annum be approved;
and

 

ii)         the
final contract term (anticipated to be 2 + 1 years) subject to
procurement outcomes be approved
topline: The Council has decided to procure frozen meals to support vulnerable residents in Runnymede and Surrey Heath.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
make a number of recommendations to the
Corporate Management Committee for proposed staffing establishment
changes in Community Services.  These
were to respond to ongoing vacancies, financial pressures, and to
prepare for Local Government Re-organisation (LGR).  In addition, approval was sought to recruit to
vacancies, new posts and to implement the changes under delegated
authority to effect the proposals in a
timely manner.
 
Members received a detailed report which
explained the financial pressures facing both Runnymede and Surrey
Heath Borough Councils, and how these might be addressed by
alterations to the staffing establishment at both Councils.
 
In essence, the proposals involved the
deletion of a number of posts across
Community Services, and the recruitment to key vacancies and new
posts, and some amendments to existing posts in consultation with
the affected individuals.  The exact
process to be followed for each role was noted.  In general terms the plan was a phased
implementation programme; to make amendments to existing posts
first, and then move onto internal and
external recruitment.
 
The Committee noted the detailed financial
implications as set out in the Officer’s report, and
commended Officers on the level of work undertaken to reach the
current position, which showed a very modest budget required to
make the proposed changes.  The recent
pay and grading review had also been taken into account for
estimated savings for Runnymede, whilst Surrey Heath’s much
higher saving was based against their existing pay structure.
 
The legal, equalities, and risk implications
were noted.
 
The Committee agreed that the sustained
reliance on a reduced capacity was no longer viable, and recognised the urgency to implement the
new structure.  Members agreed that
stabilising the service and protection of staff wellbeing was a
priority.
 
Members were pleased to support the
recommendations accordingly.
 
Resolved
that:-
 
Corporate Management
Committee be asked to approve:
 
i)         
the proposed staffing changes and revised service structures within
Community Services; and
 

ii)         an
amendment to the Council’s Establishment, as set out in the
Officer’s report; and

 

Resolved that:-

 

iii)        approval is
given to progress internal and external recruitment to the

           
revised and vacant posts as set out in the report; and

 

iv)       
authority is delegated to the Corporate Head of Community Services,
in consultation with Human Resources, to implement the changes in
accordance with the phased approach outlined, including finalising
job descriptions and managing individual staffing adjustments
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for staffing changes in Community Services to address ongoing vacancies and financial pressures.

The Committee received a report proposing a
new Repairs policy to set out the council’s approach to
delivering a high-quality, efficient, and resident-focused
responsive repairs service. It ensures compliance with regulatory,
and contractual obligations, and supports our commitment to
maintaining safe, secure, and well-maintained homes. The new policy
meets the current requirements of Awaab’s Law and the
approach laid down in the regulator’s customer
standards. 
 
Further amendments will be required to the
policy upon release of Phase 2 and Phase 3 of Awaab’s law,
which is scheduled to come into force in late 2026 and
2027. 
 
The existing policy was reviewed in 2021 and
set out three defined repair timescale obligations. These were:
 

Emergency – 4 Hours
Routine – 15 Working Days
Planned – 90 Working Days

 
The new policy had been discussed with engaged
tenants and proposed the following categories with the type of
repair issue detailed in the report:
 




Emergency


Emergency repair work will be attended and if
possible, completed within 24 Hrs.




Significant


If there are significant repairs, it will be
completed within 5 days.




Routine


All repair work will be completed within 20
days




Planned


90 days (larger fencing and more complex
works)




 
The Committee agreed to strengthen the
provisions around no access, and that the wording around guttering
repairs should be amended so that cases where harm was likely to be
caused to person or property should be escalated.  The amendments would be finalised in conjunction
with the Chair.
 
RESOLVED that the Repairs Policy with the
amendments described above be approved.

content:
The Committee received for information the
annual report for the year ending 31 March 2026 on all matters
relating to the Licensing Act 2003.
 
Members recalled that the scope of the
Licensing Authority covered the publishing of a Statement of
Licensing Policy, administering and considering applications for
licensable activities, with a view to promoting the Licensing
objectives, as well as undertaking inspection and enforcement
activities.
 
The Committee reviewed statistics for the
number of licensed premises, personal licences, applications,
variations, reviews etc.  Of note were
the slight reduction in the number of Club Premises Certificates,
and an increase in the number of Temporary Event Notices (TENs),
particularly ‘late TENs’. 
Officers considered there was no specific reason for the increase
in late TENs, but highlighted the information available on the
Council’s website, and the need to avoid giving late notices,
owing to the risk of licensable activities not being permitted if
any of the Responsible Authorities objected to the late TEN, with
no right of appeal.  Members were
disappointed that nationally there had been no progress with the
creation of a ‘Community Event Notice’ which would
assist schools and church groups especially.
 
Members noted that there had been two
applications, and one review application determined by the
Sub-Committee during the year.  The
latter had appealed revocation of the premises licence.  This had subsequently been resolved through an
agreement of a Consent Order, following a significant improvement
in the supervision and management of the premises in question.
 
The Committee was also presented with
statistics provided by Surrey Police which highlighted the increase
in incidents involving theft of alcohol from licensed
premises.  There were also a significant
number of public order offences at public houses.
 
Officers continued to undertake a structured
intelligence led approach to inspections and enforcement; in
partnership with other Responsible Authorities.  Officers re-affirmed that promotion of the
licensing objectives was paramount.
 
The Committee noted that 9 complaints had been
investigated during the year, compared with 3 in the previous
year.  In addition, Environmental Health
had received 60 complaints regarding licensed premises, an increase
of 14 on the previous year.
 
Officers reported an on-going case example of
proactive partnership working with Immigration Enforcement and
Surrey Police.
 
The Committee was pleased to note service
improvements made in conjunction with the Council’s Digital
Services team, especially the introduction of a new online form for
TEN applications and payments, and including successful debt
recovery.
 
The Committee was appraised of forthcoming
legislative changes which would need to be reflected in the
Licensing Policy when enacted and/or when statutory guidance or
secondary legislation was in place (in the case of the Tobacco and
Vapes Act 2026), which would clarify the duties and
responsibilities for the Licensing Authority.
 
The Committee agreed that it was also
important to ensure local authorities across East and West Surrey
were consistent in their policies and procedures to prepare for the
West Surrey Council.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations related to the Licensing Act 2003 for the year ending 31 March 2026.

content:
The Committee received for information the
annual report on all matters relating to Hackney Carriage and
Private Hire licensing for the year ending 31 March 2026.
 
Officers advised that the paramount obligation
of the Licensing Authority for hackney carriage and private hire
licensing was the safety of the public. 
The licensing regime was governed by the Town Police Clauses Act
1847, and the Local Government (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act
1976.
 
The Licensing regime covered Hackney Carriage
Vehicles and Drivers, Private Hire Vehicles, Drivers, and
Operators.
 
The Committee was invited to review a series
of statistics relating to the trade. 
These showed a small increase in the number of private hire
drivers, operators, and vehicles, but a small decrease in the
number of hackney carriage drivers and vehicles.
 
Members recalled that the Hackney Carriage and
Private Hire Policy had been substantially reviewed during the
summer of 2024, taking on board legislative change, and introducing
Environmental standards concerning exhaust emissions to take effect
from 1 January 2030.  In Runnymede, 89%
of the licensed fleet currently met ULEV standards; only 9 vehicles
were non-compliant.  Officers confirmed
that a new Euro 7 emission standard was due to come into force from
November 2026.  This would introduce
stricter rules for exhaust gases, and, for the first time,
regulation of non-exhaust emissions like brake dust and tyre
particles.
 
Members noted there were 4 suspensions in
2025/26, two were regarding the same driver.  Officers also reported 6 complaints, two of which
had resulted in Regulatory Committee Hearings, where one driver had
received a warning, and the other had been suspended.  Officers confirmed that they had worked closely
with the Senior Park Operations Manager at Thorpe Park, and with
Spelthorne Council to assist with revisions to Thorpe Park’s
‘Taxi Rank Regulations and Operational Expectations’
for hackney carriage drivers.  It was
hoped that the improvements made would minimise issues in the
future.
 
Officers reported on other enforcement
operations, in partnership with a number of other agencies,
including the Surrey & Sussex Police Commercial Vehicle
Unit.  Of note was an operation in
September 2025, where 70 vehicles were stopped and spoken to by
different agencies, including Transport for London, and Surrey
Police and Licensing Officers.  It was
confirmed that 2 operations were planned per annum, the first of
which for 2026/27 had already taken place.  The organisational change for Surrey Police into
East and West Surrey had not adversely affected their ability to
provide assistance with such enforcement operations.  Likewise, Licensing Officers across Surrey were
working closely ahead of Local Government Re-organisation to ensure
consistency and a smooth transition into the East and West Surrey
Councils.
 
In respect of Licensing fees and fares,
Members noted modest increases in private hire vehicles, driver
renewals and Operators’ fees and a 29% decrease in fees from
hackney carriage vehicles.  In addition,
the Committee recalled the increase from £50 to £100
for the soiling charge, which came into effect from 21 April
2026.
 
The Committee was notified of forthcoming
legislation, including the Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the
Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services)
Regulations 2026, and the English Devolution and Community
Empowerment Act 2026.  Key measures of
the aforementioned Act would establish a national framework for the
licensing of taxi and private hire vehicles.  In addition, the King’s Speech in May 2026
included reforms to modernise the relevant legislation for the
first time in more than a century.  The
Draft Taxi and Private Hire Bill sought to provide a single,
consistent national framework for England, improving accessibility
for passengers with disabilities and regulating modern booking
apps.  Members agreed this was long
overdue and most welcome.
 
The Committee also noted a graph tabled at the
meeting to illustrate the fluctuations in the numbers of drivers,
vehicles, and operators since 2014.
 
Officers were thanked for their hard work and
the report was duly noted.
topline: The Licensing Authority has decided to approve recommendations for Hackney Carriage and Private Hire licensing for the year ending 31 March 2026.
