content:
The Committee received a report proposing that
the Council consults stakeholders on whether to apply  to the Secretary of State  for a Regulation 7 Direction, which would remove
deemed consent for the display of estate agent letting or for sale
boards.  The report was accompanied by
evidence in support of such an application; for the application to
succeed, the case had to be made that that one or more of the
deemed consent provisions has had such adverse effects on the
amenity or public safety of the area that there is no prospect of
an improvement in the quality of advertising in the locality,
unless the local planning authority are given the power to control
that particular type of advertisement. 
The areas considered to be affected were Englefield Green and
Egham. 
 
It was noted that the complaints received by
the planning enforcement team are largely concerned with an
over-proliferation of residential lettings boards and that lettings
agents often fail to remove these boards within the 14 day time limit from sale or agreed letting. The
focus of complaints is on residential ‘To Let’ boards,
rather than ‘For Sale’ boards. The number of complaints
received by the Council over the last 3 years related to this
matter are 3 complaints in 2023, 6 in 2024 and 67 in 2025.
 
If an application were made and was
successful, this will mean it is for the Council to make individual
decisions on granting advertisement consent for the Class of
advertisement where deemed consent is not applied. This would allow
the Council greater control over the consenting procedure, taking
account of the impact to local amenity and enforcing any conditions
or limitations.  There is confidence
that there is sufficient resource in the Planning department to
respond to any increase in applications that may result from the
proposed Regulation 7 direction coming into force. 
 
Members welcomed the proposal to start the
process towards strengthening the Council’s powers in this
area.  The results of the stakeholder
engagement would be report back to the Committee to inform next
steps.
 
 
RESOLVED: to approve early stakeholder
engagement prior to a decision being made on whether to apply to
the SoS for the making of a Regulation 7 Direction
topline: The Council has decided to engage stakeholders before considering an application to the Secretary of State for a Regulation 7 Direction to remove deemed consent for estate agent boards in Englefield Green and Egham.

content:
Proposal: Demolition
of all existing buildings and erection of 96 residential dwellings
with associated infrastructure, landscaping and formation of new
access from Thorpe Lea Road.
 
The application site has an area of 2.81 Ha
and comprises of a commercial/office building, surrounded by
extensive areas of hardstanding providing open storage and vehicle
parking together with a residential dwelling (Kemmacott, currently
accessed via Thorpe Lea Road) in the south-east corner of the
site.  Levels across the site are
generally flat. Clockhouse Lane has a rural character, with trees
and vegetation spanning the entire length of the land and northern
boundary of the application site.
 
The report detailed the range of consultations
undertaken and responses: this included 49 responses setting out
concerns about the proposal from the public.
The application site is located within the
Green Belt where there is a presumption against development, unless
a relevant exemption applies.  A road
safety audit had been carried out and the proposal was considered
acceptable. 
 
The proposal would help to meet assessed
housing need and in other respects met the criteria for the
development of Grey Belt. The proposed mix of residential units and
density was considered to be
appropriate.  It was noted that the
figures for SANG and SAMM in the report had been transposed.
 
The site was assessed as Grey Belt as it had
been previously developed.  In view of
the changed National Planning Policy Framework in this connexion
the decision criteria for Grey Belt were explained in detail
– if the site was capable of
meeting unmet need, was a sustainable location and met the
Golden rules.  Previously Developed Land
(PDL) was now only one of the considerations – a site
considered appropriate for development could also be one that did
not contribute to the Green Belt purposes in relation to protecting
historic towns, preventing sprawl and preventing neighbouring towns
merging. 
 
In this instance, the M25 and lake to the
south of the site were restrictions to sprawl; the site sat within
existing developed areas.  Thorpe and
Virginia Water were not towns – only Egham and Chertsey were
relevant in this regard.  It was
confirmed that no special precedent was set by this evaluation.
 
Members were concerned about the appearance of
the two blocks of flats in the proposal although it was accepted
that the rear elevation would mainly be seen from the M25. It was
agreed to seek a revised landscaping plan with more detail on the
location of trees to act as a barrier to the M25 – this would
be subject specialist arboricultural advice and further negotiation
with the applicant.  The £300k
contribution for public transport was in relation to a demand-led
service provided by Surrey CC; it was noted that there were 181 car
parking spaces in the design.  The
future management of the public open spaces would be undertaken by
a Management Company that would charge residents for its
services.  There was concern about the
around the level of noise that future residents would experience
– this was mitigated by the sound insultation provided by the
proposed houses and flats. In terms of air quality, the site was
outside of the M25 Air Quality Zone.
 
 
RESOLVED:  to grant
Consent
 
1. subject to conditions 1-30 in the report,
with an amendment to condition 5 to require the submission of a new
landscaping plan;
 
2. subject to the completion of a S106 legal
agreement which secures the following:
 
• SAMM and SANG Contributions
(£23,063.88 and £47,027.18 respectively)
• Provision and management of the open
space via a management company
• Green space contribution
(£13,150.00)
• Affordable housing (50%)
• Travel Plan
• Contributions to running of DDRT bus
service (£300,000)
• Council monitoring fee
(£866.25)
 
Or
 
3. to authorise the refusal of planning
permission at the discretion of the Head of Planning if the legal
agreement has not progressed to his satisfaction within 3 months of
the committee determination, or if material circumstances arise
prior to the issuing of the decision 
notice that would in the HoP’s
view warrant the refusal of planning permission.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve the demolition of existing buildings and construction of 96 residential dwellings in a contentious decision involving concerns from the public and considerations of Green Belt development.

content:
The application had been called in to the
Planning Committee by Cllr Mullens for the reasons given in the
report.
 
The Committee heard from Ellen Taplin, an
objector.  The principal points were
that the report did not demonstrate harm to neigbouring properties;
the cumulative impact was overbearing and the reasons for the 2014
refusal of a similar proposal still held. 
 
It was noted that Roscrea is a detached
2-storey dwellings on a level plot formed by the junctions of
Vicarage Avenue, Vicarage Road and Mead Close. The dwelling has an
east-facing front elevation and is located within an elongated
rectangular plot. 
 
The rear gardens of Mead Close have a northern
aspect, facing the southern elevation of Roscrea. From these
gardens the first floor west-facing bay window of Roscrea is
clearly visible. The gardens of Mead Close are private spaces, but
there is mutual overlooking from existing first floor windows. The
proposal’s presence will be limited because of its
subservient design. The new section of hipped roof would be set
below the existing roof by between 2.2m and 3.2m. In addition, the
length of the extension has been reduced by omitting the chevron
wall along the boundary with No.3 Mead Close.
 
The judgement of the officers was that
permission should be granted. It was considered that the benefits
of the scheme to the economy during construction together with the
benefits to the homeowner will make a positive contribution to the
local economy.
 
In discussion of the proposal. the following
principal points were made:

·        
The proposed extension was 72 cm narrower with an expanse of white
wall across the width of the neighbouring garden

·        
The proposed extension was about 11m from the back door of 5 Mead
Close – close to the separation distance in the Design
SPD

·        
The perception of overlooking was a valid Planning consideration;
there was a loss of privacy and light 

·        
Any new windows if the proposal were approved would need to be
non-opening and obscured

·        
There was no significant difference from the 2014 refusal
 
The Chair put to the vote the recommendation
to grant permission, amended with acondition not to allow any
future windows on the flank wall and this was lost. 
 
A proposal to refuse permission as set out
below was approved unanimously.
 
RESOLVED: that permission be refused on the
grounds of the overbearing and unneighbourly effect on adjoining
properties in Mead Close.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse permission for a proposed extension due to concerns about its impact on neighbouring properties.

content:
The Sub-Committee was invited
to determine an application for a new premises licence in respect
of Morrisons Daily, 244 – 256 Station Road, Addlestone,
Surrey, KT15 2PS.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer
presented their report; setting out the application for which the
licensable activity was the off sales of alcohol only under a
franchise of Morrisons.
 
Officers advised the
Sub-Committee that there were five other premises located in the
vicinity which benefited from a premises licence to sell
alcohol.
 
Since submission of the
application, the applicant had revised the opening hours and
operational hours from a 06:00 hours start to 07:00 Monday to
Sunday.
 
Following discussions with the
Police and Licensing Authority, additional conditions had been
agreed, and following representations from local residents, it was
also proposed that deliveries be restricted to the front of the
premises.
 
The Responsible Authorities had
not made any objections to the application as a result of these
agreements.
 
Officers reported that there
had been 8 valid objections to the application, a further 8
partially relevant objections had been withdrawn based on
clarification of the actual activities sought and/or the changes
subsequently made to the application and agreed
conditions.
 
The Sub-Committee’s
attention was drawn to the Council’s Statement of Licensing
Policy 2026-2031, in particular sections 6 to 11, 15, and 16, as
well as the relevant guidance issued under Section 182 of the
Licensing Act 2003, in particular sections 9.42 –
9.44.
 
There were no questions posed
to the Senior Licensing Officer. 
Therefore, the Applicant was then invited to state their
case.
 
In summary, the applicant
sought to assist the community, by employing local staff and
providing a modest supermarket service to local
residents.  The applicant had readily
amended the opening hours, and accepted additional
conditions.  The applicant offered to
further revise the terminal hour if it was deemed
necessary.
 
The applicant confirmed that
spirits would be stored behind the counter, and that robust
training would be in place, including adherence to the training
requirements set by Morrisons for franchisees.  This was regularly monitored.
 
The two objectors attending the
meeting were then invited to state their case.  The priority for them was the potential for noise
disturbance, anti-social behaviour, and litter.
 
Officers advised that issues
with vehicles obstructing the forecourt owing to its layout and
positioning of bollards, which the residents thought could
constitute a public nuisance, was not a licensing issue, but which
could be taken up with the land owner.
 
The objectors thanked the
applicant for agreeing to only have deliveries to the front of the
property, and they were pleased that the applicant had, in
addition, to the other conditions as set out in the Appendices to
the Officer’s report, undertaken to provide a bin near the
entrance to the store to deter littering, and to undertake
appropriate and proportionate measures to prevent nuisance from
litter.
 
There was a brief discussion
between the two objectors and the applicant about the
objectors’ preference for alteration to the hours for the
sale of alcohol and/or hours of opening.  However, it was confirmed that such an arrangement
would require further discussion with Responsible Authorities with
respect to an additional condition, if the opening hours exceeded
those permitted for the sale of alcohol, and that the Hearing was
not the appropriate forum for negotiation between the objectors and
applicant.
 
There being no further
questions or comments, each party was invited to make a closing
statement.
 
The Sub-Committee resolved to
exclude the press and public to determine the application at
2.35pm.
 
The Sub-Committee reconvened at
2.50pm.
 
Having taken into account the
cases as presented, the relevant policy and guidance, as well as
the written and oral representations made at the Hearing, the
Sub-Committee determined that the Premises Licence should be
granted with mandatory conditions and those additional conditions
as agreed by the applicant.
 
Resolved that -
 
the
application for a premises licence in respect of Morrisons Daily,
244 - 256 Station Road, Addlestone, KT15 2PS, be granted in
accordance with the application as amended, subject to the
mandatory conditions, and the conditions agreed by the Applicant
with the Police the Licensing Authority and the Objector in
Appendices F and I of the Officer’s report
topline: The Sub-Committee has decided to grant a new premises licence for Morrisons Daily in Addlestone, Surrey, with additional conditions to address concerns raised by local residents.

content:
The Committee received for information, the
2025/26 Quarter 4 report on complaints and compliments.
 
Officers advised that there were 73 entries in
Jadu, compared with 84 this time last year, but 67 in the last
quarter.  Officers clarified that the
figures provided a snap shot, as the position could alter over the
course of the reporting period.
 
Members were asked to note that the slight dip
in response times reflected a small backlog of two weeks in March
which had now been cleared of making updates in jadu while it was being rebuilt to accommodate the
new complaint handlers.
 
At a previous meeting, Members had asked for
an update on the introduction of thresholds with regard to
complaints about refuse and recycling. 
The Committee recalled that Officers in Law & Governance and
Environmental Services had decided that an initial contact would be
treated as a service request, up to there being 3 contacts in a 6
week period about missed collections and other similar issues
without there being a reasonable explanation, such as access
issues. 
 
To support the way a contact was handled the
crews had been asked to provide evidence of access issues,
contamination or other issues preventing them from making a
collection.  In the last six months
there were 41 complaints mainly about missed collections, of which
18 were upheld, and 5 were re-classified as service
requests.  There were also a significant
number of service requests which also took time to resolve as these
were all investigated to find a resolution.  It had been decided to continue with the existing
thresholds for the remainder of Runnymede’s life; thereafter
West Surrey would assume responsibility for complaint handling and
monitoring.  Officers considered that
the complaint handling system in place was a very useful tool and
hoped it would continue into the future.
 
Officers advised that crews worked extremely
hard to provide a good service in very challenging conditions,
which is why it was positive to see some good feedback for DSO
staff in the compliments section of the report.
 
Members noted there were 28 individual
compliments in Quarter 4 the details of which were set out in the
exempt appendix.  It was agreed that
some of the compliments were obviously heart felt and reflected
well on staff.
 
Officers were thanked for the report which was
duly noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations based on the 2025/26 Quarter 4 report on complaints and compliments.

content:
The Committee’s approval
was sought for the 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement, and for it
to be presented to Full Council.
 
The Committee noted that the
Annual Governance Statement (AGS) met statutory requirements to
report publicly on the extent to which the Council was complying
with its own code of governance and should include how the
effectiveness of governance arrangements have been monitored and
evaluated in the year, and any planned changes in the coming
year.
 
Officers advised that following
consultation, updated guidance had been published in May 2025 in
the form of an addendum to the Delivering Good Governance in Local
Government framework.  This suggested
changes to the way local authorities conducted their annual review
to produce the AGS.  Officers engaged
the Council’s Internal Auditors to undertake an independent
assessment of the Council’s preparations for the 2025/26 AGS,
noting progress already made within the 2024/25 AGS, with a focus
on readiness to meet the strengthened requirements of the CIPFA
Addendum 2025.  Taking the Internal
Auditor’s findings with a gap analysis, a set of improvements
were identified.  These included
documentation of a clear process for undertaking the review, a
greater level of internal and external engagement, a revised
Officer Declaration for senior manager, development of an assurance
map, and strengthening the conclusion on whether the Council was
meeting its governance requirements in each core area.
 
The ‘Forward Look’ to
the AGS referenced LGR and preparations for the new West Surrey
Council.  The Action plan outlined
issues raised in 2024/25 for action in 2025/26 and set out the
progress made in 5 key areas.  There
were two significant issues identified in 2025/26 for action in
2026/27; these were LGR and Regulator of Social Housing
Judgement.  There were six other
governance matters for action in the coming year.  These were consistency in risk management
responsibilities, new digital systems, processes reliant on manual
data handling, lack of reliable IT assets inventory, and a review
of FOI themes and improvements considered as part of the Standards
and Audit Committee’s self- assessment exercise in
2025/26.
 
The Committee agreed that the
extensive evidence for each of the seven key Principles provided
sufficient confidence in the Council’s policies, procedures
and the effectiveness of the Council’s system of internal
control and governance.
 
Members reviewed each area of the
AGS, including the action plan and evidence examples, and agreed
that it was both informative and robust, fully endorsing it for
presentation to the full Council at its meeting in July.
 
Resolved that –
 

i)         
the draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 (Appendix A of the
Officer’s report) be approved, for signature by the
Co-Leaders of the Council and the Chief Executive and publication
alongside the Annual Statement of Accounts for 2025/26;
 

ii)        
delegated authority be given to the Assistant Chief Executive /
s151 officer, in consultation with the Chair of the Standards and
Audit Committee, to include any significant change in governance
arrangements that may occur in the period between the approval of
the draft Annual Governance Statement and the signing of the
Statement of Accounts for 2025/26; and

 

Recommend that -
 

iii)        the approved
Annual Governance Statement be presented to Full Council so that
all elected representatives have sight of the conclusions and
agreed actions in line with recommended best practice.
topline: The Standards and Audit Committee has decided to approve the 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement for presentation to the Full Council.

content:
The Committee received for information the
annual report on complaints about Councillors, and co-opted Members
for the year ending 31 March 2026.
 
The Monitoring Officer had received 4
complaints, and accepted 3 of them for further
investigation.  This compared with 7 in
the previous year.  There were no
hearings in 2025/26, and no need to appoint any external
investigator which meant there were no resource implications, as
all complaints were dealt with within existing resources.
 
At the time of writing the report, two cases
were still open, and one was closed after initial enquiries were
made of the complainant to provide further detail.  Members were updated with the news that one case
remained open and the Monitoring Officer had sought further
information in order to make his assessment of the case.
 
Members were reminded that the process for
dealing with complaints about Councillors was set out in detail in
the Constitution, and to assist customers step by step guidance was
available on the Council’s website, including a pro-forma and
 public register as required, although
the data was anonymised unless the Monitoring Officer decided that
it was in the public interest to publish more detail.
 
Members recalled the previous report in
November 2025 to the Committee which confirmed widespread support
for system reform regarding the Code of Conduct.  However, it was unlikely that there would be any
further developments with this before West Surrey
Council.  This was re-inforced by the knowledge that reference to
legislative change had not been included in the recent King’s
Speech.
 
The Committee noted that a survey of training
needs for Councillors would be conducted shortly, which could
include matters relating to the Code of Conduct if Members
wished.
 
Officers advised that if there were any
outstanding matters unresolved by Vesting Day in April 2027, if
they concerned Members of the West Surrey Shadow Authority (WSSA)
these would transfer, along with any archived material to West
Surrey Council to determine and set a retention period for
documents of this nature.  If there were
any matters relating to existing RBC Councillors, these would
‘fall’ by default when those Councillors ceased to hold
office, being no longer subject to a Code of Conduct at that
point.  Officers confirmed that the WSSA
had adopted a Code of Conduct as part of its new Constitution and
established a Standards Committee.
 
Members agreed that the report complied with
the requirement to provide a summary of complaints about
councillors and the report was duly noted.
topline: The Committee has approved recommendations based on the annual report on complaints about Councillors and co-opted Members.

content:
The Committee was presented with Grant
Thornton’s External Audit plan for the year ending 31 March
2026, for information.
 
Members were provided with a brief re-cap on
the backstop arrangements introduced by the Accounts and Audit
(Amendment) Regulations 2024 and the dates under which local
authorities were required to publish their audited financial
statements up to the year ending 31 March 2028.
 
Grant Thornton (GT) would be working towards
an internal deadline of 30 November 2026 in order to meet the
statutory deadline for 2025/26 of 31 January 2027.
 
Members noted the scope of the planned audit,
including significant risks that GT had identified.  These were management override of control,
valuation of property assets including investment properties,
valuation of pension fund net liability and implementation of new
general ledger system.
 
In terms of materiality GT had determined
Group planning materiality to be £1.5m, which equated to 2.5%
of the Council’s prior year gross group operating costs for
the year.  Following this for the
Council, GT had determined planning materiality to be
£1.425m, using the same benchmark as the Group, capped at 95%
of Group Materiality.  With regard to
uncorrected omissions or misstatements; ‘clearly
trivial’ had been set at £75K for the Group, and
£71.3K for the Council.
 
Officers from GT highlighted their risk
assessment regarding Value for Money arrangements, audit logistics
and details of how their fieldwork would be carried out and
when.
 
Members noted the proposed fee of £222K
for the Council, subject to the Council delivering a good set of
financial statements and working papers, no significant changes to
the scope of the audit, and management co-operation and provision
of evidence in a timely manner.  It was
noted that the proposed fee for 2025/26 with regard to the new
general ledger system implementation testing was to be
confirmed.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The UK council has decided to approve Grant Thornton's External Audit plan for the year ending 31 March 2026.

content:
The Committee was presented with the
Council’s Corporate Risk Profile for Quarter 4 of 2025/26, in
line with the approved risk management framework.  Officers sought to provide assurance on the
Council’s principal risks, how they were managed, and how the
risk profile had changed since the last update.
 
Officers reported that all service areas
reviewed their risks during February and March 2026, overseen by
the Corporate Leadership Team (CLT), to ensure consistency and
appropriate challenge.
 
Members noted that at the end of Quarter 4
there were 261 recorded risks across service, project and contract
risk registers.  There were 86 risks
which scored above the escalation threshold of 10
post?mitigation.  In addition, of these,
29 were classed as ‘significant’, scoring above 15.
 
Members were referred to the Risk Dashboard
which reflected the scale and complexity of the Council’s
activities, rather than any deterioration in risk controls.
 
The Committee was advised that the majority of
significant risks continued to sit within Financial, Operational
and People categories which was consistent with the Council’s
wider operational environment.  Members
noted that there were ongoing financial pressures across local
government, increased regulatory scrutiny, particularly in Housing,
and workforce pressures, including uncertainty linked to Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR).
 
Risks scoring above the threshold had been
reviewed by CLT to determine whether they should be escalated to
the Corporate Risk Register.  Officers
confirmed that at the end of Quarter 4, 36 risks were formally
designated by CLT for inclusion on the Corporate Risk Register, as
set out in the Appendix.  They had been
sorted by post?mitigation score.  In
addition, two risks were newly added in Quarter 4.  These were the Cost of provision of Temporary
Accommodation, and Failure to recruit high calibre, quality key
staff.  However, Officers stressed that
both additions reflected emerging pressures rather than failures in
existing controls.
 
Members noted that 11 risks had trended
upwards, 19 risks had trended downwards, and there was one
upward?trending risk sitting on the Corporate Risk Register.
 
As reported elsewhere, the most notable change
related to housing regulatory compliance, following the Regulator
of Social Housing’s inspection and C4 judgement. Members were
aware that a corporate Housing Improvement Programme was now in
place to address this.
 
Officers advised that two of the five newly
identified risks arose from arose from internal audit
work.  Although these currently scored
below escalation thresholds, they were included for transparency
and to demonstrate continuous improvement in the risk management
system that learning from audit activity was now captured.
 
The Committee was informed that Officers were
asked to review risks in light of LGR, which was considered to be a
compounding factor across several workforce, operational and
data?related risks.  Members were
assured that these impacts were being monitored closely and
reported regularly to CLT.  In addition,
Officers explained that the LGR Implementation Planning Board had
oversight of all associated risks by keeping risk registers which
were discussed in the various workstreams set up to transition the
East and West Surrey Councils.
 
Members agreed that overall, the report
demonstrated that risks were being actively reviewed and
challenged, escalation was occurring in line with the agreed
framework, emerging issues were being identified early, including
through internal audit, and the Council maintained clear visibility
and oversight of its principal risks.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to review and approve recommendations for managing risks in its Corporate Risk Profile.

content:
The Committee noted the Internal Audit Annual
Audit Conclusion for 2025/26.
 
SIAP were pleased to report that in their
opinion, sufficient assurance and advisory work had been carried
out in order for them to form a ‘reasonable’ conclusion
on the adequacy and effectiveness of the internal control
environment.  In their opinion the
Council’s framework of governance, risk management and
control were reasonable, and audit testing had demonstrated
controls to be working in practice. 
 
In addition, SIAP reported that where
weaknesses had been identified through internal audit review, they
had worked with management to agree appropriate corrective actions
and a timescale for improvement.
 
SIAP made reference to the Regulator of Social
Housing’s report and judgement. 
Officers were satisfied that the Council was working with the
Regulator to build on the existing improvement plan, noting that
the Council had self-referred having identified an historical rent
setting issue prior to the regulatory inspection.  The establishment of the Housing Improvement
programme and board was clear evidence of engagement and an
intention to maintain performance standards.  Members considered there would be clear signs of
progress to report by the end of March 2027.
 
SIAP assured that provision had been made
within the 2026/27 programme to follow this up in discussion with
the Council’s Corporate Leadership Team to determine the
specific scope and timing of the audit.
 
The Committee was advised that in respect of
acceptance of risk, SIAP were not aware of any instances where
management had accepted a level of risk that was felt to exceed the
Council’s risk appetite or risk tolerance.
 
With regard to SIAP’s own performance,
although some audit reviews had been technically late, all had been
completed for the year.
 
Members asked what would happen in terms of a
handover to the West Surrey Council. 
Officers sought to re-assure the Committee that the 2026/27 audit
plan was on track for final reporting in March 2027.  If there were any outstanding actions or
recommendations arising during the year these would be collated
accordingly.
 
SIAP thanked Officers for their collaborative
approach, which was echoed by Members, and the report was duly
noted.
topline: The UK council has approved recommendations from the Internal Audit Annual Audit Conclusion for 2025/26.

content:
The Committee was asked to approve the
Council’s Annual Self Assessment
against the Ombudsman’s complaint handling code, and key
performance indicators for 2025/26.
 
Officers presented an assessment of the
Council’s compliance with the complaint handling code. It was
noted that compliance could be demonstrated with regard to each of
the 9 tests; ranging from adoption of the Ombudsman’s
definitions of service requests and complaints, through to Scrutiny
and Oversight by the Committee.
 
Officers provided some detail on particular
sections including exclusions; the main one being that any
complaints about RBCI or RBCS; were regarded as external
complaints, but both companies were expected to follow the
corporate complaints policy and procedures.  Other exclusions included service requests,
duplicate complaints, and where there was another form of appeal
such as penalty charge notices.
 
The Committee was advised that the Council
accepted a total number of 296 complaints in 2025/26.  Of these, an average of 81% were responded to
within the given deadlines.  It was
noted that overall 37% of Stage 1 complaints were upheld, and 10%
were upheld at Stage 2.
 
Officers highlighted the accessibility of the
complaints process, noting an increase in complaints.  In response to the Council’s resources being
stretched the Committee was advised that Corporate Heads were
recently redesignated as stage 2 complaint handlers, and in their
place about 35 managers and other trained staff had been appointed
to deal with stage 1 complaints.
 
It was agreed that for a relatively small
organisation, timeliness and outcomes were supported by the
information provided which included a detailed list of service
improvements.  Members highlighted
performance in Housing as consistent with learning points across
the organisation.  The people dealing
with complaints were commended for their dedication to resolving
the various issues arising.
 
Overall, the Committee considered that the
annual assessment was fair and reflective of the Council’s
performance with regard to complaints, and could be regarded as a
positive achievement by all involved.
 
Officers extended particular thanks to
colleagues in Customer and Digital Services, Housing and
Environmental Services.
 
Members were content to approve the assessment
and requested that a summary of the feedback from the Committee be
presented as its response to the report, as required by the code
for publication on the Council’s website.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the Council’s
annual assessment against the Ombudsman’s complaint handling
code and associated key performance indicators for 2025/26 be
approved, and the Committee’s response be summarised and
published on the Council’s website
topline: The Council has decided to approve the Annual Self Assessment against the Ombudsman's complaint handling code for 2025/26.

8a)         Local
Code of Corporate Governance – Recommendation from
the   Corporate Management
Committee 
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 
Corporate Management Committee on 12 February 2026, first
considered by the 
Standards and Audit Committee 29 January
2026  seeking approval for the adoption of Local Code
of Corporate Governance for 2026/27.
 
Councillor R. King
proposed the recommendation in the report, Councillor L. Gillham
seconded and the matter was put to the vote
 
 
RESOLVED that:
 
the Local Code of
Corporate Governance for the period 2026/27 be adopted
 

8b)      
Housing Payments Policy – recommendation from Corporate
Management
Committee        
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 
17 March 2026 Corporate Management Committee meeting.
 
The report sought
approval of a new Housing Payment (HP) Policy for 2026/27 to
replace Discretionary Housing Payments (DHP) as part of the
Government’s Crisis & Resilience Fund (CRF), which would
consolidate DHP and the Household Support Fund into a single
funding stream from 1 April 2026.
 
The recommendations
in the report were proposed by Councillor R. King, seconded by
Councillor L. Gilham and the matter was put to the vote.
RESOLVED that:
 
                        
i.        
the Housing Payments Policy for 2026/27 be APPROVED and adopted as
the Council’s formal policy for administering Housing
Payments under the new Crisis & Resilience Fund framework.
                       
ii.        
Authority be delegated to the Corporate Head of Customer, Digital
& Collection Services, in consultation with the Assistant Chief
Executive (Section 151 Officer), to make any minor amendments
required to ensure operational compliance with updated Department
for Work and Pensions guidance and Management Information
requirements
 

8c)       Whistleblowing
Policy         
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 
17 March 2026 Corporate Management Committee meeting.
 
The report put
forward a revised Whistleblowing Policy and Procedure which had
been reviewed and updated in accordance with good practice and
recent changes to employment legislation.
 
The draft policy
had been considered by the Council’s recognised Trade Union
who supported its adoption.
 
The recommendation
in the report was proposed by Councillor R. King, seconded by
Councillor. L. Gillham and put the vote.
 
 
RESOLVED that:
 
The revised
Whistleblowing Policy be APPROVED
 

8d)      Larchwood
Drive and Kings Lane, Egham – recommendation of the Corporate
Management Committee
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 
17 March 2026 Corporate Management Committee meeting.
 
The report provided
an update on progress since the January 2026 meeting of the
Corporate Management Committee (CMC) and outlined the range of
options considered for two key operational assets: 57 Larchwood
Drive and Kings Lane Open Space as identified in work commissioned
from Montague Evans to assess feasibility and options appraisals of
the two sites following a request for such an exercise by the
committee.
 
Following detailed
evaluation, the report recommended that 57 Larchwood Drive be
declared as surplus to operational requirements and planning
permission pursued for residential use, with the strongest market
option being 9 residential units.  The report also
highlighted the benefits of delivering a new, community and
recreation facility at Kings Lane which would provide high quality
amenities for local residents and strengthen the offer
for communities across the borough, whilst providing a fit for
purpose base for community activities currently provided at 57
Larchwood Drive.
 
The recommendations
in the report were prosed by Councillor R. King and seconded by
Councillor L. Gillham
 
The matter was
discussed and council expressed thanks to those involved in
delivery of community activity at the site and those that had
helped to progress the matter to this point.  Council welcomed the proposals.
 
The matter was put
to the vote.
 
RESOLVED
that:
 
                        
i.        
a supplementary revenue estimate for 2026/27 in the sum of
£375,000 to facilitate a twin tracked planning approach for
Larchwood Drive and Kings Lane Open Space be APPROVED
                      
ii.        
the redevelopment of Kings Lane be subject to a strategic CIL bid,
subject to planning permission, and obtaining vacant possession of
the pavilion building at Kings Lane be AGREED; all these aspects
are highlighted in Section 17 of report
                     
iii.        
a capital provision in the sum set out in Option 3 in confidential
Appendix A be included in the Capital Programme for 2027/28 for the
redevelopment of Kings Lane to be released, subject to a future
report setting out a full business case, costings and funding
assessment be APPROVED
                     
iv.        
where recommendations (i) and (ii) have
been approved, agree to procure a design and build contract for a
mixed-use community and leisure facility on Kings Lane be APPROVED
[approval conditional on the above having been achieved]. The
maximum contract value is noted in exempt Appendix A.
                      
v.        
Subject to the above, and the provision of an alternative venue, 57
Larchwood Drive be AGREED as surplus to operational requirements
and bring back to a future committee the principal of disposal and
method of disposal.
                     
vi.        
the allocation of up to £20,000 from the Englefield Green
S106 monies for Community Support Facilities if required, for
interim works required to enable continuation of use of the
Community Hub at Larchwood Drive, whilst the above is progressed be
AGREED.
                    
vii.        
the allocation of all remaining Englefield Green S106 monies, for
Community Support Facilities, totalling £308,640, plus any
underspend from monies allocated in (vi) to be allocated to
non-building elements of the project relating to Kings Lane, as a
contribution towards the total costs be AGREED.
 
 

8e)       Procurement
Strategy – recommendation of the Corporate Management
Committee        
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 16
April 2026 Corporate Management Committee meeting
 
The report sought
approval of the adoption of the updated Procurement Strategy and
associated policies set out in Appendices 1 – 4.  It explained that the update was necessary as a
result of recent changes to procurement legislation and changes
were largely related to ensuring that the council met its duty to
remove barriers for small and medium sized enterprises.
 
The recommendation
in the report was proposed by Councillor R. King, seconded by
Councillor L. Gillham and put to the vote.
RESOLVED that:
 
the updated
Procurement Strategy and associated policies, set out in Appendices
1 – 4 subject to the correction of typographical errors as
noted by Corporate Management Committee be APPROVED.
 
8f)      Annual Review of RBC
Constitution & In-Year
amendments         
 
Council received a
recommendation from the 
16 April 2026 Corporate Management Committee meeting.
 
The report sought
agreement to proposed changes to the Constitution, as set out in
appendix 1 to come into effect at the beginning of the municipal
year i.e. 20 May 2026 save for that proposed change to be effected
‘in year’ and set out as such in the appendix, to come
into effect immediately following the council meeting on 30 April
2026 be agreed.
 
The recommendations
in the report were proposed by Councillor R. King and seconded by
Councillor S. Ringham
 
The matter was
discussed.  It was established that CMC
had heard, in error, that the Constitution Member Working party had
considered all of the proposed changes but that this had not been
the case.  In light of this the wording
associated with the recording of officer decisions was debated and
advice was received from the Monitoring Officer.  
 
It was agreed that
a 5-minute adjournment be observed for further advice to be
received and the wording to be considered.  On recommencement of the meeting, it was agreed
that an amendment be made to the wording of proposal 2l as
follows:
 
“A Reportable
Decision is a delegated officer decision which is taken:
(i) Under a specific delegation
contained in a council or committee resolution or is taken under
general delegations and will be, or is likely to be: (ii)
significant in terms of its effects on communities (as opposed to
an individual), or (ii) an exception to policy, or would be
regarded as novel, repercussive or contentious, or (iii)
sufficiently important and/or sensitive so that it is reasonable
for a member of the public to expect it to be recorded and
published, or (iv) involve, or is likely to involve the Council in
legal proceedings against another person or affects the rights of
an individual, or will (v) award a contract or incur expenditure
that will affect the council’s financial
position more than 25% of the Council’s annual spend or
annual income for the service or function to which the decision
relates or is over £250k;”
 
The matter was put
to the vote
 
           
RESOLVED that:
 
proposed changes to
the Constitution, as set out in appendix 1, subject the
the amendment set out above, to come
into effect at the beginning of the municipal year i.e. 20 May 2026
save for that proposed change to be effected ‘in year’
and set out as such in the appendix, which would come into effect
immediately following the meeting be APPROVED.
 
 

8g)           Standards
and Audit Annual Report – recommendation from the Standards
and Audit Committee
 
Council received a
recommendation from 
the 12 March 2026 Standards and Audit Committee meeting.
 
The annual report
of the Standards and Audit Committee is considered in accordance
with recommended best practice from CIPFA to local authorities to
provide assurance to those charged with governance that the
Standards and Audit Committee has fulfilled its purpose and can
demonstrate its impact both internally and to the public. The CIPFA
position statement was appended to the Officer’s report.
           
The annual report
set out the Committee’s:
· terms
of reference

· membership details

· highlights, and a summary of work undertaken during
the year including:
· external and
internal audit
· the
governance framework
· oversight of
complaint handling
· risk
management
· external
review and self-assessment
· performance
and effectiveness
 
Following consideration at the Standards and
Audit Committee the election of Councillor Cai Parry as Chair of
the Committee and Councillor Elaine Gill as Vice-Chair at the March
meeting were reflected and the results of the self-assessment
exercise undertaken in March included.
 
The amended report had been circulated to all
members with the agenda for the meeting.
 
It was proposed by Councillor C. Parry,
seconded by Councillor C. Parry and put to the vote
 
RESOLVED that:
 
the Standards and Audit Committee Annual
Report 2025/26, as amended, be APPROVED

The Committee received an update on a range of
operational and maintenance matters affecting the Green.
 
Car parking
 
Officers reported
that the Crown Estate had now communicated with Officers regarding
car parking, a full written response on this would be sent when
appropriate advice had been received from Counsel.   This response would be conveyed to the
Committee when received.
 
The Committee was
asked to note that the Council’s Environment and
Sustainability Committee had resolved at its meeting in February
2026, that the Englefield Green car park should be excluded from
the recreational charging scheme and Council’s Off-street
parking orders.
 
Tree
planting
 
Officers reported
that The Crown Estate had now given their consent for the planting
of six Acer Campestre Queen Elizabeth II trees.   The planting of these trees would take place
in the next planting session.
 
 
Woodland Management
Plan
 
The Crown Estate had
now given their consent to the Woodland Management Plan which had
previously been approved by this Committee.
 
 
Bollards
 
Officers reported
that in order to comply with the conditions of the Crown Estate the
corroded metal drop bollard located on the pathway from the Cricket
Club would need to be replaced with a wooden bollard.
 
Litter
bins
 
Consent had now been
received for the installation of 16 Glasdon Origin Curve 110 litter
bins.   To comply with the Crown
Estate the following conditions would be adhered to:
 

·        
Litter bins that are removed and not
replaced will have their concrete bases and anchors removed and the
ground made good; and

·        
Concrete surfaces and anchors would be
repaired, maintained and kept in good condition where litter bins
were replaced.
 
 
Clock
 
The Committee was
advised that the clock at the Englefield Green Cricket Club had now
been repaired.  A new internal system
had been installed whilst retaining the clocks external
appearance.
 
All works which had
now received Crown Estate consent would be progressed by Officers
through the appropriate procurement processes, using the Englefield
Green ring-fenced funds and in line with the legal framework that
protected the Green as an open and unenclosed space.
 
Mr Mc Gregor-Johnson
(Residents’ Representative) expressed his dissatisfaction
regarding the current condition of the Green.  He was disappointed not to see an item on the
agenda regarding remedial measures for the Green.    Mr Bromilow (Residents’
Representative) stated that he had contacted the Chair of the
Committee and asked him to request Officers write a report on
remedial measures for the Green.
 
The Chair of the
Committee advised both residents representatives that due to
operational and staffing issues, along with a significant event
happening in the Borough prior to publication, there had not been
the capacity for a report to be written.
 
Mr Bromilow
expressed his extreme dissatisfaction with the way his request had
not been responded too, nor had he been advised prior to
publication of the agenda that his item would not be
included.  The Chair advised the
Committee that he had responded to Mr Bromilow on the
matter.   It was noted that service
from Residents’ Representatives was very much appreciated but
processes had to be followed, and on this occasion, unfortunately
there were not the staff resources to prepare a late
report.
 
Mr Bromilow advised
the Committee that he wished to resign as Residents’
Representative with immediate effect and left the
chamber.
 
Members thanked
Officers were thanked for all their work in relation to the
Green.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for operational and maintenance matters affecting the Green, despite resident dissatisfaction with the current condition and lack of inclusion of remedial measures on the agenda.

The Committee was updated on the grant of the
lease to the Englefield Green Cricket Club to regularise their
occupation of the pavilion and use of the cricket facilities at
Englefield Green Recreation Ground.
 
The Committee was advised that the Cricket
Club had occupied the pavilion at Englefield Green for many years,
most recently under a ten years’ licence to occupy, granted
on 27 November 2014.  Since expiry of
the 2014 licence, negotiations had been taking place on the new
terms for the club’s occupation of the pavilion and adjacent
storage shed.  During negotiations the
club had continued to have occupation of the pavilion and adjacent
storage shed.
 
Officers advised the Committee that the
Cricket Club was structured as an unincorporated association,
governed by a constitution adopted on 1st January
2024.  The Cricket Club, therefore, had
no separate legal personality, and could not enter into contracts
with third parties.  Authorised
representatives of the Cricket Club must, therefore, enter into any
legal agreements on behalf of the Club, and they were at risk of
being held personally liable for the obligations incurred.
 
Officers had agreed the Heads of Terms, for a
new lease for the pavilion and storage shed, with non-exclusive
ancillary rights for use of the square/outfield and a right to use
a designated storage area for the screens.
 
Approval of the Heads of Terms were agreed by
the Corporate Management Committee in November 2025, since then
some progress had been made.
 
The Constitution of the
Cricket Club had been provided to the Council, however, it was not clear that the document
authorised their representatives to act as signatories on behalf of
the Cricket Club.  Further enquiries had
been raised;
 
The names of the current
Secretary and Vice Chair of the Cricket Club had been provided as
the persons who will enter into the lease on behalf of the Cricket
Club; and
 
A draft of the lease had been
issued to the members of the Cricket Club whose contact details had
been provided to Council’s legal Officers.
 
Council Officers were currently awaiting
details of the solicitors engaged to act for the Cricket Club in
negotiating a new lease or (in the alternative and the minimum
requirement of the Council)  evidence of
the identity of the Cricket Club’s representatives and
evidence that they had engaged solicitors or a competent third
party to act for the Cricket Club in the registration of the
lease.
topline: The Council has decided to approve a new lease for the Englefield Green Cricket Club's occupation of the pavilion and storage shed.

content:
The Committee was asked to consider a report
which sought approval for three updated enforcement policies to
ensure the Council was fully prepared for the new statutory duties
coming into force under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025.
 
The Act had introduced a significant shift for
local housing authorities. Under Section 107, the Council now had a
statutory duty to enforce landlord legislation as defined in that
section of the Act. This meant that, for private sector housing,
the Council could no longer rely on informal advice as its default
starting point for all offences. When a breach was identified, the
Council must now actively consider formal enforcement action
subject to the duty. Our existing housing policies were written
before this change so therefore no longer reflected the new legal
framework.
 
The report therefore proposed adopting three
revised standalone policies: the Environmental Services Enforcement
Policy, the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy, and the
Private Sector Housing Civil Penalty Policy.
 
It was important to emphasise that the amended
main Environmental Services Enforcement Policy continued to operate
under the existing graduated approach, guided by the
Regulators’ Code. For the majority of Environmental Services
functions, informal resolution, advice and proportionality remained
entirely appropriate. The only change was that private sector
housing had now been separated out, because the Renters’
Rights Act required a different, more formal enforcement starting
point. Separating the policies ensured clarity and prevented the
stricter housing requirements from unintentionally affecting other
service areas.
 
The revised housing policies aligned us with
the expanded civil penalty framework and with national model
policies developed by the Association of Chief Environmental Health
Officers. This promoted consistency, transparency and
defensibility, and helped avoid inconsistent approaches between
authorities.
 
It was expected that there would be an
additional workload as these duties came into force. The government
had provided initial New Burdens funding, and a separate resources
report would be brought to Committee once the full implications and
future funding position was clear.
 
Subject to approval, the revised policies
would take effect from 1 May 2026, ensuring the Council was fully
aligned with the new enforcement expectations from day one.
 
 
 
Resolved
that: 
 
The existing
overarching Environmental Services Enforcement Policy be revised
with the adoption of the below standalone policies:
 

-       
Environmental Services Enforcement Policy,

-       
Private Sector Housing Policy, and

-       
Private Sector Housing; Civil Penalty Policy
topline: The Council has decided to approve updated enforcement policies to comply with the Renters' Rights Act 2025.

The Committee was advised that this report
asked for a variation of the approved capital programme for vehicle
replacement scheduling due to a reliability review. 
 
Members would recall that in July 2025 the
Committee approved a program to replace 7 vehicles over a period of
3 years.   The replacement of the
3.5t Precinct Sweeper was originally scheduled for financial year
2027/28.   The HIAB was not
included at the time as it was believed it would continue to be
functional through to Local Government Reorganisation.

Unfortunately, both assumptions were no longer the
case.  Both vehicles had had significant
downtime, which impacted the service provided to residents
significantly.
Officers believed further investment in these
vehicles was unsustainable and high risk.
 
Members received an options appraisal in
relation to both the precinct sweeper and HIAB.  The appraisals detailed various options available
to the Council.   Having reviewed
the options Members supported the Officers recommendation to
replace both vehicles as the most cost effective approach,
 
 
Resolved
that: 
 
i)              
Approval be given to bring forward replacement of 3.5 tonne
precinct sweeper by one year to ensure continuity and approve the
commencement of the procurement process as detailed in the
report.
 
ii)            
Approval be given to commence the procurement process to
purchase a used HIAB as detailed in the report.
 
iii)           
The Corporate Management Committee be requested to approve a
supplementary capital estimate for the sums detailed in the report
for the purchase of one new EV precinct sweeper and one used
HIAB.
 
iv)           
The Corporate Management Committee be requested to remove the
budget set aside for the precinct sweeper in the 2027/28 capital
programme, as detailed in the report.
topline: The Council has decided to bring forward the replacement of a precinct sweeper and commence the procurement process for a used HIAB.

The Committee received a report which sought
approval for Officers to commence a procurement exercise to
purchase liquid fuels including HVO (Hydrotreated Vegetable
Oil).   The term of the contract
would be 5 years at the approximate value detailed in the
report.
 
In May 2024 the majority of fleet transitioned
to HVO to reduce carbon emission. 
 
The current contract expires on
30th September 2026.  
Renewing the contract would ensure continuity of service and no
disruptions to current operational services for Refuse collections,
Street Cleansing and Grounds Maintenance etc.
 
The purchase of HVO aligned with the Climate
Change Action Plan as this reduced tail pipe emissions by up to 90%
in comparison to standard diesel.
 
The proposed procurement directly supported
the Council’s objectives and ongoing reduction of Scope 1 and
2 emissions.
 
 
 
 
Resolved
that: 
 
i)              
Approval be given for Officers to commence the procurement
process to source a supplier to provide the Council with Liquid
Fuel
 
ii)            
A 5-year contract as detailed in the report be approved
topline: The Council has decided to procure liquid fuels, including HVO, for a 5-year contract to reduce carbon emissions and ensure continuity of operational services.

content:
The Committee was asked to consider the future
of the Dog Control Public Space Protection Order, which was due to
expire on 13 June 2026, and to approve a three?year extension of
the existing Order without variation.
 
The PSPO was first introduced in 2017 to
replace the former dog fouling legislation that had lapsed
nationally. It was last extended in 2023 and continued to provide
the Council with essential powers for dealing with dog fouling and
certain forms of dog?related anti?social behaviour across the
borough.
 
Under the Anti?Social Behaviour, Crime and
Policing Act 2014, a PSPO could only remain in force for a maximum
of three years unless it was formally extended. To extend it, the
Council had to be satisfied that the activities covered by the
Order continued to have a detrimental effect on the quality of life
of people in the area, and that the behaviour was persistent,
continuing, or unreasonable. Based on the evidence, these tests had
clearly been met.
 
Between April 2023 and March 2026, the Council
received 260 complaints related to dogs and dog fouling. The
existing Order required people in control of a dog to remove
faeces, to put a dog on a lead when directed by an authorised
officer, and not to take dogs into fenced children’s play
areas. These remained proportionate and necessary measures to
protect public health and ensured open spaces could be enjoyed
safely.
 
A full consultation was carried out during
February 2026, it was promoted online, through social media, at
public meetings, and through direct engagement with residents in
parks and open spaces. Whilst the number of responses was modest
— which was consistent with previous consultations —
the feedback was overwhelmingly supportive. Eighty per cent of
respondents felt the PSPO was successful or very successful, and
100 per cent supported extending it for a further three years for
the entire area of the Borough.
 
There are no additional financial implications
arising from this decision. The PSPO functions primarily as a
deterrent tool: it sets clear expectations for responsible dog
ownership, provides a legal basis for intervention when needed, and
supported officers in addressing the most problematic behaviour.
The Order also included appropriate exemptions for people with
disabilities who relied on assistance dogs.
 
If the PSPO was allowed to lapse, the Council
would lose the legal powers needed to address dog fouling,
exclusion areas, and dogs not being placed on a lead when directed.
Extending the Order ensured continuity, supported health and
wellbeing objectives in the corporate business plan, and helped
maintain clean and safe public spaces for residents and
visitors.
 
The Officers recommendation was therefore to
extend the existing Dog Control PSPO for a further three years from
14 June 2026.
 
The Committee fully endorsed this
approach.
 
 
 
Resolved
that: 
 
The existing Dog
Control PSPO be extended, without variation, for a further three
years.
topline: The Council has decided to extend the existing Dog Control Public Space Protection Order for a further three years without variation.

The Committee was asked to consider a report
which sought approval to commence a procurement exercise to appoint
a new supplier for wheeled bins and caddies.  The proposed contract would be for a period of 3
years, up to the value detailed in the report.
 
Officers advised the Committee that the
current contract expires on 30 September 2026.  The Council had a statutory obligation to provide
refuse & recycling wheelie bins to its residents under sections
45 & 46 of the EPA Act 1990.
 
The contract would cover all sizes of wheelie
bins, both 2 wheeled and 4 wheeled as well as internal (7 litre)
and external (23 litre) caddies.
 
Members were advised that in March 2025 the
existing food waste service had been expanded to include flats and
communal properties.   In the same
month it had become mandatory for local authorities to provide food
waste collections to all residents as part of the Simpler Recycling
Legislation.
 
The procurement process would be undertaken
through approved frameworks thereby ensuring best value,
competitiveness and compliance. 
Frameworks used would require bins to contain a proportion of
recycled materials.
 
Noting that existing specifications would be
retained Members approved the Officers recommendation.
 
Officers were asked to continue to publicise
and encourage residents to recycle through the Council’s
website and social media platforms.
 
 
Resolved
that: 
 
i)              
Approval be given for Officers to commence the procurement
process to source a supplier to provide the Council with Wheeled
Bins and Food Caddies
 
ii)            
A 3-year contract as detailed in the report be approved

content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine an
application for a new Premises Licence under section 17 of the
Licensing Act 2003, in respect of KFC, 79 Station Road, Addlestone
KT15 2AR.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer’s report
was noted.  Officers confirmed that the
application concerned the licensable activity of Late Night
Refreshment (LNR) only. 
 
Members were advised that since submission of
the application, and following negotiation, the application had
since been amended to ‘Delivery Only’ and a number of
conditions agreed.  As a result, the
Responsible Authorities had withdrawn their formal
representations.  However, two residents
had not withdrawn their representations, which were considered
partially valid in respect of the Licensing Objectives.  All parties had been served the papers for the
Hearing which included full details of the objections and
subsequent discussion.
 
There being no questions of the Senior
Licensing Officer, the Applicant’s representative was then
invited to state their case.
 
The Sub-Committee’s attention was drawn
to additional conditions within the proposed operating schedule
which specifically addressed the Licensing Objectives of the
Prevention of Crime and Disorder and the prevention of Public
Nuisance.  The additional conditions
were also set out in the Appendices, within emailed correspondence
between the Applicant and the Senior Licensing Officer.
 
The applicant’s representative sought to
demonstrate active engagement with residents to address their
concerns, which were also summarised for the benefit of the
Sub-Committee.  In essence, the
applicant considered that amending the application to
‘delivery only’ removed the potential for a number of
the objections; such as anti-social behaviour, and accumulation of
rubbish.  The applicant confirmed that
refuse was collected regularly under a commercial contract, and
that if the application was granted, careful monitoring would take
place.
 
It was stressed however that concerns about
parking and associated matters were not within the remit of the
Licensing Act.  However, the applicant
undertook to monitor the situation and could make effective
representations to the third party delivery firms if problems
arose, although it was noted that the business could not control
where people, including delivery drivers, parked.
 
The applicant’s representative confirmed
that their client ran several London businesses with no reviews or
sanctions.
 
The applicant was asked where, if there were a
number of drivers, they would wait while orders were being
prepared.  It was confirmed that orders
were prepared to be collected as soon as they were ready to shorten
‘dwell time’, but there was room in the premises for
drivers without them having to congregate outside.
 
The resident was then invited to state their
reasons for objecting to the application.
 
The resident explained that the main issues
were the volume of rubbish in the vicinity of the premises, and
access to their property via a private road leading from Station
Road.  The resident had encountered
difficulties on a number of occasions where delivery drivers had
blocked access when they were either going to work or returning
therefrom.  They had also  been subject to verbal abuse and threats when they
had challenged their behaviour which was unacceptable.
 
Regarding the build up of rubbish, the
applicant agreed there were waste problems in the area to the rear
of the commercial premises, but that it wasn’t necessarily
emanating from KFC, and that granting the licence would not make
matters worse.
 
In respect of driver behaviour, the applicant
confirmed that all such incidents should be reported and they could
also feedback to the relevant companies if there was a persistent
issue, to effectively ban someone from attending their premises if
they caused a problem.  In addition, the
applicants referred to the driver ‘hand off’ time which
if longer than 2-3 minutes would adversely affect the
business.  This could be monitored and
reported back to the delivery companies.  As a family business, the applicant wanted to work
with the residents and escalate if necessary any problems with
delivery drivers.  The resident
appreciated what they described as an ‘olive branch’
but still had concerns about parking issues.
 
The applicant confirmed that after 23:00 to
01:00/03:00 hours, the front door of the premises could not be
locked for fire safety reasons, but the illuminated light would be
switched off to dissuade late night customers, and clarifying that
it would be ‘delivery only.’
 
The Sub-Committee expressed sympathy for the
resident and appreciated the proposed steps to address the matters,
whilst acknowledging that parking itself was not a licensing
issue.  Parties were advised that
regulation of the private access road rested with the land owner to
whom representations should be made by all concerned.
 
There being no further contributions, the
closing statements of those present were noted and the
Committee’s attention was drawn to the relevant guidance
under section 182 of the Licensing Act, as well as the
Council’s Statement of Licensing Policy.
 
The meeting was adjourned at 14:45 and the
press and public excluded to allow the Sub-Committee to determine
the application.
 
The meeting re-convened at 14:49.
 
The Sub-Committee was satisfied that with
reference to the application and taking into consideration all
relevant representations and subsequent discussion, the applicant
had addressed the relevant Licensing Objectives, with the
additional conditions as set out in the agenda papers.  The decision of the Sub-Committee was to grant the
application accordingly, there being no valid grounds to
refuse.
 
All parties were thanked for their attendance
and confirmation of the decision would be issued in writing within
7 days of the meeting.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the application for
a premises licence in respect of KFC, 79 Station Road, Addlestone.
KT15 2AR, be granted for the licensable activity of late night
refreshment
topline: The Sub-Committee has decided to grant a new Premises Licence for a KFC in Addlestone, addressing concerns raised by residents.
