content:
Proposal: Full
planning application for a residential development of 35 units (18
apartments and 17 dwellings) and no. 2 traveller pitches with
associated landscaping and open space; new access and associated
works to facilitate the development.
 
Members’
attention was drawn to the addendum which cited three further
letters of objection. The application was then outlined to members.
The site formed part of a wider residential site in the local plan
for housing and gypsy and traveller pitches. The new application
would provide 35 additional residential sites and two gypsy and
traveller pitches, and great weight should be allocated to the
application because of this. It was confirmed that there would be
no negative impact on biodiversity or the highways in the area.
Consideration had been given to housing design and housing mix.
 
Queries were raised
over the reduction from 40 to 35 units, and the perceived lack of
three- and four-bedroom homes within the scheme when it had been
noted there was a scarcity of these in other parts of the
borough.
 
Officers noted that
this application was more constrained than the neighbouring
development because of the need to provide two allocated gypsy and
traveller pitches at 500m2 each, and
provide a root protection area for the veteran tree.
 
It was noted that
the original plan had included less of the flood plain, whereas the
final site included more of the flood plain, and the number of
housing units had to have been reduced accordingly this had also
had an impact on the mix. It was noted that the under delivery in
terms of units and mix was not so significant as to cause
significant concern and was for good planning reasons.
 
In response to
concerns over the phrasing of ‘high quality planting’
to replace trees that would be removed from the site, it was
confirmed that this would also include trees.
 
In response to
objections from the Thorpe Lea Residents’ Association, it was
noted that the application complied with the Council’s
relevant design and parking standards; that it was intended for
trees to be planted to replace those that were lost, that there was
a biodiversity enhancement plan in place, and that the suggestion
about residents only being able to turn left was not supported by
county highways.
 
It was also
confirmed that all flats would have one parking space, and houses
would have two. In response to questions about cycle routes, it was
confirmed that there were other schemes which intended to bring
cycle ways to the area.
 
RESOLVED THAT:
 
The Planning Committee authorised the Head of
Planning to:
 
To
consider comments received from Dickson Searle in respect of the
Housing Viability Assessment to determine whether the scheme can
financially support affordable housing and either
 
A) Grant planning permission in
accordance with this advice subject to conditions as set out in
section 12 and a S106 Legal Agreement to:
 
(i)
Either secure the relevant affordable housing or a claw
back
(ii) To secure the required
financial contributions towards the SAMM and the SANG in respect of
the Thames Basin Heath SPA.
(iii) The provision of 2 Gypsy & Traveller pitches including
a clear phasing for their timely Delivery and a local connection
test.
(iv) Secure management
arrangements and provide a management plan for the maintenance of
all public amenity space (including any verges), the open space
(including the 10m buffer to the neighbouring watercourse to the
east) and the equipped play area.
(v) Secure a Travel Plan and
Monitoring Fee.
(vi) Provision of £50
worth of free travel for car club vehicles for each residential
unit and the provision of one year free
membership of a local car club for the first occupants of the
residential units.
vii) To prevent a ransom strip
and to protect connectively (cycle and pedestrian) with the
adjacent site Thorpe Lea Manor.
 
Or
 
B) To refuse planning permission at the discretion of the
HoP should the viability issue not be
satisfactorily resolved within 4 months of the committee date
and/or the S106 does not progress to his
satisfaction.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to authorize the Head of Planning to grant planning permission for a residential development of 35 units and 2 traveller pitches.

content:
Proposal:
Demolition of the existing office building and the erection of a
5-storey building comprising a mixed use
development including parking at ground floor level, retail at
first floor, and student accommodation across the upper floors
consisting of 128 ensuite bedspaces. Construction of a new
vehicular access onto Church Road following the closure of the
existing access and associated new landscaping across the site.
 
Members’
attention was drawn to the addendum which included an updated
recommendation. The application was then outlined to members. The
development would provide 128 student bedsits within a sustainable
development. The development was not considered harmful to the
street scene or wider town centre. Two letters of objection had
been received.
 
Discussion centred
around parking which had been allocated to the retail store, and
not the student accommodation. It was noted that SPD parking
guidance recommended parking at one space per ten students and one
space per two members of staff however it was noted that this was
guidance. A minority of members suggested that they would wish for
this parking to be provided and the
spaces allocated to the retail store reduced accordingly.
 
Officers stated
that the standards were guidance and
also maximums. It was also noted that allocation of parking
spots to the retail store did not encourage new trips into the
area, but supported those who already
visited a supermarket in the area, and therefore was shifted demand
rather than new demand. It was considered that the location of the
development meant that students were unlikely to need their cars,
as it was within walking distance of campus, supermarkets the
station and a full range of services for daily life. It was also
considered 
that more harm could potentially arise by reducing the
allocated parking for the retail store, as this would increase the
risk of traffic could back up onto the public highway at peak times
on a critical part of the network and in proximity to a town centre
and level crossing. There were concerns around how to allocate
spaces to such a small proportion of the students (circa 12 spaces
for 128 bed spaces), and how would this
work operationally.
 
Members noted that
there had been problems in the nearby Magna Square development
regarding the turning circles and conditioning for refuse
collection, alongside an under provision of disabled parking
spaces. It was asked if the condition could be strengthened to
ensure adequate provision of both. Officers thanked members for
this insight and noted that there was still opportunity for these
points to be strengthened in negotiations with the developer.
 
Concerns were also
raised over surface water drainage, and it was confirmed that this
would be considered under condition ten, which would ensure any
runoff rates were not greater than the existing situation.
 
Members also
requested an additional condition be placed on the development to
ensure there were noise limits on delivery vehicles late at night
given the supermarket’s proximity to the student
accommodation. An additional condition for the delivery management
plan for noise was agreed to be added to the development.
 
Discussion returned
to student parking, with it being suggested by a minority of
members that students be allocated parking to remove pressure on
residential streets which was a perceived problem in other areas.
It was noted that such amendments were material, and that given the
likely impact of such a suggestion officers were not comfortable
with it being a change imposed by condition without discussion with
the applicant, it did not seem that there was an incentive for the
developer to agree this change as there was currently no objection
from the County Highway Authority.
 
Whilst the option
of deferring the application to allow further consultation with the
developer was discussed, some members had concerns that this was
unlikely to change the outcome, and that it may delay the item
unnecessarily which could lead to an appeal from the developer and
the risk of costs. No deferment was proposed.
 
 
RESOLVED THAT:
 
The Planning Committee
authorised the Head of Planning to grant planning permission
subject to:

-       
Cycle parking scheme for students

-       
Provision of disabled parking for
students

-       
Bus stop improvements

-       
A refuse and recycling scheme and
 
The removal of the requirement
for a Travel Plan.
The list of 32 conditions
listed on page 70 of the agenda read in conjunction with the
amended and updated conditions in the addendum
 
Alongside the new condition of
a delivery management plan for noise
topline: The Planning Committee has authorized the construction of a mixed-use development with student accommodation, despite concerns about parking allocation and potential traffic issues.

content:
Proposal:
Development of site to deliver data centre campus (sui generis use)
consisting of (a) data centre buildings (b) energy, power, and
water infrastructure (c) site access and internal roads (d) site
security arrangements (e) hard and soft, green and blue,
landscaping and (f) other ancillary and auxiliary forms of
development (application includes elements approved under ref.
RU.21/0780 and already constructed)
 
Officers outlined
the proposal to provide a data centre campus including site access
and internal roads, and site security arrangements. A number of changes were outlined compared to the
previously permitted scheme which has been largely constructed on
site. These included the increase in the height of the central
office/ ancillary block, an increase in height of the northern data
centre building, a new five storey data centre building, and an
additional fourteen standby back-up generators proposed which would
be double stacked on existing. One letter of objection had been
received from Chobham Common, which highlighted concerns around
electricity and water supply which had been addressed by the
developer.
 
Queries were raised
around the fuel usage fuel usage for the back-up generators. A
member raised that it was noted some authorities had chosen not to
allow diesel use in their applications due to habitats concerns.
Officers thank the member for this insight and it may be useful for similar future
proposals. In this case however Officers noted the generators are
proposed to run on HVO fuel and are simply for back up purposes in
case of electricity supply failure, and so it was unlikely that
this impact would be significant or material as the generators were
anticipated to be used infrequently, as a result a condition was
not considered necessary on this occasion. 
 
 
RESOLVED THAT: 
 
The Planning Committee authorised the Head of
Planning to:
 

1.1)        
Grant planning permission subject to the completion of a Section
106 legal agreement and amended planning conditions as set out in
section 12 of the report and addendum
 

1.2)        
To refuse planning permission at the discretion of the Head of
Planning should the S106 not progress to his satisfaction.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to grant planning permission for a data centre campus development, despite concerns raised by local stakeholders.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
increase the Hackney Carraige vehicle soiling charge from £50
to a maximum of £100 following a request from members of the
Trade.
 
Members were advised that the vehicle soiling
charge (which was a supplementary charge) had not been increased
since its introduction in 2006, it was out of step with other West
Surrey authorities, with whom the Council would be combining in
April 2027, and did not reflect the true cost or inconvenience to
the Trade of rectifying such incidents.
 
Following the request, and a previous general
expression of support by the Committee, Officers had consulted the
Trade, and received 4 responses, all of which were in
support.  Officers had benchmarked with
other Surrey authorities and TFL, as well as taken into account
inflation, and the cost of local hand car wash operators and
professional valet services.  The
Committee agreed that £100 was fair, reasonable, and
proportionate.
 
Officers had also taken the opportunity to
update the wording of the policy to be more specific in the
definition of and consequences of vehicle soiling.
 
The Committee noted the timescale for
advertising, subsequent consultation, and if no objections were
received that the change would take effect in April 2026.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the Hackney Carriage
vehicle soiling charge be increased from £50 to £100
and the description of the charge is amended from
‘discretionary soiling charge’ to ‘soiling the
carriage interior leaving it unfit for immediate subsequent hiring
(not shown on the meter)’
topline: The Committee has decided to increase the Hackney Carriage vehicle soiling charge from £50 to £100.

content:
The Committee received a report providing an
update on progress since the January 2026 meeting of the Corporate
Management Committee (CMC) and outlining the range of options
considered for two key operational assets: 57 Larchwood Drive and
Kings Lane Open Space as identified in work commissioned from
Montague Evans to assess feasibility and options appraisals of the
two sites following a request for such an exercise by the
committee..
 
Following detailed evaluation, the report
recommended that 57 Larchwood Drive be declared as surplus to
operational requirements and planning permission pursued for
residential use, with the strongest market option being 9
residential units.  The report also
highlighted the benefits of delivering a new, community and
recreation facility at Kings Lane which would provide high quality
amenities for local residents and
strengthen the offer for communities across the borough, whilst
providing a fit for purpose base for community activities currently
provided at 57 Larchwood Drive.
 
Phil Turner (PT) Assistant Chief Executive
(Place) presented the report and suggested that the proposals set
out therein supported a strategic,
balanced approach to asset management and directly aligned with the
core aims of our Corporate Business Plan.
 
The position remained, as set out in the
January report, that there was no satisfactory evidence, after
extended engagement, that the proposals put forward previously by
the Englefield Green CIC would be financially viable or
deliverable.  PT recognised the
excellent work of volunteers delivering services at the Larchwood
site but concluded that officers could not support continued
pursuit of the CIC redevelopment proposals as an outcome for the
Larchwood Drive Site.  
 
PT drew the attention to members of some of
the considerations regarding funding set out in the report
and in particular a proposed future bid
for strategic CIL subject to the usual approval processes.
 
PT assured members that the council would
engage with appropriate stakeholders regarding proposals for the
management of any new facility at Kings Lane. He also made a
correction to paragraph 11.3 of the report which incorrectly state
that the Englefield Green Residents Association formed part of the
CIC, which it did not, and asked that the correction be noted.
 
Finally, PT referred to the anticipated costs
set out in the exempt appendix to the report, and the financial
request in the recommendations for initial estimates and surveys
prior to planning application submission, a capital provision would
be made until such time as a full project appraisal had been
conducted.
 
Councillor R King clarified the correction to
the report at 11.3 to read “In addition other stakeholders
could support the management of a future facility at Kings Lane and
they will be identified”
 
Councillor R. King proposed the
recommendations as set out in the report and Councillor L. Gillham
seconded.
 
The matter was discussed.
 
Officers and residents were thanked for their
hard work in this area and the importance of a such community
facilities as those proposed in this report was stressed. In
addition, volunteers at the Larchwood Drive site were thanked for
their involvement and it was recognised that their efforts had been
key to moving the matter forward.
 
That the proposals were welcome given
that the CIC proposals were not considered viable.
 
In response to questions received the
committee heard that:
 
RBC had in place a Multi-service agency agreement with Montague Evans
and would build team to work at pace to secure planning for the
proposals.  Key to that process would be
a consultation to ensure that any application would meet the needs
of the community. 

That the report was purposely vague in
relation to provision of services currently provided at Larchwood
Drive in order that alternative provision during delivery of a new
facility was guided by the needs and wants of those utilising and
delivering provision.
 
That issues of accessibility to the Kings Lane
site would be part of the planning process, including elements of
design such as levelling, widening or lighting and was likely to be
a phased or conditioned element of any planning approval.
 
Following consideration of the exempt
appendices in Part II, the meeting returned to public session and
the matter was put the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 

      
i.        
a supplementary revenue estimate for 2026/27 in the sum of
£375,000 to facilitate a twin tracked planning approach for
Larchwood Drive and Kings Lane Open Space be APPROVED

    
ii.        
the redevelopment of Kings Lane be subject to a strategic CIL bid,
subject to planning permission, and obtaining vacant possession of
the pavilion building at Kings Lane; all these aspects are
highlighted in Section 17 of report be AGREED

   
iii.        
a capital provision in the sum set out in Option 3 in confidential
Appendix A be included in the Capital Programme for 2027/28 for the
redevelopment of Kings Lane to be released, subject to a future
report setting out a full business case, costings and funding
assessment be APPROVED

   
iv.        
where recommendations (a) and (b) have been approved by the
Committee, it be AGREED to procure a design and build contract for
a mixed-use community and leisure facility on Kings Lane [approval
conditional on the above having been achieved]. The maximum
contract value is noted in Appendix A.

    
v.        
Subject to the above, and the provision of an alternative venue, 57
Larchwood Drive be AGREED as surplus to operational requirements
and bring back to a future committee the principal of disposal and
method of disposal.

   
vi.        
the allocation of up to £20,000 from the Englefield Green
S106 monies for Community Support Facilities if required, for
interim works required to enable continuation of use of the
Community Hub at Larchwood Drive, whilst the above is progressed be
AGREED

  
vii.        
the allocation of all remaining Englefield Green S106 monies, for
Community Support Facilities, totalling £308,640, plus any
underspend from monies allocated in (f) to be allocated to
non-building elements of the project relating to Kings Lane, as a
contribution towards the total costs be AGREED.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to declare 57 Larchwood Drive surplus and pursue residential use, while developing a new community facility at Kings Lane Open Space.

content:
The Committee received a report putting
forward a revised Whistleblowing Policy and Procedure which had
been reviewed and updated in accordance with good practice and
recent changes to employment legislation for recommendation to Full
Council for adoption.
 
Kate Enver (KE), Corporate Head of HR &
OD, introduced the report.  She reported
that the Whistleblowing Policy had been revised as part of the
council’s scheduled policy cycle and reflected requirements
set out in the recently introduced Employment Rights Act 2025, most
notably the explicit inclusion of sexual harassment as a type of
wrongdoing that can be raised through whistleblowing routes.
 
She stated that the draft policy had been
considered by the Council’s recognised Trade Union who
supported its adoption.
 
Finally, KE informed members that should the
policy be approved, it would be communicated to the whole RBC
workforce by various channels, including a webinar for all staff,
with in person sessions for others and an updated intranet page to
ensure that the policy was properly embedded within the
organisation.
 
The recommendation within the report was
proposed by Councillor R. King and seconded by Councillor L.
Gillham.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 
The revised Whistleblowing Policy be Approved
for presentation to Full Council.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve a revised Whistleblowing Policy for presentation to Full Council.

content:

approval of the allocation of £21,970.00 neighbourhood CIL
funding to the tree planting project in Englefield Green Village,
in a bid submitted by Englefield Green CIC, subject to a number of

Stephanie Broadley (SB) Assistant Planning

.

the allocation of £21,970.00

content:

content:
Having declared a conflict of interest in the
matter to be discussed Councillor R. King left the meeting for the
duration of this item
 
The Committee received a report seeking
approval of previously allocated SCIL funds to deliver standalone
elements of the Egham Hythe LSI scheme, independent of any further
funding, to guarantee that well-supported elements of the scheme
can be delivered without delay, as recommended by the Developer
Contributions Advisory Group at its meeting on 5 March 2026.
 
Stephanie Broadley (SB) Assistant Planning
Policy Manager (Policy and Infrastructure) presented the report and
explained the history of the scheme and the problems encountered in
attempting to secure further funding for the scheme as originally
planned.  The report set out alternative
proposals to deliver elements of the scheme not reliant on
additional funding.  Surrey County
Council had confirmed that delivery of a reduced scope scheme at
this stage would not compromise pursuit of the wider scheme aims in
the future and it would remain on the SCC prioritisation
framework.
 
The recommendations within the report were
proposed by Councillor L. Gillham and seconded by Councillor R.
Milstead.
 
In response to a question the committee heard
that the SCC had not committed at this stage to a detailed timeline
for decisions on which element of the project would be delivered
but that it would be agreed this year and SB assured members that
any information would be shared with them in a timely
manner. 
 
SB also confirmed that the Chertsey LSI scheme
bid continued, and the outcomes of the initial engagement phase had
recently been published by SCC, but no further timeline details
were able to be confirmed at this stage.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 
the use of £600,000 of allocated
strategic CIL monies to deliver standalone elements of the first
phase of the Egham Hythe LSI scheme be APPROVED.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve the use of allocated funds for standalone elements of the Egham Hythe LSI scheme.

content:

topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve recommendations after discussing confidential matters.

content:
The Committee received an urgent report tabled
under the provisions of paragraph 1.3 of Part 3a (Committee
Responsibilities) of the Constitution to facilitate a decision
needed urgently and that could not reasonably be delayed until the
next Meeting of the Council. 
 
The report sought approval to the
Council’s participation in a response from Surrey local
authorities to an invitation from the Government to establish a
Foundation Strategic Authority (FSA) for Surrey.
 
Mario Leo (ML), Corporate Head of Law and
Governance introduced the item for members and explained the
chronology of consultation and other events to the point of the
meeting.  He explained what an FSA was
and how the creation of such authorities aligned with the
governments longer term commitment to mayoral devolution.
 
On meeting to discuss the government’s
consultation request there had been a consensus amongst Surrey
local authorities that an expression of interest to form an FSA
should be submitted and a letter indicating that desire had been
drafted.  Support for the position from
the Committee would allow Runnymede to be a signatory on that
letter.
 
The recommendation within the report was
proposed by Councillor R. King and seconded by Councillor L.
Gillham.
 
The matter was discussed and the comments
received were supportive of the proposal to form an
FSA.  In response to questions the
Committee heard that:
 

      
i.        
At this time the FSA proposal supported by Surrey local authorities
covered the geographical area of the county of Surrey only

    
ii.        
That support for an FSA in no way precluded mayoral devolution in
the future.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 
 
Runnymede Borough Council be a signatory to a
letter to the Government expressing a wish to submit an Expression
of Interest for establish a Foundation Strategic Authority for
Surrey be AGREED.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to have Runnymede Borough Council participate in the establishment of a Foundation Strategic Authority for Surrey.

content:
Having declared a conflict of interest in the
matter to be discussed Councillor L. Gillham left the meeting for
the duration of this item

approval of the allocation of neighbourhood CIL funding to two
schemes in Thorpe as recommended by the Developer Contributions
Advisory Group (DCAG) at its meeting on 5 March 2026.
 
The schemes were set out in the report as:
 

      
i.        
Thorpe C of E Primary School - Early Years Foundation Stage
Playground Regeneration for Outdoor Learning - £39,000.00
Neighbourhood CIL, with £21,000.00 of ‘Your Fund
Surrey’ match-funding applied for;

    
ii.        
Thorpe Neighbourhood Forum – Thorpe Heritage Walls Project -
£75,043.20 Neighbourhood CIL.
 
Stephanie Broadley (SB) Assistant Planning
Policy Manager (Policy and Infrastructure) presented the
report.  She referred to the projects
seeking approval for CIL funds to be allocated and drew the
attention of the committee to Appendix 2 of the report which set
out recommendations from the DCAG to reject three schemes
previously deferred for decision-making and continue to defer two
schemes for future consideration for neighbourhood CIL funding.
 
The recommendations within the report were
proposed by Councillor R. King and seconded by Councillor D.
Whyte
 
The proposals were discussed and comments were
supportive of the recommendations and of the thorough discussions
at DCAG which provided assurance for members.  The committee spoke of the continued relevance of
the two deferred schemes within appendix 2.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that
 

      
i.        
the allocation of Thorpe neighbourhood CIL monies to two schemes as
recommended by the Developer Contributions Advisory Group,
summarised in paragraph 2.3 and Appendix 1 of the report be
AGREED.

    
ii.        
the remaining recommendations of the Developer Contributions
Advisory Group for the rejection of three neighbourhood CIL funding
applications previously deferred for decision-making; and the
continued deferment of funding decisions for two CIL applications,
as set out in Appendix 2 of the report be AGREED.

content:
Having declared a conflict of interest in the
matter to be discussed Councillor J. Mavi left the meeting for the
duration of this item.
 
The committee received a report which sought a
decision on whether to consent to a request received to relinquish
the right of the Council to appoint Nominative Trustees to the
Chertsey Combined Charity
 
Mario Leo (ML), Corporate Head of Law and
Governance presented the report.  He
explained the intended purpose of Council appointed Nominative
Trustees to Charities in general and the circumstances specific to
the undertaking in relation to Chertsey Combined Charity, from whom
the request to relinquish had been received.
 
ML continued, he set out the options available
to the Committee in its decision making and the potential outcomes
of each and set the decision in the context of the LGR and the
creation of a West Surrey Authority from April 2027.
 
Councillor King proposed and Councillor
Gillham seconded.
 
The matter was discussed with views heard
noting the events leading up to this request, supporting
relinquishing of powers, identifying the potential benefit of
reduced workload of this nature for elected members post LGR when
the number of councillors in the Borough would be significantly
reduced, and proposing that the wishes of the charity should be
respected.  
 
A named vote was proposed by Councillor Mann
and seconded by Councillor Cressey and was duly undertaken by the
monitoring officer. 
 
The vote asked whether members wished to agree
to surrender the right of the Council to appoint Nominative
Trustees to the Chertsey Combined Charity
 
The result of the named vote was as
follows:
 
For:
Councillors R. King (Chair), L. Gillham (Vice Chair), M. Cressey,
T. Gates, T. Gracey, C. Howorth, C. Mann, R. Milstead, I. Mullens,
M. Smith and D. Whyte
Against:
None

Abstentions: None
 
It was
RESOLVED:
 
that the
surrender of the right of the Council to appoint Nominative
Trustees to the Chertsey Combined Charity be AGREED
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve the surrender of the right of the Council to appoint Nominative Trustees to the Chertsey Combined Charity.

content:
The Committee received a report introducing a
new Housing Payment (HP) Policy for 2026/27 to replace
Discretionary Housing Payments (DHP) as part of the
Government’s Crisis & Resilience Fund (CRF), which would
consolidate DHP and the Household Support Fund into a single
funding stream from 1 April 2026.
 
Linda Norman (LN), Corporate Head of Customer,
Digital & Collection Services presented the report.  She explained that the new HP scheme presented an
administrative transition and largely mirrored existing DHP rules,
ensuring continuity for residents while aligning with updated
national guidance. Runnymede Borough Council would continue to
administer Housing Payments, with Surrey County Council delivering
other CRF elements and eligibility, application processes, and
decision-making criteria remain essentially unchanged.
 
LN explained that the new framework removed
the previous limit on council “top-ups” and placed
greater emphasis on proactive identification of residents
struggling with housing costs.
 
The recommendations within the report were
proposed by Councillor R King and seconded by Councillor L Gillham,
there being no questions or comments, the matter was put to the
vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that it be recommended to Full
Council that:
 

      
i.        
the Housing Payments Policy for 2026/27 be APPROVED and adopted as
the Council’s formal policy for administering Housing
Payments under the new Crisis & Resilience Fund framework from
1 April 2026.

    
ii.        
delegated authority to the Corporate Head of Customer, Digital
& Collection Services, in consultation with the Assistant Chief
Executive (Section 151 Officer), to make any minor amendments
required to ensure operational compliance with updated Department
for Work and Pensions guidance and Management Information
requirements be AGREED.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve a new Housing Payment Policy for 2026/27 under the Crisis & Resilience Fund.

content:
The Committee received a report
providing a summary of the 2026/27 Service Area Plan (SAP) for
Assets and Regeneration for approval.
Alex Williams (AW), Corporate Head of Assets and Regeneration,
presented the report.  She explained
that the SAP set out how the Assets and Regeneration service would
support the Corporate Business Plan and ensured that resources were
focussed where they would have the greatest impact over the next
year toward the Council’s priorities.
She
described the income generated by the service, circa £27m per
annum and assured members that focus would remain on strengthening
capacity following the non-statutory best value review and ensuring
best value across the property portfolio.
AW
continued to set out external pressures being managed in order to
deliver against priorities such as carbon reduction initiatives,
improvements to the Civic Centre and necessary works at the
depot.
Finally, she reported that items identified as requiring budget
growth had been included in the Council’s approved budget for
2026/27 but that capital provision would require further
consideration by Committee to release the funds during the year as
per the Council’s Financial Regulations.
The
recommendation within the report was proposed by Councillor
R.King and seconded by Councillor L.
Gillham.
The
plan was discussed, in particular regard was had to the mission
statement and Carbon reduction and in response members heard that
the mission statement, although lengthier than those in other
service area plans was not considered to be an issue that would
preclude it from being approved.
The
matter was put to the vote.
It
was RESOLVED that:
the
2026/27 Service Area Plan for Assets and Regeneration be
APPROVED.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve the 2026/27 Service Area Plan for Assets and Regeneration.

content:
The
Committee received a report setting out the 2026/27 Service Area
Plans (SAP’s) for Finance, Procurement, HR/OD and Comms,
Legal and Governance and the CEX Office for approval as well as,
subject to the SAP approvals, the Council’s Corporate Action
Plan for 2026/27 which was compiled from planned activity in all
Service Area Plans and was for noting.
Sarah Hall (SH), Head of Business Planning, Projects and
Performance presented the report and associated plans for approval
and reminded members of those plans considered by other service
committees and approved for inclusion in the Corporate Action
Plan.
SH
reported that the Corporate Action Plan had 183 planned activities
included within it and that these were additional to the core
activities of the Council.  All activity
was planned for delivery by the end of the calendar year to allow 3
months contingency for completion before Runnymede BC ceased to
exist in April 2027.
She
reminded members that items identified as requiring budget growth
had been included in the Council’s approved budget for
2026/27 but those that required capital provision would be
considered by the relevant Committee prior to release of funds
during the year as per the Council’s Financial Regulations
and finally, explained that the Corporate Action Plan was the start
of the ‘Golden thread’ which would run through the
Service Area Plans, to individual objectives to ensure delivery of
the council’s objectives over its final year.
The
recommendations within the report were proposed by Councillor R.
King and seconded by Councillor L. Gillham and no comments or
question being received, the matter was put to the vote.
It
was RESOLVED that:

the 2026/27 Service
Area Plans for Finance, Procurement, HR/OD and Comms, Legal and
Governance and the CEX Office be APPROVED
the Corporate Action
Plan that lists the activities approved for delivery in 2026/27
across all service areas be NOTED
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve the 2026/27 Service Area Plans and Corporate Action Plan for Runnymede BC.

content:
The Committee was presented with their Annual
Report for 2025/26 for onward recommendation to the full Council on
30 April 2026.
 
The report set out the Committee’s terms
of reference and remit and Officers highlighted some of the key
events of the Committee’s year. 
These included embedding the Council’s revised complaints
policy, procedures, and reporting requirements in line with the
Ombudsman’s Complaints Handling Code, continued development
of the Council’s Risk Management framework, oversight of
internal audit arrangements and finally completion of the external
audits by BDO for the years 2019/20 through to 2022/23, the
Corporate Peer Challenge reviews, and strengthening the
relationship with the new External Auditors, Grant Thornton.
 
Members reviewed the work undertaken in
2025/26, and noted the timeline and narrative for the
Council’s dealings with external and internal
audit.  Matters relating to Governance
were noted, including the Committee’s participation in the
Government’s Consultation on the Code of Conduct.
 
Prior to submission to full Council, Officers
would make an amendment to the report to reflect the recent change
in the membership of the Committee, and the outcome of the
self-assessment exercise.
 
The Committee was pleased to commend the
report, and thanked Officers for their clear conveyance of complex
areas.
 
Recommend that
–
 
the draft Standards
and Audit Committee Annual Report 2025/26 be amended as agreed to
reflect the results of the self-assessment exercise and endorsed
for referral to Full Council
topline: The Standards and Audit Committee has decided to approve and endorse their Annual Report for 2025/26.

content:
The Committee was advised of the results of
Quarter 3 for complaints and compliments in 2025/26.
 
Officers reported that there were 67 entries
in Jadu for complaints in Quarter 3 of 2025/26.  This compared with 79 in Quarter 3 of 2024/25, and
87 in the previous quarter of 2025/26.
 
Members reviewed the table containing data
requested by the Ombudsman which would be presented at year end at
the next meeting.  Members were pleased
to note that the majority of complaints at Stages 1 and 2 continued
to be responded to within the stipulated 15 working
days.  An increase in the reporting of
service improvements was also deemed useful and informative.
 
With regard to compliments, 28 individual
compliments were recorded in quarter 3, a slight decrease from the
previous quarter, but a vast improvement on the figure for the same
quarter in 2024/25.  Officers
highlighted positive feedback for colleagues in Housing and
Customer Services especially.
 
Members were advised that to align with the
reporting regime, Quarters 1 and 2 of 2026/27 would be reported in
November 2026, and the final report at the Committee’s last
meeting in March 2027.
 
Officers were asked to consider the customer
journey for setting up a ‘one account’ with the Council
and any particular feedback could be shared with colleagues in
Digital Services.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Council has reviewed complaints and compliments data for Quarter 3 of 2025/26.

content:
The Committee was asked to note progress with
the Internal Audit plan for 2025/26.
 
Officers reported that the timetable was being
adhered to, with 80% of the year’s programme complete, and
that there had been no ‘limited’ audit opinions issued
since the previous update. 
 
There had been two adjustments to the plan, to
remove Fraud Framework and Financial Management of RBCI following
review and alignment of risk and resource.
 
Since preparation of the report, Members were
assured that a recommendation with regard to the ‘use of
volunteers’ audit had now been completed. 
 
The Committee was advised where there were
overdue items categorised as medium and low priority; these
totalled 5 and 3 respectively and were in the areas of Housing,
Disabled Facility Grants, and Decision Making and
Accountability.  Three revised target
dates had been agreed with the relevant client departments.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve the recommendations for the Internal Audit plan for 2025/26.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought for
the accounting policies for the financial year 2025/26, used in the
production and presentation of the Council’s annual Statement
of Accounts.
 
Officers had reviewed the accounting policies
and highlighted to the Committee one major change as a result of a
Thematic Review of Non-Investment Asset Valuation for financial
reporting by HM Treasury.  A change had
been made to the accounting policy relating to the valuation of
Property Plant and Equipment in the accounts.  Officers advised that a formal revaluation was
required on a rolling basis every five years (as before) and in the
intervening years, assets would be revalued using indexation.
 
The Committee was content to approve the
accounting policies with this update.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the Council’s
accounting policies for the financial year 2025/26, as set out in
Appendix A of the Officer’s report be approved
topline: The Council has decided to approve accounting policies for the financial year 2025/26.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought for
the ‘Informing the audit risk assessment’, introduced
by Grant Thornton in response to revised financial reporting
standards.  This document was produced
ahead of the main audit.
 
Officers presented each of the detailed
inquiries and the Management responses thereto and Members were
invited to make comments or suggest amendments if necessary.
 
The Committee was satisfied with the document
as presented and no such amendments were made.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the
document “Informing the audit risk assessment for Runnymede
Borough Council 2025/26” be approved, and the external
auditors be notified if there are any additional matters that the
Committee considers may also impact on the planned audit work and
context for the financial year ending 31 March 2026.
topline: The Runnymede Borough Council has decided to approve the 'Informing the audit risk assessment' document for the financial year 2025/26.

content:
The Committee was asked to
participate in two self assessment
exercises in order to consider the Committee’s level of
effectiveness in 2025/26.
 
Officers had, as in the previous
year, taken CIPFA’s model of assessment.  This set out key indicators covering all aspects
of governance, risk control and audit that were within the
Committee’s scope and influence.
 
Members reviewed the assessment,
noting actions from the 2024/25 assessment, and any areas for
improvement in 2026/27, which would then be fed into the
Council’s Annual Governance Statement.  The main areas for action were connected with
Local Government Re-Organisation (LGR), such as bringing reports
forward like the Internal Auditor’s Annual Assurance Opinion,
reviewing the risk register and actions arising therefrom as
overseen by the Council’s Continuous Improvement Programme
Board.  It was acknowledged that the
greatest area of risk associated with LGR was recruitment and
retention.  The other area of focus was
monitoring progress against an action plan to support the outcome
of the Housing Regulator’s inspection.
 
Officers highlighted where
actions had not been possible to complete, including concluding the
complaint in respect of BDO, undertaking some benchmarking work
regarding risk generally, and a review of the Council’s
Anti-Fraud and Corruption Policy.
 
In the second assessment, Members
were taken through a set of 29 questions and asked to record a
score against each in terms of the Committee’s compliance
therewith.  In the majority of areas it
was agreed no further improvement was needed and Members were
generally content.  It was agreed that
the opportunity for the Committee to meet privately with the
auditors was important, but that in 2025/26 they had not felt it
necessary.  The Committee did not
include any lay representatives. 
However, it was agreed that with only one year to go it would not
be productive to pursue this any further.  Officers undertook to survey the Committee in May
at the start of the municipal year about training needs as that had
not taken place in 2025/26.
 
Officers confirmed that feedback
from the exercise including those areas of improvement as
identified, would be included in the Annual Governance Statement,
and the final scores of the second assessment shared with
Members.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the
Standards and Audit Committee considers the self-assessment
exercises set out at Appendices A and B of the Officer’s
report, to evaluate its effectiveness during 2025/26 and identify
any areas for improvement during 2026/27.
topline: The Standards and Audit Committee has decided to evaluate its effectiveness and make improvements for the upcoming year.

content:
The Committee was provided for information,
with a progress report on completion of the 2025/26 External Audit,
and an update on developments in the External Audit sector
generally.
 
Officers advised that in respect of the 2023/4
and 2024/5 External Audits, work was substantially complete, now
that the former Auditors, BDO had issued their opinions on the
audits from 20219/20 through to 2022/23.  For both 2023/24 and 2024/25, a modified opinion
was expected, but not by the back stop date of 27 February, owing
to the delayed issue of prior year audit opinions by the
Council’s previous auditors. 
However, Officers were confident that future dates would be
achieved.
 
With regard to 2025/26, planning work was in
progress, and with the introduction of some early testing in key
areas such as fees and charges, grant income, operating expenditure
and similar, for months 1 to 9, Officers were very comfortable, and
could re-assure the Committee accordingly.  Members also found the Audit Deliverables timeline
useful in this regard.
 
Officers from Grant Thornton confirmed their
intention to present the External Audit Plan for 2026/27 to the
next scheduled meeting of the Committee in May 2026, or if not, to
July.
 
Officers would be taking into account the
Housing Regulator’s judgement, and in terms of the Value For
Money assessment, no significant risks had been identified yet.
 
The Committee noted various sector updates;
notably Grant Thornton’s report entitled ‘After the
Backstop: Reset, recovery and reform in the audit of Local
Authority accounts.  Legislative change
included the Fair Funding Review, Renter’s Rights Act and a
proposed new duty of candour and standards regime.
 
The Committee noted the Audit Fees for the
year ending 2026 were £222,349, derived from the procurement
exercise carried out by PSAA in 2022.
 
Officers were thanked for their report and for
their positive interactions with the Council.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for external audits and plan for future audits.

content:
The Committee received for information the
results of the External Quality Assessment of the Council’s
Internal Auditors, SIAP.  The assessment
was carried out by an Independent person, John Chesshire, of JC
Training Ltd, from September to December 2025.
 
Members were advised that the assessment was
both comprehensive and broad in scope, and carried out in
accordance with the provisions of the Global Internal Audit
Standards in the UK Public Sector.
 
The assessment had 5 domains, 15 principles
and 52 standards; Members agreed this was rigorous and were pleased
to learn that SIAP had been very favourably assessed, fully
achieving 46 of the 52 standards, and generally conforming in the
remaining 6, so a very positive outcome.
 
Officers confirmed that there were of course
opportunities for improvement which had been made into an Action
Plan, containing 9 areas for SIAP to work on over the coming
months.
 
Members found the feedback from the interviews
carried out with Stakeholders (a mixture of Audit Chairs, Chief
Executives, and other Senior Managers, and SIAP employees)
particularly helpful and encouraging.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations following a very positive assessment outcome of its Internal Auditors, SIAP.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought for
the Internal Audit Charter and Internal Audit Plan for 2026/27.
 
Officers reported that there were no changes
to last year’s Charter, and that as required by the Global
Internal Audit Standards for the UK Public Sector, it covered the
internal audit function’s mandate, organisational position,
reporting relationships, scope of work, types of service, and other
specifications.  These were set out in
full in the appendix to the Officer’s report.
 
Members reviewed the planned audit programme
for 2026/27, noting, that it was a unique year as Runnymede was
about to enter into its last year before
vesting day of the new West Surrey Council on 1 April 2027.
 
Officers from SIAP advised that they had
already met with the Section 151 Officers in West Surrey to
identify future synergies.
 
With regard to the audit plan, Officers aimed
to finish the audits in the programme by the end of January 2027,
so that their final Annual Assurance report could be presented to
the last scheduled meeting of the Committee in March
2027.  It was acknowledged that there
were tighter timescales, but Officers felt confident it was
achievable, having consulted the Senior Leadership Team in respect
of the areas on which it was proposed to focus.
 
One area highlighted by Members was the
Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) Disbursement. Clarification was
sought with regard to Neighbourhood and Strategic CIL balances post
re-organisation.  Officers thought that
funding for Neighbourhood CIL would carry forward, ringfenced to
the local areas but that Strategic CIL would be absorbed into the
wider pot for West Surrey.  A report on
CIL was due to be considered by Corporate Management Committee.
 
Members were assured that continuity of the
plan itself was being considered, and audit work undertaken, in
case SIAP were not the provider going forward.
 
Officers confirmed that there was contingency
(32 days) and flexibility in the plan should priorities change
owing to Local Government Re-organisation.
 
The Committee was content to approve both
documents accordingly.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the Internal Audit
Charter and Internal Audit Plan for 2026/27 be approved

from the funding originally awarded, leaving a contingency of

communities in the borough, whilst maintaining a link to the
original themes.  These were discharge

funding for the Health and Wellbeing partnership.  Officers had taken the opportunity to seed fund or
pilot new initiatives, or to support ongoing delivery of community
activity.  For example continuation of the youth hub, installation
of an accessible pathway at St Ann’s Hill and improvement
works in parks and recreational spaces.
 
As a precautionary measure it was recommended
that delegated authority be given to the Corporate Head of
Community Services to re-allocate funding to another project if the
original one could not go ahead, in consultation with the Chair and
Vice-Chair of the Committee.

2026/27.
 
Officers advised that the Service Area Plan
had been written with an eye towards the extensive preparations
that would be needed over the coming months for the establishment
of the West Surrey Council.  It was
intended that all identified work objectives would be completed by
the end of Quarter 3 to allow for their closure and transfer to the
new authority.
 
The Service Area Plan objectives aligned with
the Council’s Corporate Business Plan for 2026/27 and were
focussed on promoting active lives within the
community.  Taking a semi-commercial
outlook allowed Officers to make discretionary services
sustainable, providing high social value to residents.
 
Community Services had a wide remit with 18
service areas from prevention services to community engagement,
each with a set of objectives for the year to be delivered across
the team.  There were 33 planned
activities, 16 of which were in progress, and 17 had not yet
started.  Of the 33 projects, 7 were due
to be completed by 31 March 2026, and 26 carried forward into
2026/27.  The details were set out in
full in the Appendix to the Officer’s report.
 
Officers confirmed that ‘holding
lines’ in the plan existed in case there were projects or
initiatives that arose during the year from other projects such as
the Youth Development Fund and Englefield Green Section 106
infrastructure.

to Chertsey Museum, Community Alarms and Telecare, Community Halls,
Community Safety, Community Transport, Social Centre services,
Handyperson and Home Improvement Agency, Homesafe Plus, Meals at Home, Safer Runnymede,
Social Prescribing and Open Spaces Development.
 
The Committee was content to approve both
documents and looked forward to receiving an update at a future
meeting.

i)         
the Community Services, Service Area Plan for 2026/27 be approved;
and
 

ii)         the Key
Performance Indicators for Community Services for 2026/27 be
approved

financial projection as set out in Appendix A of the
Officer’s report be approved

content:
Members were asked to endorse the
Council’s response to a petition which had been referred by
full Council to the Committee for consideration concerning planting
and maintenance of trees and hedges on Council owned land.
 
The Committee recalled that the petition
prayer read:
 
‘Runnymede Borough Council to approve
the planting and maintenance of trees and hedges by voluntary
groups on selected land owned by Runnymede Borough Council in
accordance with the RBC Climate Change and Nature Action
Plan.’
 
Officers highlighted how climate,
sustainability and biodiversity matters had taken a more prominent
position both in the minds of residents and the wider community, as
well as being a priority in the Council’s own policies and
activities, as stated in the Corporate Business Plan for
2026/27.
 
Officers cited some of the activities already
undertaken under the climate change agenda including the
Biodiversity action plan, and acknowledged the valuable input of
existing voluntary groups in the borough such as the Friends of
Gogmore Park and Holme Farm.
 
However, Officers did not feel they had
sufficient resources to implement what was being asked of them at
this time which was a policy for supporting volunteers in this
particular endeavour, and taking into
account going into Local Government Re-organisation. Officers
considered it should be a matter for the new West Surrey Council to
address. 
 
Some Members disagreed with this, and wanted to see more active encouragement of
volunteer groups either in a more formal setting or through
informal agreements.  In addition, some
Members considered that the Council could provide a clear framework
under which voluntary groups could operate to avoid inappropriate
planting either by location or species; which had happened in some
cases, and which had resourcing and financial consequences.
 
Officers considered that financial liability
falling onto the Council was also a factor if volunteer groups were
having taken on a project, were then unable to maintain
it.  Officers stressed that they were
not against new planting schemes and ideas but that the wording of
this particular petition perhaps
broadened the scope too widely for the Council to support it.
 
After a lengthy debate, as summarised above,
it was moved and seconded that a decision on the petition was
deferred.
 
Officers agreed to consider the request for a
potential policy and framework for community groups in respect of
appropriate planting and maintenance projects in the borough, and
if after discussion it was considered realizable, to submit a
report to a future meeting of the Committee.
topline: The Council has decided to defer a decision on approving the planting and maintenance of trees and hedges by voluntary groups on council-owned land.

Members were informed that repairs performance

to improve performance, a new tender will be advertised this
year for additional provision for void and
minor works across the HRA stock to supplement the existing

The Corporate Head of Housing reported that the main

provide some performance information.  There had been a
change of senior leadership within the main contractor, and housing
has a commitment to resolving all the IT integration
issues as a priority. Housing has its own link to their
system, so we continue to have oversight of all
activities and housing has its own reporting.
 
The Corporate Head of Housing went on to report that
arrears were at 2.17% at the end of December compared to 2.32% the
previous year, which in the economic climate is a
positive result.
 
As of this week gas is at 99.89% and all other
compliance checks completed as required. 
 
Category 1 Hazards are at 48 (40 homes) these
will continue to be received throughout the stock condition survey
and are all being addressed. 
 
New contracts are
being procured for additional fire risk works.
The Corporate Head of
Housing advised that the Committee will receive updates at
every Housing Committee Meeting.
  
As reported in January, void timescales were improved
in Q3, however during Q4 there is some impact of the Christmas
period when contractors were not working, with the current average
time at 39 days.
 
The Chair welcomed the large number of additional KPIs now
being provided to monitor performance in key areas. Members
appreciated the work undertaken.
 
The Chair asked if Members had comments or questions

what the triangulation was between the report and

carry out a 10 percent
quality testing on the existing electrical contractor

 
2)            
We will be tendering
for an additional contractor to carry out the tests.
 
3)            
There had not been an
instance where a pass had been challenged through the quality

Officers are confident that contractors can do the work
immediately
  
Page 11 of the reports illustrated the number of disrepair

In response to Members’ questions on Medium Risk Fire

The Officer gave an outline of the Housing
Development Programme Update Report and presented slides.
 
Members were advised of progress on current
Housing Revenue Account development activity. HRA have a target to
deliver 125 new homes as part of the Housing Strategy. The status
and number of homes towards this target was outlined in paragraph
1.1 of the report.
 
Ripley Avenue and The Crescent bid is
ongoing in planning terms. We are waiting the outcome of the bids
LAF4. (Homes England).  Park side
regeneration is not included in the target of 125.
 
Thorpe Lea Manor, Egham, this is
nearing completion. Air source heat pumps have been installed, and
this would go towards achieving electric savings within the
apartments. The building will have electric charging points. 
The principle of purchasing S106 opportunities was agreed at
Housing Committee in September 2024, along with approval to
purchase 13 homes at Thorpe Lea Manor. 
 
LAHF3, The purchase of all four of the
Local Authority Housing Fund 3 (LAHF3) programme ahead of
completion schedule and grant funding deadline of end of March
2026.  The LAHF3 grant funding received has covered 64% of the
project costs. The funding requires two properties to be let to
refugee status families and two let as temporary accommodation.
 
Strategic Purchases The purchase of two
strategically placed homes has been completed within the estate
with a proposed redevelopment. These will be used as temporary
accommodation whilst the regeneration plans are developed. 
The purchase of a DIYSO (Do It Yourself Shared Ownership) share in
a 3-bedroom family house in Chertsey had completed. This will be
advertised on the letting system. A fourth family home in
Englefield Green (freehold owned by the Council) is in the
conveyancing process.
  
Garages at The Crescent and Ripley Avenue,
Egham Members have previously approved a successful bid to the
Council Housebuilding Support Fund to accelerate this site towards
a planning submission by end March 2026.  The site area
comprises 8 bedsits on The Crescent, 52 garages between Ripley
Avenue and The Crescent and a previously purchased plot of land
adjacent to the garages. Designs are evolving and a public
consultation event was held on 3rd February. 65 people attended
this informal consultation and feedback on our proposals was mixed
with general agreement that there was a housing need in Runnymede,
but a perception that homes should not be multiple storeys in this
location.  Parking around the site (due to students) is
already problematic and although our scheme would be self-contained
for parking, the perception is that our proposals could make
matters worse for residents. Architects are now working on designs
following feedback received in readiness for a pre-application
meeting with Local Planning Authority. Emerging designs are ongoing
to review height of the apartment blocks within the site, but they
will provide 2-, 3-and 4-bedroom homes in two blocks. There will
also be a terrace of 2 three bedroom and 2 four-bedroom homes which
will replace the 8 bedsit properties which face onto The
Cresent.
 
The Chair thanked the Officer for the report,
showing good progress on the properties mentioned.
 
Members were impressed by the size of the
dwelling and the mixed tenure for the community. Members thanked
Officers for securing of the sites mentioned.

conducted by Viewpoint Research who are experienced in
carrying out these surveys and provide assurance that the
methodology and technical requirements are
compliant.  The survey form was emailed to all tenants
who have an email address on our system and the remaining tenants
were sent a form through the post. A small number of telephone

Low satisfaction was also reported with
maintenance of communal areas.  Works streams to address each

The overall satisfaction score is 72%, an

A summary of the report will be uploaded to

Issuing Electrical
Installation Condition Reports (EICRs) to Tenants
 
The Head of Housing Compliance gave an outline
of the report Issuing Electrical Installation Condition Reports
(EICRs) to Tenants.
 
This report provides an update on the
Council’s arrangements for issuing Electrical Installation
Condition Reports – or EICRs – to tenants, following
the extension of the Electrical Safety Standards in the Private
Rented Sector (England) Regulations 2020 to the social rented
sector in 2025.
 
By way of context, these Regulations require
landlords to:

Inspect and test electrical
installations at least every five years
Obtain a valid EICR following each
inspection
Complete any C1, C2, or further
investigation works within statutory timescales
And crucially, provide a copy of the
EICR to tenants within 28 days of inspection, or before occupation
for new tenancies.

 
For social landlords, these duties apply:

From 1 November 2025 for new
tenancies
From 1 May 2026 for existing
tenancies

 
This brings the social rented sector fully in
line with the private rented sector.
 
The Council already undertakes five-yearly
EICR inspections across the housing stock.
 

For new tenancies, copies of valid
EICRs are already issued at sign-up.
We are therefore compliant with the
current legal framework.

 
Historically, the council  did not routinely issue EICRs to tenants in
existing tenancies, as this was not previously a statutory
requirement. To meet the new requirements, we are strengthening
processes in three key areas:
 

Updated procedures – A formal
operating procedure will be in place to ensure EICRs are issued
within 28 days of inspection and prior to occupation for new
tenants.
System integration and automation
– We are working with our contractor and our asset management
system, NEC, to enable electronic and, where required, postal
distribution of EICRs with automated tracking and clear audit
trails.
Monitoring and audit – Regular
internal monitoring will track issue dates and evidence of
distribution, ensuring we can demonstrate compliance to regulators
and auditors.
topline: The Council has decided to strengthen processes for issuing Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICRs) to tenants in the social rented sector.

further afield.
 
An engagement had been undertaken at the Fire
Walk at White Lodge where sponsored volunteers had crossed burning
coals.  Their efforts had raised over
£8500 for the centre on the night.
 
Two stage performances had been attended
the  Wizard
of Oz, staged at Magna Carta School and the Pond Grainger
Performing Arts show, Dance from the
Heart and she was pleased to announce that the latter had offered
to stage a fund-raising evening for her chosen charities on Friday
27th March at The Fleming Theatre, TASIS,
Thorpe.  In relation to fundraising
activities, she also asked that councillors ‘save the
date’ of 15th May 2026, with an announcement
expected shortly of an exciting event.
 
St John’s Church Egham had recently
licenced The Reverend Lydia Corbett as vicar and the Mayor had spoken at her first service to welcome
her.
 
A visit had been undertaken to Rivermede Care home in Egham to listen to speaker,
Louis Alexander who the Mayor described
as inspirational.  In his early
twenties, Mr Alexander had already run marathons in 5 continents
and swum across 5 oceans and he held a
World Record. Mr Alexander’s inspiration was his grandfather,
who had a distinguished army career, but suffered from dementia in
later life and his aim in his endeavours was to raise money for
dementia care and research, a cause for which he had already raised
many thousands of pounds.
 
Finally, the Mayor related her latest
engagement, at Woking Football Club, where the Mayor of Woking has
held a fund-raising event.

content:
The Corporate Management Committee received a
report which sought agreement to proposals to Council on the
adoption of a Members’ Allowances Scheme for the 2026/27
financial year
 
Mario Leo, Corporate Head of Law and
Governance presented the report and explained the legal landscape
within which this decision was sought, the options available to
Councillors and any associated issues and costs of each option.
Members heard that implementing the provisions
if the 25/26 scheme for 26/27 would equate to a
‘freeze’ on the allowance received.
 
It was proposed by Councillor R. King that the
recommendations in the report be approved and seconded by
Councillor L. Gillham 
 
Members of the Committee welcomed the
opportunity to limit resource requirements for the last 10 months
of the Councils life and suggested that it was an opportunity to
reflect their commitment to public service.  Members who
might experience difficulties as a result of the
‘freeze’ would be encouraged to inform their Group
Leader.
 
Members noted that the difficulties in
establishing an IRP, detailed within the report, potentially
highlighted a system wide issue.
 
It was RESOLVED that it be recommended to Full
Council that:
 

(i)      The 2025/26 Members’
Allowances Scheme be withdrawn with an end date of 31 March 2026
inclusive.

(ii)     That the provisions of the
current Members’ Allowances Scheme be agreed for 2026/27 with
an implementation date of 1 April 2026 inclusive.

(iii)     That the Corporate Head of Law
and Governance be delegated authority to implement the 2026/27
Members’ Allowances Scheme to give effect to the above and
undertake any necessary measures to do so (such as advertising it
in a local newspaper, authorising the recovery of payments made,
etc).
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the adoption of a Members' Allowances Scheme for the 2026/27 financial year.

content:
The Committee received a report setting out
results for Quarter 3 2025/26 against the Corporate Key Performance
Indicator Set intended to provide Members with a snapshot of
performance across key areas of business in
order to act as a general ‘health check’ and
provide an ‘early-warning’ mechanism for action to be
taken where need was identified.
 
Sarah Hall (SH) Head of Business Planning,
Projects and Performance, introduced the report for the benefit of
the Committee.  She referred to the
thresholds for categorisation as ‘red’
‘amber’ or ‘green’ and detailed the numbers
of indicators reported in each category, being 6, 6 and 17
respectively.
 
SH also provided an account of each
‘red’ indicator as follows:
 

·      
H1: Proportion of non-emergency repairs completed within target
timescale – delays largely related to sub-contractor capacity
and the use of alternative providers, where possible, was improving
performance.

·      
H2: Average number of calendar days to re-let a void property -
still reported outside of target but showing a positive direction
of travel and significantly improved from quarter 2.

·      
H6: Proportion of homes that do not meet the Decent Homes Standard
– work in progress but not complete meant that the target was
on track to report as ‘green’ by year end.

·      
H7: Proportion of homes for which all required gas safety checks
have been carried out – the target was 100% and currently 2
houses were non-compliant.  One was
scheduled to be certified shortly but the other was subject to
access issues being resolved.

·      
ES4: Number of street cleansing reports – improvements had
been achieved despite still reporting outside of target, in
addition a number of reports received in
quarter 3 were seasonal in nature, relating to leaves in gutters
and drains.

·      
AR2: fire risk recommendations on operational sites outstanding
– work underway to replace fire alarm system at the Civic
centre. Current system fully operational.
 
The Chair thanks SH and opened the item for
questions and comments.
 
The committee welcomed the positive overall
performance and the direction of travel described by SH.
 
In relation to street cleansing the committee
heard that improvements to data collection were to be introduced to
eliminate multiple reporting from the data and improve the
council’s ability to identify trends and local
need.  Finally, it was reported that the
Environment and Sustainability Committee would consider the street
cleansing matters agreed as part of the budget considerations, in
due course.   
 
There were no further comments or questions
and the report being for information only the item was
concluded.
topline: The council has decided to approve recommendations based on positive performance indicators for Quarter 3 2025/26.

The Corporate Management Committee received a
report which, following the Stage 2 consultation on the Community
Governance Review for the Englefield Green Neighbourhood Village,
presented the final recommendations for the establishment of a
parish council for Englefield Green for consideration and agreement
to recommend to Council.
 
Kath Richards (KR), Electoral Services
Manager, presented the report for the benefit of members and set
the recommendations in context, describing the work undertaken to
date.
 
Councillor R King proposed the recommendations
set out in the report and Councillor P. Gahir seconded
 
The committee heard a message of thanks from
residents to KR and her team and to the councillors for their
support to date.  Committee members agreed that getting
to this stage was a positive achievement and welcomed the focus on
local democracy that it would allow.
 
Following a question from a committee member
it was confirmed by the Corporate Head of Law and Governance that
the recommendations before the committee would not impact on the
Green and the lease arrangements with the Crown associated with
it.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
 It was RESOLVED that it be recommended
to Full Council:
 

(i)      to approve
the Final Recommendations as set out in Appendix A to the report,
in accordance with the provisions of Local Government and Public
Involvement in Health Act 2007.

(ii)     to request officers to formulate
an appropriate budget for the proposed parish council for the
financial year 2027-2028.

(iii)     to request officers to clarify
the position as to which allotments situated in the area falling
within the area of the proposed parish council would transfer to
the proposed parish council and under what legal provisions.

(iv)    to report back to Full Council at a
future date to seek authority to make recommendations to the
proposed West Surrey Shadow Authority in respect of making an Order
under the provisions of the Local Government and Public Involvement
in Health Act 2007 for the creation of the new parish council.
topline: The Corporate Management Committee has decided to recommend the establishment of a parish council for Englefield Green following a Community Governance Review.

content:
The Committee received a report for
information, the purpose of which was to provide an opportunity to
for members to review and scrutinise treasury management policy and
activities.
 
In line with the responsibilities of the
Corporate Management Committee delegated from Council, the report
reflected on the Council’s treasury management activity and
performance during the year to 31 December 2025 focusing on
financing, liquidity, cash and risk management. The report also
reflected on the review of the Council’s treasury and
investment strategies, along with prudential indicators, and
compliance with the limits set for 2025/26.
 
Paul French (PF) Corporate Head of Finance
presented the report.  He noted that
members would be familiar with the regular quarterly report format
and referred to the council’s borrowing position as set out
therein.  He reported that
£302,000 had been repaid against the council’s annuity
loan and the investment portfolio had returned an average interest
rate of 4.28%, well in line with the treasury benchmark set out in
report. Although interest rates were falling and this would impact
performance it would be, to some extent, offset by some good
short-term investment rates secured with local authorities.
 
Finally he referred members to the investment
total which ended the quarter at £84m, an increase fo
£13m on the previous quarter which was mainly due to
collection of council tax receipts not yet due to be paid to the
council preceptors until quarter 4 which would reduce the total at
that time. 
 
A full list of borrowing and investment was
set out in appendix A to the report.
 
PF concluded by assuring members that the
council had operated with the Treasury Management strategies and
reported that a ‘substantial’ internal audit opinion
had recently been received. 
 
The Chair and committee thanked PF for the
report and being for information only the item was concluded.
topline: The Council has decided to review and approve recommendations for its treasury management policy and activities.

content:
The Committee received a report setting out
the quarterly monitoring information for Q3 2025/26 as set out in
both the Asset Management and the Capital and Investment
Strategies. 
 
Alex Williams, Corporate Head of Asset
Management and Regeneration introduced the report.  She highlighted key messages from the report that
described how the Assets and Regeneration Team managed the
council’s property portfolio, mitigating risk appropriately
while strengthening income and long term value through a strategy
of proactive management as opposed to passive ownership.
 
AW reminded members of recent regearing
reports considered by the Committee and reported on recent
successful auctions that would be reflected in the next update
 
She drew the attention of members to some to
KPI 002 relating to rent arrears and explained the reason for a
spike in arrears for quarter 3 which related to the rent due date
falling on 25th December when many businesses were
closed.  The council, unlike many other
landlords, did not currently have a short period of grace before
rent due was classed as ‘in arrears’ but she said that
in the future this would be applied in order that members received
‘true’ representations through the data reported.
 
Finally, AW referred members to the section of
the report relating to the benchmarking tool ‘MSCI’
which the council utilised to check performance against the UK
wider market.  She reported that during
the most recent review of the MSCI data, an anomaly was identified
in the information used to calculate the portfolio’s total
return. Once the anomaly was removed, the portfolio’s total
return was restated at 7.9%, compared with the MSCI benchmark of
6.5%. While this represents a lower level of outperformance than
previously reported, the portfolio continued to outperform the
benchmark overall and following the correction, the
portfolio’s net operating income growth increased from 1.77%
to 2.1%, providing further assurance of the underlying strength and
resilience of the Council’s income performance.
 
The Chair thanked AW and opened the matter for
comments and questions.  No such
comments or questions being received and the report being for
information, the item was concluded.
topline: The council has decided to approve recommendations based on the quarterly monitoring report for asset management and investment strategies.
