content:
The committee received a report seeking
approval of the Corporate Key Performance Indicator Set or
2026/27.
 
Sarah Hall (SH) Head of Business Planning,
Projects and Performance introduced the report and highlighted the
following changes from the current set for 25/26:
 

·      
The full set had been increased from a total of 43 indicators to 45
indicators.

·      
Three indicators from the 25/26 set had been removed relating
to:
o  
C4: Percentage of community alarms equipment upgraded to digital
solution – proposed for removal as the project had been
completed.
o  
H3: Satisfaction with the overall reactive repairs service received
(% of total number of responses returned) – proposed for
removal as new wider and more strategic measures were proposed.
o  
H10: Anti-social behaviour cases opened (including hate incidents)
relative to the number of social housing dwellings - cumulative
result – proposed for removal. This information would
continue to be reported to Housing Committee as it was a regulatory
requirement for it to be collected but was
considered to be operational in nature and therefore better
reported in that way.

·      
Several new indicators were proposed as follows:
o  
Community Services - C4: The number of completed referrals to the
HIA resulting in completion of works or another agreed outcome with
resident.
o  
Housing Services - Two new CKPIs (Replacing H3 and H10) are
proposed to be added from Housing.
§ 
(new) H3: Proportion of significant damp and mould hazards
investigated within 10 working days; is a new statutory requirement
under Awaabs law and a high-profile
issue.
§ 
(new) H10: Proportion of homes for which all required fire risk
assessments have been carried out by date due; is a compliance
indicator,
o  
Assets and Regeneration - Two new CKPIs (AR4 and AR6) were proposed
to measure building compliance of operational assets managed by
Assets and Regeneration.
SH also drew out some of those indicators that
would be amended for 2026/27 including:
o  
The proposed move to annual reporting for the proportion of homes
that did not meet the Decent Homes Standard to ensure steady
reporting and align with regulator reporting requirements
o  
Annual reporting of recycling indicators in
order to reflect seasonal variations in the wider context of
recycling throughout the year.
o  
A change to the description of H9 outstanding high risk Fire Risk
Assessment actions; ‘overdue’ high-risk Fire Risk
Assessment actions to allow for the distinction between outstanding
and overdue in relation to statutory compliance to be properly
reflected.
o  
Amendments to ES4 to focus on litter bin reports (as opposed to
general detritus) to improve the accuracy and reliability of
data.

 
Finally, SH confirmed that the new Corporate
Key Performance Indicator Set would be in place from 1 April 2026
if approved.
 
Councillor R. King proposed the
recommendations within the report be approved. The motion was
seconded by Councillor L. Gillham.
 
The committee considered the
report.  Following comments and
questions received from Committee members SH confirmed that reports
of graffiti were not currently reported as part of the Corporate
KPI set for 2025/26 but that reporting
was recorded and could be reported to the appropriate service
committee.  It was agreed that this
would be desirable.
 
It was RESOLVED that
 
i)         
the proposed 2026/27 Corporate Performance Indicators descriptions
as shown in Appendix A of the report be APPROVED;
ii)         the
proposed 2026/27 quarterly/annual targets be APPROVED
iii)        data collected on
reports of graffiti be reported to the appropriate service
committee during 2026/27.
topline: The UK council has decided to approve the Corporate Key Performance Indicator Set for 2026/27, with updated and new indicators for performance measurement.

The Committee was advised that the report was
to update Members on recent public consultation regarding the
proposed introduction of a recreational parking tariff at a number

The Council had received a series of formal
representations, the majority of which related to Abbeyfields,
together with an objection concerning Englefield Green.  Subsequent enquiries confirmed that Abbeyfields
was situated on land held in trust for charitable purposes and was
therefore not owned by the Council.  In
the case of Englefield Green, the Crown Estate had advised that it
was unable to grant consent for the implementation of parking
charges or associated infrastructure due to the site’s Town
and Village Green status.
 
Therefore, Officers advised the Committee that
in light of these legal and land-ownership contraints, alongside the concerns
raised through the consultation, Officers recommended that both
Abbeyfields and Englefield Green should be excluded from the
recreational charging scheme and from inclusion within the
Council’s Off-Street Parking Orders with effect from 1 April
2026.
 
The Committee fully supported the Officers
recommendation.
 
 
Resolved that:
 
Abbeyfields and Englefield Green car parks be
excluded from the recreational charging scheme and inclusion in the
Council’s Off-Street Parking Orders; and
 
The draft order to take effect from 1 April
2026

content:
The Committee received a report which provided
a mid-year update on delivery of the Environmental Services Service
Plan for 2025/26 and sought approval for the proposed Service Area
Plan for 2026/27.
 
The proposed 2026/27 plan had been developed
in the context of significant organisational change as the Council
prepared for Local Government Reorganisation and the creation of a
new West Surrey Unitary Authority from April 2027.  The service was, therefore, focused on both
sustaining high-quality delivery for Runnymede residents now and
ensure a smooth transition and strong legacy.
 
For the current year plan there were now 23
activities in scope, 8 of which had been completed, 1 due to be
completed by end of March, and 5 continuing into 2026/27
A further 8 activities had been archived due
to the impacts of Local Government Reorganisation.
 
Work already completed included delivery of
the Air Quality Plan, the roll-out of food waste collection
capability for flats, completion of the borough-wide tree audit, a
programme of bridge inspections, a pumping station and fleet
review.
 
Key ongoing areas of work into 2026/27
included the bus shelter infrastructure replacement programme,
refurbishment of the Chertsey Depot, delivery of the Memorial
Testing programme and delivery of the HIT project in Green
Spaces
 
Additionally, strong environmental benefits
had already been realised this year by enhanced data from the tree
audit, expansion of food waste recycling, progress on air quality
communications and increased electrification of the fleet.
 
Members thanked Officers for all the good work
done across the department, particularly noting that the bus
shelter replacements and closed topped bins had been positively
received by residents.
 
With regards to the public toilet review, the
Committee was advised that specific work was underway, this work
would initially identify and trial appropriate products that would
be less susceptible to vandalism.
 
The bin replacement programme was ongoing with
the 1st tranche being the replacement of high street
bins, replacement of bins in the Borough’s parks would
follow.
 
 
 
 
Resolved that:
 
The proposed 2026/27 Service Area Plan and
Mission Statement be approved.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the proposed Service Area Plan for 2026/27 for Environmental Services in Runnymede.

content:
The Committee was asked to review a report
which sought their approval to optimise the route across the DSO
collection rounds.
 
Runnymede’s in-house refuse, recycling,
food and garden waste collections operated across 40,700 dwellings
and 34,380 collection points.  There had
been significant dwelling growth in the borough in recent
years.  To date this dwelling growth had
been absorbed into existing rounds, however, this was causing some
rounds to be excessively long.  The last
major reroute was done in 2018 when the Bartec system was
introduced.  When the Bartec contract
was renewed in 2025 the route optimisation software had been
procured at the same time.
 
Currently, crews on several rounds regularly
exceeded the 7 ½ hours duty time.  In addition, they missed the statutory 20-minute
breaks which put the Council at risk of non-compliance with the
Working Time Regulations. 
 
The Committee was asked to consider 3 options
which had been tested using Bartec data.
 
Model 1 – Do nothing
Model 2 – Optimise Existing Rounds
Model 3 – Full Redesign including Day changes
 
The Committee was advised that Option 1 was
not feasible as this option would not alleviate the current
practices.   Option 3 would give
significant disruption to residents, increase customer service and
depot workload, require additional staff and have no significant
CO2 impact, as the fleet would remain unchanged.
 
Officers, therefore, advised the Committee
that Option 2 was the preferred option. 
Option 2 would cause minimal resident disruption, would balance
workloads across a two-week cycle, remove the need for an agency
loader every other Thursday and provide some capacity for
growth.
 
Officers were thanked for the report and
Members expressed their thanks to the team for covering the
significant increase in workload.

It was noted that equal treatment of staff was
important and would make working for us more attractive going
forward.
 
 
Resolved that:
 
Option 2 detailed in the report be
approved
topline: The Council has decided to approve route optimisation for refuse, recycling, food, and garden waste collections to address excessive duty times and non-compliance risks.

content:
The Committee was advised that the Tree
Management plan outlined how Runnymede managed the risks associated
with its tree stock.  The plan was
supplemented by the Tree Management policy for Housing which had
been approved in 2002 along with any subsequent updates to that
policy.
 
The management plan only applied to Council
managed land and did not include Highways which currently fell,
until LGR under SCC.  The plan explained
how records were kept, how inspections were prioritised and how
works were commissioned.

Tree data was managed using Ezytreev tree
management software.  This month the
first full audit of the Council’s entire tree stock would be
completed.  From an initial estimate of
30,000 trees, 225,000 trees and tree groups had been plotted on
Exytreev.
 
Tree maintenance works would be carried out by
either,  In-house Officers supported by
the grounds maintenance team for ground-based work and Contractors
for complex works or works at height.   This combination ensured both planned and
emergency tree works could be delivered.
 
There were 3 types of inspection:
 
Level 1 – basic tree inspection, which
enabled someone to recognise and report
               
a defect to a professional Arboricultural Officer for further
inspection
Level 2 -  Visual
tree inspection VTA
Level 3 -  Detailed
tree inspection
 
98% of inspections were VTA’s.
 
Every inspection was logged on Ezytreev, which
automatically amended (if necessary) the risk status of a tree, and
specified when the next inspection should take place.  Works were carried out in descending order of
priority as set by Ezytreez.
 
The Committee was pleased to note the tree
audit was coming to a conclusion and that concurrent remedial work
had been undertaken. 
 
 
Resolved that:
 
The tree risk management plan at Appendix A be
approved.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the Tree Risk Management Plan for managing and maintaining its tree stock.

content:
Councillor J. Hulley had submitted a motion in
accordance with Standing Order 15 which had been published with the
agenda for the meeting. 
 
Councillor J Hulley spoke to the motion and
reported that following liaison with Co-Leader Councillor R King a
‘friendly amendment’ to the motion tabled had been
agreed which he would speak to and which Councillor R King would
second.
 
The motion sought to support Neighbourhood
plans, which he said had long been one of the most meaningful ways
to shape the area in which a person lived, forming part of the
statutory framework around planning for local areas.
 
Neighbourhood Plans, he contended, faced an
uncertain future and it was his belief that proposed reforms to the
wider planning system, alongside uncertainty regarding the future
funding of neighbourhood planning, risked weakening the voice of
local communities by making Neighbourhood Plans less effective and
this should be resisted.
 
Councillor J Hulley proposed the motion as
amended.
 
Councillor R. King spoke to the amended
motion.  He thanked Councillor Hulley
for his contribution and for accepting, in particular, the
inclusion of the term ‘character’ in the motion as this
was, he believed, what local people wanted to protect.  He did believe there was a role for certain
targets in planning, but that local involvement was critical.
 
He spoke of the current government and planned
proposals for planning reform and did not believe that there were
plans to end neighbourhood planning as part of this but he did
agree that there was an opportunity to show support for those
smaller areas where finance could be a barrier to developing key
local aspects of a community.
 
Councillor R King seconded the motion as
amended.
 
Councillors considered the amended motion and
showed support for neighbourhood plans, siting examples form areas
within the borough where plans had been produced and acknowledging
the risk that finances could pose to the production of additional
plans in the future.
 
Runnymede Borough
Council acknowledges that:


a)            
Neighbourhood planning can empower local communities to shape
development, character and growth of their areas through the
creation of Neighbourhood Plans.

b)            
The preparation of Neighbourhood Plans require significant time,
expertise, and financial resources, with the associate set-up and
support costs that can present barriers for neighbourhood forums,
community groups and smaller parish councils or those with limited
precept income  

c)             
Neighbourhood Plans contribute to more democratic, locally informed
planning decisions and support the delivery of sustainable
development aligned with community needs and aspirations.
 
 Therefore, this Council resolves to:
 

1.         
Call upon His Majesty’s Government, as part of a future
Spending Review, to consider reintroducing targeted
“seed” funding to support the development of
Neighbourhood Plans for neighbourhood groups and parish councils
with insufficient precepts to cover the costs of plan
preparation


2.         
Write directly to Matthew Pennycook, Minister of State for Housing
and Planning to communicate this resolution of this council and
recognise that Neighbourhood planning can empower local communities
to shape the development, character and growth of their areas, and
seek guidance on the timeline within which this funding could be
considered, the process for submitting any evidence or support for
a specific funding request, and the role local political
representatives, councillors and our two local MP’s could
play in making the case for this funding.
 
The motion was carried, and
 
Resolved that:
 

1.         His
Majesty’s Government be called upon, as part of a future
Spending Review, to consider reintroducing targeted
“seed” funding to support the development of
Neighbourhood Plans for neighbourhood groups and parish councils
with insufficient precepts to cover the costs of plan
preparation
 

2.         Matthew
Pennycook, Minister of State for Housing and Planning be written to
directly, to communicate this resolution of this council and
recognise that Neighbourhood planning can empower local communities
to shape the development, character and growth of their areas, and
seek guidance on the timeline within which this funding could be
considered, the process for submitting any evidence or support for
a specific funding request, and the role local political
representatives, councillors and our two local MP’s could
play in making the case for this funding.
topline: The Runnymede Borough Council has decided to support Neighbourhood Plans to empower local communities and shape sustainable development.

content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine
whether the Hackney Carriage Driver named in the report was still
deemed to be ‘fit and proper’ to hold a licence,
following an alleged incident at a local entertainment venue in the
borough.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer, assisted by the
Council’s Taxi Licensing Officer, were invited to present
their report.
 
Members learned that the driver was first
licensed in Runnymede in 2011 and had a combined licence for both
Hackney Carriage and Private Hire vehicles.  The driver had four previous complaints on record
which had been addressed by Officers under delegated
authority.  Of these, two incidents
regarded ‘attitude of driver’, the most recent was
recorded in March 2015 which resulted in a written warning.
 
Members were appraised of the events and the
alleged behaviour of the driver on 18 October 2025, which the
Senior Operations Manager at the venue had reported to the
authority the day after on 19 October 2025.
 
Members reviewed the statements made by the
staff and the driver, and as the driver was present at the meeting,
there was an opportunity for Members to ask them questions, and for
the driver to do the same.  However,
there were no representatives present from the venue which had
lodged the complaint, so the Sub-Committee relied on the written
evidence before them to consider the matter.
 
The driver queried whether there was any CCTV
footage provided by the venue.  Officers
confirmed there was.  However, it was
not of any evidential standard on which to rely, as it was taken
from a distance and with no audio.  The
driver disputed the time stated that they remained at the venue,
again the CCTV footage finished at about 20 minutes so could not be
evidenced either way.  The driver also
commented on the length of time between the alleged incident and
when they were called in for interview. 
Officers apologised for the delay which was in part due to the
length of time to receive statements from the venue.
 
The driver was invited to state their case,
and this was duly noted.  The driver emphasised that they were professional
and had acted in a respectful manner.
 
The driver was asked whether their perceived
behaviour was an over-reaction borne from the upset of the
situation and whether they had been agitated.
 
The driver confirmed that there was some
confusion over the apparently changed policy for parking at the
venue which put prospective customers at some distance from the
location to which drivers were directed to ply for
hire.  The driver had found this
frustrating because in order to attract
customers they needed to be in a prominent position in the car
park.  The driver had attempted to
explain this to the staff in question but with no result.
 
Each party was invited to make a closing
statement, which was duly noted.
 
The Sub-Committee was adjourned at 12 noon
in order to determine the case in
private session.
 
Members were directed towards the relevant
sections of the Council’s Hackney Carriage and Private Hire
Licensing Policy, in particular the
paramount importance of public safety. 
Members also took into account the Institute of Licensing
‘Suitability Guidance’, the Local Government
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1976, other legal implications and
reviewed their options which could be exercised under the
aforementioned Act.
 
The Sub-Committee reconvened at 12:25.
 
The Sub-Committee’s decision was that
based on the evidence, and the balance of probability, an incident
had occurred to justify that the driver should be issued with a
written warning in respect of their behaviour.  The Sub-Committee considered that the
driver’s behaviour had fallen below that expected of a
Hackney Carriage Driver.  The fact that
they had exited their vehicle to move barriers,
and spoken to staff in the manner alleged crossed the
boundary of acceptable behaviour.
 
The Sub-Committee did appreciate that the
driver was frustrated and deserved to earn their living which could
have influenced their conduct.  However,
this was outweighed by the unacceptable actions taken and lack of
appropriate professional behaviour.
 
Resolved that
–
 
in respect of the
driver in question, informal action be taken, in the form of a
written warning to be issued for the reasons provided verbally to
the driver at the meeting
topline: The Council's Sub-Committee has decided to issue a written warning to a Hackney Carriage Driver following an alleged incident at a local entertainment venue.

content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine
whether the Hackney Carriage Driver named in the report was still
deemed to be ‘fit and proper’ to hold a licence,
following an alleged incident at a local entertainment venue in the
borough.
 
The Senior Licensing Officer was invited to
present their report.
 
The Sub-Committee was informed that the driver
was first licensed as a Private Hire Driver in 2011, and became a combined Hackney Carriage and
Private Hire Driver in 2013.  Members
were appraised of the history of ‘issues’ of concern
going back to December 2014.  Seven of
the eight recorded incidents involved the driver’s behaviour,
the most recent being in February 2025, for which a written warning
was issued.
 
Members were advised of the events and the
alleged behaviour of the driver on 18 October 2025.  The Senior Operations Manager at the venue
reported the alleged incident to the Licensing Team on 19 October
2025, which Officers then investigated. 
This included obtaining witness statements from three members of
staff at the venue and interviewing the driver.
 
Members reviewed the statements made by the
staff and the driver.  However, as the
driver nor representatives of the venue were present at the
meeting, there was no opportunity for Members to ask them
questions.  The Sub-Committee relied on
the written evidence before them to consider the
matter.  Members’ attention was
drawn to the statements made in the Driver’s interview under
caution and the email explaining why they could not attend the
meeting, due to ill health.
 
The Sub-Committee determined the case in
private session.
 
Members were directed towards the relevant
sections of the Council’s Hackney Carriage and Private Hire
Licensing Policy, in particular the
paramount importance of public safety.  Members also took into
account the Institute of Licensing ‘Suitability
Guidance’, the Local Government (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Act 1976, other legal implications and reviewed their options which
could be exercised under the aforementioned
Act.
  
The Sub-Committee’s decision was that
based on the evidence, and the balance of probability, a serious
incident had occurred to justify that the driver should be
suspended until such time as they had completed and provided
written evidence of attendance of a specific course on ‘Taxi
Driver Proficiency’ to be delivered by The Blue Lamp
Trust.
 
The Sub-Committee considered that the
driver’s behaviour had fallen significantly below that
expected of a Hackney Carriage Driver and that they did have a
history of such behaviour. 
 
Members were also concerned about the impact
of the driver’s behaviour on the staff at the
venue.  This was considered intimidating, and had caused distress and
anxiety.  The fact that the driver had
physically moved barriers, disregarded instructions, and spoken to
staff in the manner alleged, and allegedly driven at speed in the
car park, was unacceptable behaviour.
 
In serving the suspension, the driver would be
advised of their right of appeal and confirmation that the
suspension would take effect at the end of the period of 21 days
beginning with the day on which the notice was given.
 
Resolved that
–
 
in respect of the
driver in question, their Hackney Carriage Driver’s Licence
be suspended until such time as the driver could provide written
confirmation of attendance of a specific course on ‘Taxi
Driver Proficiency’ to be delivered by The Blue Lamp
Trust.
topline: The Sub-Committee has decided to suspend a Hackney Carriage Driver's Licence following an alleged incident at a local entertainment venue.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
make a recommendation to full Council in respect of the
Council’s Risk Appetite Statement for 2026/27.
 
Members were asked to note that following
consultation with all of the Council’s Corporate Heads and
Corporate Leadership Team it was agreed that the broad Risk
Appetite Statement and each of the principal risk categories should
remain unchanged from 2025/26.  Members
concurred with this view.
 
Officers considered that no significant change
had occurred to justify an alteration to the risk appetite
positions which accompanied the Council’s overarching Risk
Appetite Statement, as set out below:
 
“Risk Management is a continuously
evolving process, whereby the Council constantly seeks to refine
and improve process, in order to support the delivery of its
objectives and take a proportionate approach to risk. Identifying
its risk appetite enables the Council to take a balanced approach
in respect of risk by understanding the risk levels it may
tolerate, and therefore target its scarce resources at the
management of risks that cannot be tolerated. Effective risk
management supports informed decision-making through the
determination of the nature and extent of the principal risk
exposure of the Council and how much risk it is capable of
absorbing to achieve its objectives.
 
It is often not possible to manage all risk to
the most desirable level, but the setting of risk appetites means
that risks can be managed to a tolerable level.
 
In addition to having an overarching risk
appetite statement, the Council has developed statements to
describe its attitude to accepting risk in each of its principal
risk categories; recognising that risk appetite is not a single,
fixed concept but that there will be a range of appetites for
different risks and that these appetites may well vary over
time.”
 
With the approach of Local Government
Re-organisation, Members agreed that the statement was more
relevant than ever.
 
Officers advised that in delivering its new
Corporate Business Plan 2026/27 the Council was not proposing to
take on any new functions which might encompass risks falling
outside of these categories. While it would be participating in the
implementation programme for LGR, the existing risk categories
could appropriately accommodate the classification of risks
relating to this work. Governance, Legal, People, Technology,
Information, Security and Programme risks categories would all be
appropriate in this sphere.
 
Members reviewed each of the risk categories
and agreed that the following risk categories had been classed as
‘cautious’: Strategy, Governance, Legal, Property
Compliance, Risks arising from investment property holdings,
financial, commercial, Data and Information Management,
Security, Project/Programme, and Reputational and the remaining as
‘open’: Operations, People, and Technology.
 
The Committee agreed with the Officer’s
recommendation that principal risk categories should remain
unchanged from 2025/26.  Their rationale
was in essence that retaining those risks as ‘cautious’
was prudent whilst allowing for innovation in those risks that were
‘open.’
 
Recommend that
–
 
the overarching Risk
Appetite Statement for 2026/27, and the supporting risk appetite
level for each of the Council’s principal risk categories, as
set out in Appendix A to the Officer’s report, be approved
for recommendation to full Council
topline: The Council has decided to approve the Risk Appetite Statement for 2026/27.

content:
The Committee was asked to approve the
Council’s audited Statement Of
Accounts for 2024-25 as set out in the Appendix to the
Officer’s report.
 
Members recalled that the Accounts provided an
overview of the Council’s financial position, performance,
and cash flows over a specific period in a prescribed format, and were reminded that they had been
published on the Council’s website on 30 June, in accordance
with the statutory deadline.
 
Officers advised that the Statement of
Accounts used the same data as reported to the Corporate Management
Committee in the Provisional Outturn report in July
2025. 
 
It was noted that the difference between them
was purely the technical presentation and the requirement to add
transactions to conform to international accounting standards
(which were then reversed back out through the Movement in Reserves
Statement). 
 
Officers reported that there were no major
changes to the Council’s figures or assumptions made in that
July report.
 
Officers highlighted the two main changes to
the 2024-25 accounts, from the previous years accounts approved
by the Committee in May 2025.
 
The first relatesd
to the introduction of IFRS16 on leases.   This had been the subject of various
committee reports, including to the Standards and Audit Committee
when it adopted the Accounting Policies for 2024/25 in March last
year, which were changed to ensure the accounts were prepared in
accordance with the new regulations.
 
The second item which was drawn to the
Committee’s attention was the change in the Council’s
pension liability. 
 
Officers explained that under Accounting
Standards, when a pension benefit obligation became an asset, the
amount that could be recognised in the accounts was restricted to a
pension asset ceiling.  This recognised
that any asset arising at the date of the balance sheet would most
likely lead to a refund to the employer, or reduced contributions
in the future.
 
The Committee was advised that at the balance
sheet date, the value of the Council’s share of the pension
fund assets stood at £140m, with liabilities of £115m.
This left the Council with a net pension fund asset of
£25m.  The Council’s
actuary, Hymans Robertson, carried out the necessary calculations
to determine what the pension asset ceiling amounted to and,
allowing for the credit ceiling adjustment, this left the fund with
a net liability of £2.7m. 
 
Members were referred to further detail set
out in the Narrative statement and notes to the accounts.
 
Officers confirmed that during the audit, two
minor adjustments were made to the notes in the draft accounts, and
these were set out in the audit findings report elsewhere on the
agenda.  Members were assured that these
adjustments did not have any effect on the bottom lines of the main
statements.
 
The Committee appreciated that not having been
fully audited for over five years, the depth and rigour of current
audit requirements and requests necessitated a realignment of
practices and the Council’s approach over time, working
collaboratively with Colleagues in Grant Thornton.
 
Members were also directed to the content of
the Management Letter of Representation as set out in Appendix B to
the Officer’s report. 
 
Officers agreed to amend the reference from
‘Chairmen’ to ‘Chairs’ under the
‘Useful Information’ section of the accounts.
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
the Statement of Accounts for 2024/25 be approved, noting that the
Statement of Accounts will be disclaimed; and

 

ii)         the
Management Letter of Representation be noted
topline: The Council has decided to approve the audited Statement of Accounts for 2024-25.

content:
The Committee was presented with the 2024/25
audit findings report prepared by the Council’s external
auditors, Grant Thornton.
 
Officers reported there had been some delays
in the receipt of some supporting evidence and transaction listings
within the agreed timeframe which had restricted Grant
Thornton’s ability to perform certain substantive
testing.  This was in the area of
employee benefit expenditure, other service expenditure and support
service recharge balances and was attributable to an aging ledger
system which the Council was due to replace shortly, meaning that
Officers were unable to produce the data requested in the required
format.
 
With regard to the Value for Money assessment,
and based on interim work undertaken, Grant Thornton was satisfied
that the Council had made proper arrangements for securing economy,
efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.
 
The Committee reviewed key findings, including
a detailed action plan which contained a number of
recommendations.
 
The Management response to each recommendation
was noted, and it was anticipated that although some of the issues
would still be present for the 2025/26 audit, now that Officers
understood some of the requirements, great strides could be made in
addressing the auditors’ concerns.  It was also hoped that the new Financial
Management System would be of significant assistance.
 
The Committee noted the core audit fees of
£216,293 and additional work related to the IFRS 16 amounting
£5,500, the latter being subject to approval from the
PSAA.
 
Overall, Members were assured that significant
work could be undertaken for the 2025/26 audit and in the required
format.
 
Officers from Grant Thornton were asked to
amend the typo under ‘Other findings’ with regard to
the Valuation of land and buildings as at 31 March 2025.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for improvement based on the 2024/25 audit findings report.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought for
the Local Code of Corporate Governance for 2026/27 to be
recommended to the Corporate Management Committee.
 
It was noted that the Code of Corporate
Governance was based on seven core principles, supported by
documents such as the Code of Conduct, Financial
Regulations.  These were in place to
allow the Council to achieve its intended outcomes while acting in
the public interest at all times.
 
Officers advised that no changes to the
previous Code of Corporate Governance were proposed because it
still reflected the governance systems currently in place and the
various policies and strategies.
 
It was agreed that although Local Government
Re-organisation was a major development and its impact would be
significant, Runnymede Borough Council would cease to exist on 31
March 2027, so there would be no need for a code to be adopted in
2027.
 
Members were content to recommend the Local
Code of Corporate Governance for 2026/27 accordingly, with the
assurance provided that the various links in the Code would be
checked and updated prior to submission to the Corporate Management
Committee.
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that –
 
the Local Code of
Corporate Governance for the period 2026/27 be approved, and
recommended to full Council for adoption

enable the replacement of the balcony panels along with replacement

measure and replaced with temporary timber boarding.  A suitable replacement system had now been found
which would eliminate the issue of repeated glass shattering,
allowing the safe reinstatement of the balconies for tenant use,
and restoring the building’s original appearance. The
proposals would also ensure full compliance with health and safety
requirements.

content:
The committee received a report which proposed
the introduction of a Council Tax premium on second homes in
Runnymede from 1 April 2027.
 
This measure aimed to ensure fairness,
encourage better use of housing stock, and generate additional
income to support local services. The recommendation was intended
to reflect Runnymede’s commitment to financial sustainability
and an equitable policy, with implementation timed to coincide with
the formation of the new West Surrey Council.
 
Linda Norman, Corporate Head of Customer,
Digital and Collection Services, presented the report and explained
that 12 months’ notice of the implementation of such
proposals must be given and that as all other councils due to be
incorporated in to the new West Surrey Council currently had such a
policy this would enable the new authority to align the approach
should they wish to from April 2027.
 
Councillor R. King proposed the
recommendations within the report be adopted. The motion was
seconded by Councillor D. Whyte.
 
 
The committee sought assurances regarding
classification and appeal processes and were satisfied with the
careful consideration of the former and the inclusion of proposals
for the latter.
 
The matter was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that it be recommended to Full
Council to APPROVE the amendment as follows:
 
i)          with
effect from 1 April 2027, in accordance with Section 11C of the
Local Government Finance Act 1992, the Council will apply a council
tax premium of up to 100% on dwellings that are substantially
furnished and not anyone’s sole or main residence (second
homes)
topline: The committee has decided to introduce a Council Tax premium on second homes in Runnymede from 1 April 2027.

content:
The committee received a report providing an
update on the council owned asset at 57 Larchwood Drive, Englefield
Green, and outlining the current position following discussions
with the existing occupier, River Church, and the Englefield Green
Community Hub CIC.
 
Recent requests from the Community Hub CIC,
including consideration of a potential freehold disposal, together
with ongoing negotiations with both parties, required the future
use of the asset to be reviewed more holistically. The report made
members aware that the matters raised went beyond existing
delegated authority and departed from previous committee approvals
relating to the property. Accordingly, it was proposed that work
was undertaken to consider options for the asset in the round, to
explore alternative options to support community use, and approval
was sought for funding to support such work.
 
Phil Turner, Assistant Chief Executive (Place)
and Alex Williams, Corporate Head of Assets and Regeneration
presented the report for the benefit of members.  They drew attention to an error in the report at
2.2 which incorrectly stated that Full Council had considered
relevant matters in September 2023.  The
matter was considered in September 2023 but by the Community
Services and Corporate Management Committees.
 
The presenters went on to describe, briefly,
the history of relevant negotiations, the current use of the
building, which was valued and which the report addressed, and the
proposals for feasibility work and further reporting to the
committee.
 
Councillor R King proposed an amendment to the
wording of recommendations d) in the report as follows to recommend
that the committee:
 
Agree that the council ceases engagement with
Englefield Green Community Hub CIC regarding redevelopment
proposals for the site whilst options are being explored, with a
view to further engagement should it be appropriate, once the
council has determined the future of the asset
 
Subject to that amendment, Councillor R. King
proposed the recommendations within the report be adopted. The
motion was seconded by Councillor D. Whyte.
 
The committee was supportive of the efforts
being made by officers and reflected on the upcoming local
government reorganisation and the importance of decision making in
relation to this building at a local level where the needs of this
community were understood.
 
The recommendations were put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 
i)         
the current position in relation to the council owned asset at 57
Larchwood Drive be NOTED.
ii)         the
status of negotiations with River Church as the current occupier
and with Englefield Green Community Hub CIC be NOTED
iii)        the delegation
of authority to the Assistant Chief Executive (Place), in
consultation with the Chair and Vice Chair of the Committee, to
formalise the ongoing occupation of River Church by way of a
licence arrangement be AGREED. This arrangement would be terminable
on reasonable written notice and would be without any statutory or
contractual obligation on the council, or its successors in title,
to provide alternative accommodation (noting the council’s
intention to explore options to support the continuation of
community services)
iv)        that the
council cease engagement with Englefield Green Community Hub CIC
regarding redevelopment proposals for the site whilst options are
being explored, with a view to further engagement should it be
appropriate, once the council has determined the future of the
asset be AGREED.
topline: The council has decided to review the future use of a council-owned asset at 57 Larchwood Drive, Englefield Green, following requests from stakeholders and negotiations with existing occupiers.

content:
The Officer gave a brief overview of the
Flexible Fixed Term Tenancy as outlined in the report.
 
The report recommends that the Council stop
issuing flexible fixed term tenancies (FFTT) and allow existing
FFTT to become secure at the end of their term.
 
This will affect 783 tenants as well as future
tenants who would have been issued this type of tenancy. This will
increase housing security for those residents affected whilst
creating additional resource capacity and financial efficiencies
for the Council.
 
The Localism Act of 2011 required local
authorities to develop a Tenancy Strategy. Within that, local
authorities had the discretion to implement flexible tenancies. The
Council implemented flexible tenancies in April 2014. FFTT were
issued to all new general needs social housing tenants, in line
with the terms set out within the tenancy policy. These tenancies
were routinely issued for 10 years, although some circumstances led
to two and five-year tenancies being issued. Each of these
tenancies were preceded by a one-year introductory tenancy.
 
There are significant difficulties with taking
any form of enforcement action on FFTTs specifically ASB and so
they do not facilitate good management of the
stock.  
 
Officer asked that Members approve the
recommendations in the report.
 
The Chair thanked the Officer for the report
and Members echoed their appreciation
 
Chair moved and seconded by Cllr King.
 
All Members would like to see residents get
decent housing. It is recognised that some tenants have more rooms
and earn money from subletting some of their home and they should
be encouraged to move.
 
The Officer said that incentives were
available for all tenants to downsize and for
those who don’t have the money to
move additional financial assistance can be provided. When a fixed
term tenancy is due to end and the household has to be
assessed it is difficult for the Council to establish whether
a household still requires social
housing particularly when there are adult children in the
house and it would require a high level of
investigation to provide information that would enable the
process to be fully transparent and fair. To
date all fixed term tenancy reviews have resulted in
a new tenancy being offered.  
 
These are the reasons why fixed term tenancies
have been stopped.
 
 
Members requested that reports be
received earlier as a number of the reports had been to
follow. The Chair addressed the late submission of reports and
will take maximum steps to avoid this in the
future.
 
Chair moved to vote and it was carried out
unanimously.
 
 
RESOLVED THAT:
 
The Council will cease to issue Flexible Fixed
Term Tenancies and allow all existing FFTT to become secure at the
end of their term.
topline: The Council has decided to stop issuing Flexible Fixed Term Tenancies and allow existing ones to become secure at the end of their term.

and Community Development during 2025/26.
 
Officers provided statistics of participation
in a number of events including the Surrey Youth Games,
Sportability Festival, and the Ace
Youth Project, the Foxhills Holiday
Camps programme, and positive feedback arising therefrom.
 It was noted that the transition from
the Specsavers Surrey Youth Games to the more localised Surrey
Community Games had maintained positive engagement with young
people, particularly those from deprived wards, whilst fostering
confidence and physical activity. 
Inclusivity had also been maintained.
 
Members were updated on tennis provision in
the borough as well as ‘fitness in the park’, Junior
Rangers, Runnymede in Bloom, the International Older People’s
day event, Holiday and Food provision, the Runnymede Sport and
Physical Activity Forum, and the Community Action
group.  Positive feedback from these
activities was welcomed by the Committee.
 
Officers highlighted the creation of the
Runnymede Family Network and Community Engagement, such as the
opportunity to engage with the A320 contractors.  Priority issues continued to be fly-tipping,
anti-social behaviour.  Funding
opportunities continued to be explored, including promotion of CIL
opportunities, and Members welcomed plans to launch a Mental Health
Forum.
 
Members noted that Self-Management of
facilities by local sports clubs continued to be explored.
 
The Committee thanked Officers across
Community Development who had successfully delivered a diverse
range of projects throughout the borough in 2025, effectively
supporting children, young people, and adults, which had enriched
community involvement and collaborative working with partner
organisations.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations for various activities under Leisure and Community Development in 2025/26.

content:
The Committee considered a report concerning
Health and Wellbeing Place Based funding and the mechanism for its
distribution in 2026/27.
 
The Committee was advised that a sum of
£50,000 had been allocated to each of the Boroughs in north
west Surrey to deliver meaningful support to new and/or existing
community interventions, services or projects which would
contribute to the health and wellbeing of residents and communities
in the context of the ‘Wider Determinants of
Health’.
 
It was reported that such projects, focussing
on the seven areas of deprivation in the borough, should also align
with the Council’s Health and Wellbeing Strategy, and
complement the work of the Community Action Groups, the Health and
Wellbeing Partnership, under the North West Surrey Alliance as it
was re-structured into West Surrey Place.
 
Officers proposed a two tier model to process
and consider applications for funding on a one-off basis various
new projects or new extensions to existing projects which were
considered to deliver the most benefit based on value, outcomes and
environmental/sustainability and biodiversity
implications.  The model mirrored the
Section 106 Englefield Green Small Awards process, which Members
approved of as being the most transparent.  It was hoped that projects within Englefield Green
would still be eligible for consideration following boundary
changes.
 
Members reviewed the data presented on
guidance and health inequalities, and noted that the three priority
themes were Healthy Behaviours, Healthy Minds, and Healthy Lives,
each of which would have its own workstream, overseen by the Health
and Wellbeing Partnership.  In giving
consideration to applications, all parties would need to take into
account existing provision, gaps in provision, partnership working
opportunities, and Health inequalities.
 
With regard to qualifying criteria, although
it was accepted that an organisation not being constituted could be
a barrier, there were opportunities for them still to deliver with
another constituted body managing the budget and taking the
lead.
 
Officers agreed to clarify whether the
Runnymede Borough dashboard produced for 7 of the borough’s
wards could be provided for the remaining 7 wards.
 
It was agreed that awards below a threshold of
£5,000 would be determined at Corporate Head level, in
consultation with partners, including the Chair of Community
Services Committee, and above by the Community Services
Committee.
 
Officers were asked to keep Members informed
of projects that were awarded funding below the £ 5,000
threshold, through the Service Plan updates, on a quarterly
basis.
 
The Committee was very supportive and approved
the intention to allocate all funding available before the demise
of Runnymede Borough Council.
 
In order to facilitate this, approval from
Corporate Management Committee would be sought accordingly.
 
Resolved that
–
 

i)         
the process to work in partnership with Public Sector agencies,
VCSE sector and communities, is launched in January 2026 as
detailed within the report, with outcomes to be reported to
Community Services Committee at the end of the financial year
2026/2027;
 

ii)         the
themes that will inform the direction of the partnership are
adopted as set out in the report; and
 

iii)        funding awards
to support the outputs of the partnership, from the NWS Alliance
Place-Based funding of £50,000, be authorised as follows:

 
·        
delegated authority be given to the Corporate Head of Community
Services in consultation with the Chair of Community Services
Committee, and Chair of the Health and Wellbeing Partnership for
proposals up to £5,000; and
 
·        
by approval from Community Services Committee for proposals over
£5,000; and
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management that –
 
a Supplementary
Revenue Estimate in the sum of £50,000 be approved, to be
funded from the grant received from the North West Surrey Health
and Care Alliance
topline: The Committee has decided to allocate £50,000 to each Borough in north west Surrey for community projects to improve health and wellbeing.

content:
The Committee considered a report concerning
Open Space Development projects and how they could be delivered
using the Community Infrastructure Levy, NHS, and Section 106
funding.
 
Members recalled that in November 2025,
Corporate Management Committee approved a number of bids from Open
Space Development for strategic CIL and Neighbourhood CIL
funding.
 
The Committee was advised that a number of
projects to make improvements to the borough’s recreational
facilities had been identified following community engagement to
determine local priorities.  These
were:
 
Abbeyfields Play
Area
Edgell Close Play Area
Murray House Play Area
Chertsey Recreation Ground Trim Trail
Frank Muir Project
Gogmore Park MUGA
Gogmore Park Outdoor Gym
 
Each project was described in detail and
Members were supportive of each.  It was
agreed they demonstrated a commitment to ensuring that the designs
and activities developed through the programme supported children
and young people with disabilities, enabling them to participate
fully in outdoor play, nature-based activities, and community
events, as well as encouraging people of all ages to
participate.
 
Members agreed that these projects presented a
significant and timely opportunity to create more inclusive,
accessible, and engaging spaces for all members of the
community.
 
Members were advised that the sources of
funding were a mixture of Community Infrastructure Levy, Youth
Development Fund, NHS, Pump Prime and Section 106, totalling
£500,000 Capital and £55,000 Revenue
budget.  Approval of the financial
arrangements would therefore be sought from Corporate Management
Committee.
 
In response to a
specific question, Officers agreed to follow up on progress with
colleagues in Environmental Services a previous request to re-paint
the line markings in Aviator Park.
 
Resolved that
–
 
i)         
the proposed improvements, or development of new play areas and
open spaces set out in this report be approved;
 

ii)        
commencement of the procurement processes for the required services
be approved;

 

iii)        a total
contract value as detailed in paragraph 4.2 of the report be
approved;
 

iv)       
the committee agrees to carry forward £48,000 from the
2025/26 Youth Development budget from 2025/26 to 2026/27 to
progress these works; and
 

v)         to note
that in addition to CIL funding, Officers have submitted a match
funding bid using the NHS fund to support the delivery of the
proposed outdoor fitness unit at Gogmore Park. Should the NHS
funding not be forthcoming, the scheme will be curtailed to match
available funds; and
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that:
 

vi)       
a supplementary Capital Estimate in the sum of £500,000 be
approved, for the proposed improvements to the open spaces play
areas to be funded from the sources set out in paragraph 4.2 of the
report to Community Services Committee; and
 

vii)       a
supplementary Revenue Estimate in the sum of £55,000 for the
proposed improvements to the open spaces play areas be approved, to
be funded from the sources set out in paragraph 4.2 of the
aforementioned report
topline: The Committee has decided to approve improvements and development of new play areas and open spaces in the borough.

content:
The Committee considered proposed health and
safety works to facilitate the installation of Heathervale Skatepark, which were associated with
its proposed location and that of the existing cricket pitch.
 
The Committee was advised that the proximity
of the existing cricket pitch at Heathervale posed a potential risk to other park
users, particularly users of the proposed skate park.  Expert advice had been taken from Labo Sport with
a full report appended for information. 
A number of options arose therefrom for Members’
consideration to mitigate/reduce that risk.  These included: not to proceed with the skatepark,
take no action and proceed with the skatepark, close the skatepark
when cricket was being played, proceed with permanent netting
between the skatepark and cricket field, either at the height
recommended, or at a lower height, or finally install a metal cage
around the skatepark.
 
Members discussed at length the potential
risks to park users that cricket and other activities might
present.  For example, it was noted that
the skatepark at Heathervale was not
being replaced on a like for like basis.  Therefore, had the skatepark remained the size it
was in Aviator Park, the risk would be significantly
reduced.  Members also speculated about
how other local authorities addressed these risks and whether they
were likely to be in a similar position to Runnymede.
 
Officers advised that Labo Sport recommended
installation of permanent netting, 15 metres high and 39 metres
wide, between the skatepark and the cricket pitch.  Some Members expressed concern about the potential
for damage, vandalism, and anti-social behaviour, as well as the
visual impact of surrounding the cricket field with netting,
whether all net, or part solid, part netting.  This had to be balanced with the health and safety
issues that had been identified and the fact that installation of
the skatepark was a long awaited aspiration of a number of Members
and residents.
 
During the discussion, the wider Parkside
Regeneration project was raised. 
Members were assured that Heathervale
would remain as a much valued park, and there were no plans to
reduce its footprint or add to its infrastructure.
 
After a thorough debate, including
consideration of whether to defer a decision to allow for other
options to be considered and costed, it was agreed that Corporate
Management Committee should be furnished with further information
to assist their decision.
 
Financial and legal implications were noted,
with some Members questioning whether a permanent net was good
value for money in the current circumstances.
 
On balance, Members approved the
recommendation as set out below to proceed with the installation of
the proposed netting which it was considered would not set a
precedent for other such facilities in the Council’s
possession requiring similar measures. 
There was a feeling that it would be desirable to make progress in
a timely manner.
 
Officers were asked to, if possible, collate
supplementary information for Corporate Management Committee on the
anticipated lifespan of the proposed netting, the cost of
installation of a lower net, the feasibility and approximate cost
of a part solid wire mesh base and upper netting, the breakdown of
the cost of installation and on-going maintenance, and further
details of treatments available to extend longevity of the proposed
netting.
 
Officers agreed to, if time allowed, contact
Surrey Cricket about the feasibility of re-siting the cricket pitch
and include in the reference to Corporate Management Committee or
to report back at the meeting.
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that –
 
a supplementary
capital budget estimate of £30,000 be approved, to complete
additional health and safety works required as part of the
installation of the skate park at Heathervale.
topline: The Council has decided to proceed with the installation of permanent netting between the skatepark and the cricket pitch at Heathervale to mitigate potential risks to park users.

content:
The Committee was presented with the
Council’s first Biodiversity Report, which was a legal
requirement of Section 102 of the Environment Act 2021.  The report detailed the Council’s collective
plans thereunder to meet the statutory biodiversity duty up to the
beginning of 2031, and for actions taken already for the period 1
January 2023 to 1 January 2026.
 
Officers had collated responses from the
Council’s service areas and Corporate Heads, noting that some
areas had limited opportunities to deliver
enhancements.  Therefore, much of the
focus was on areas where direct impacts could be made via land
management and habitat enhancements for the benefit residents
through biodiversity improvement.  It
was noted that there was distinction to be made between meeting
climate change targets and the commitment to biodiversity.
 
Officers (the various responsible Officers
across the Council), were asked to submit updates on future actions
set out in the Biodiversity Report to the Climate Change and Nature
Member Working Group.
 
Officers (the various responsible Officers
across the Council), were instructed to consider engagement with
and participation by Councillors in the various initiatives.
 
In response to a specific question, Officers
were asked to communicate with Ward Members and Volunteer Groups in
advance of works carried out by the Green Spaces Team and to
provide an explanation to Ward Members in respect of recent works
undertaken at Gogmore Farm Park and subsequent impact on the
environs.
 
Officers were requested to, if possible,
obtain data on trees from the Green Spaces Team as presented to the
Climate Change and Nature Member Working Group for inclusion in the
Biodiversity Report prior to publication on the Council’s
website.
 
Members were asked to note that local
government re-organisation was likely to have an impact on the
delivery of some of the actions and objectives in the
report.  This was something which the
new authority would need to take forward in terms of deciding on
the reporting periods and reporting actions.
 
Members welcomed the report and thanked
Officers for their work to bring it to fruition.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the publication of
the Biodiversity Report be approved
topline: The Council has decided to approve the publication of its first Biodiversity Report, outlining plans to meet statutory biodiversity duty up to 2031.

content:
The Committee was presented with
a comprehensive report in private session seeking approval for a
waiver to the relevant standing orders for contracts to procure
replacement vehicles for the Council’s Community Meals
service.
 
Members valued the service
because it provided daily hot meals as well as contact face to face
with some of the borough’s most vulnerable
residents. 
 
Members recalled that the current
lease for the four specialist electric vehicles; each fitted with
diesel ovens, expired in May 2026. 
These vehicles were essential for delivering meals directly from
frozen to hot at the point of
delivery.
 
Officers explained that there
were three options.  These were
to:
 

·        
Extend the current lease for 24 months with
Novuna Vehicle Solutions. 
 
This maintained the existing
delivery model, ensured continuity through Local Government
Reorganisation, and avoided service disruption.  It also delivered a small annual saving and
aligned with the Council’s Climate Change
Strategy.
 

·        
Move to a new model which involved cooking meals in
a central kitchen and transporting them in hot boxes. 
 
Members agreed that this option
should be discounted for now due to infrastructure and resource
constraints.  However, the Committee
recognised the fact that this would be the likely future delivery
model if the service is retained by West Surrey Council.
 

·        
End the service.
 
Officers reported that this had
already been discounted following Member consultation.  This was due to the significant impact on
vulnerable residents.
 
The recommended option to enter a
direct lease with Novuna for two years
was supported by the Committee.  This
required a waiver under Contract Standing Orders because
Novuna was currently the only UK known
supplier of these specialist vehicles. 
 
Officers confirmed that the
proposed arrangement was within existing budgets and mitigated risk
by maintaining proven business continuity.
 
Members were pleased to approve
the proposed procurement route and agreed that this approach
secured uninterrupted service, supported independence for older
residents, and provided time for the new authority to undertake a
full options appraisal.
 
Resolved that –
 
a
waiver of the relevant Standing Order for contracts be approved,
in order for the Council to enter into a 2 year lease
agreement for the four Meals at Home vehicles currently operated by
the Council
topline: The Council has decided to enter into a 2-year lease agreement for replacement vehicles for the Community Meals service.

content:
The Committee was appraised of forthcoming
works by the Environment Agency (EA) to Bell Weir, downstream of
Runnymede Pleasure Grounds. 
 
The refurbishment had been granted planning
consent via permitted development under application number
RU.23/1652 and affected the Pleasure Grounds as the EA had notified
the Council of its intention to proceed under its statutory powers
under Sections 165 and 172 (Schedule 20) of the Water Resources Act
1991 to use part of the Pleasure Grounds as a temporary compound
for their works.  These were estimated
to last up to 2 years.  The works were
part of a wider flood alleviation and infrastructure improvement
programme.
 
The Committee, sitting as Trustees of the
Pleasure Grounds, was advised that the Council had no legal
authority to prevent the EA from entering the land and taking up
temporary occupation under the aforementioned Act and that
colleagues in Assets and Regeneration were working to ensure that
disruption was minimised and that the public interest was protected
through ongoing engagement, transparency, and positive
communication.
 
Members were provided with a Location Plan,
Compound Layout Plan and Proposed Site Entrance.
 
It was noted that any damage or loss was
experienced as a result of the EA’s use of the land,
compensation could be claimed after the works had been
completed.  It would therefore be
important for the Landlord to carry out a photographic schedule of
condition on behalf of the Trustees, prior to the EA taking
occupation of the site.  In addition,
Officers from Assets and Regeneration, Community Development, and
Green Spaces, would also engage with the EA in respect of the
proposed removal of trees and other tree related issues.
 
In response to a specific enquiry, Officers
would contact the Environment Agency to confirm engagement with
French Bros. operating ferry trips from the Pleasure Ground
mooring.
 
Officers agreed to request the EA to arrange a
QA session on Microsoft Teams with Councillors at an early
stage.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Council Trustees have approved the Environment Agency's use of part of the Pleasure Grounds for flood alleviation and infrastructure improvement works.

content:
The Committee considered a report in private
session outlining options for the procurement of replacement
vehicles for the Council’s Community Transport
Service. 
 
Members were advised that Officers had
undertaken a comprehensive options appraisal; each option was
described in the report which was available on the Council’s
Intranet.  The Committee reviewed each
option, noting that procurement of electric vehicles was not viable
at this time, and that leasing instead of purchase would not
currently provide value for money.
 
Members were asked to note that the chosen
option provided a number of compelling advantages.  These were:
 

Rapid lead time
Infrastructure in place and
resilient (HVO tank with diesel back-up)
No fundamental range risks
Slower decline in depreciation
making resale value greater in percentage terms
Reliable and resilient maintenance
arrangements
a long-wheel based vehicle to
support the transport of our most disadvantaged (those with larger
electric wheelchairs) alongside other residents. This would provide
more space for wheelchairs, walking aids and passengers to
transport together safely

 
The proposed option did however have a few
disadvantages which Officers summarised as; unidentified underlying
mechanical issues, and wear and tear. 
In addition, although carbon impact was mitigated with HVO, it was
not considered a long-term solution. 
The financial implications included that there was a Capital Budget
of £255,000 available for the replacement of Community
Transport Fleet in the current financial year.  This was previously approved by Members in June
2024.
 
The Committee was assured that the procurement
route was required to comply with the Council’s Contract
Standing Orders and Public Contracts Regulations 2015 and that
using a Framework Agreement satisfied CSO requirements for
competitive tendering and lawful expenditure.  Officers cautioned that failure to adhere to CSOs
could expose the Council to legal challenge and reputational
risk.
 
In response to a specific question, Officers
were asked to consult the Depot Transport Manager regarding the
most lucrative and environmentally friendly method of vehicle
disposal.
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that –
 
i)         
the procurement of three Community Transport vehicles in the sum
reported (plus VAT) be approved, from the approved budget held in
the Capital Programme;

 

ii)         to
commence a procurement process via a compliant Framework Agreement,
in accordance with Contract Standing Orders; and

 

iii)        for the Pump
Prime Fund in the sum reported earmarked for electric vehicle
charging in the June 2024 report for use in the 2025-26 financial
year, be returned to the central Pump Prime Fund to be spent on
other agreed initiatives.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the procurement of replacement vehicles for the Community Transport Service.

content:
The Committee considered a report concerning a
proposal to appropriate a residential property at Chertsey
Recreation Ground from the open spaces portfolio under the
provisions of Section 122(1), (2A) Local Government Act
1972. 
 
The intention was to facilitate leasing the
Lodge at Chertsey Recreation Ground to one of the Council’s
fully owned companies to allow its management and leasing on
residential Assured Shorthold Tenancies (AST), or such other
residential tenancies as permitted by law should the ability to
grant ASTs be limited or removed by statute.
 
The Committee was advised that exercise of
appropriation would transfer the land from one ledger to another
and there were four considerations to be undertaken which were set
out in full in the Officer’s report.  These concerned identification of the purpose for
which the Lodge was held, why it was no longer required for that
purpose, why it was required for the new purpose, and consideration
of any objections received to the newspaper
advertisements.  Any objections received
in writing would be submitted to a future meeting of Corporate
Management Committee.
 
The Committee reviewed the proposed Heads of
terms to RBCI Ltd, noting that the current annual estimated
expenditure charged to the Green Spaces budget for the vacant
property was £3,658.96.  Members
agreed that this was unsustainable and that the proposed use
presented an opportunity to generate much needed income.
 
Members were pleased that proceeding with this
piece of prudent housekeeping would provide a single residential
dwelling and generate income with which to maintain the property
and pay into the general fund. 
Appropriation to the general fund was required to enable it to be
used for residential letting.
 
The Committee was advised that if the proposal
was approved by Corporate Management Committee it could generate
income of an estimated £8,920 in 2025/26 rising to
£19,500 in 2026/27 for the general fund.
 
The Committee was content to approve the
proposed course of action accordingly.
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that –
 
the
intention to appropriate the use of the Lodge at Chertsey
Recreation Ground from Open Space for general fund purposes, and
that should appropriation be approved:-
 
i)         
the intention to appropriate the use of the Lodge be formally
advertised;
 

ii)         any
objections of substance or raising legal issues to such
appropriation be reported to Corporate Management Committee for
their review; and

 
iii)        agree to the
Heads of Terms in Appendix B to RBCI Ltd
 
if no
objections to such appropriation are received then Officers be
authorised to complete the appropriation process without reporting
back to the Corporate Management Committee and a Memorandum of
Appropriation be prepared and signed by the Corporate Head of Law
and Governance to record the appropriation of the Lodge at Chertsey
Recreation Ground to general fund purposes.
topline: The Committee has decided to appropriate a residential property at Chertsey Recreation Ground for leasing purposes to generate income.

content:
The Committee was asked to consider an
application from Horton’s Steam Fair Ltd to hold their
vintage fairground on the Green from 3rd –
4th October 2026.
 
Hortons had requested access to the Green from
the 30th September to the
7th October, 8 days in
total.   4 days to set up, 2
operational days and 2 days to break down.
 
The Committee recalled Hortons had previously
used the Green and no issues had arisen, in addition the Green had
been left in a pristine condition. The Committee was keen to
support a traditional fair, which continued on from the tradition
of Carters Steam Fair historically using the Green for many
years.
 
 
Resolved that:    The application from
Horton’s Steam Fair to hold a vintage
                            
fairground on the Green be approved.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve Horton's Steam Fair's application to hold a vintage fairground on the Green.

content:
The Committee was asked to consider an
application from Beach’s Funfair to hold their funfair on the
Green from 17th – 19th April 2026.
 
Beach’s had requested access to the
Green from the 14th April to the 20th April,
7 days in total.   4 days to set
up, 2 operational days and 1 day to break down.  Potential alternative dates of 26th
– 28th June had also been included in the
application.
 
The Committee voiced some concerns regarding a
fair using the Green in April as the weather could often be wet,
which in turn would cause damage to the Green. Officers were asked
if there was a provision to cancel the event due to unsuitable
weather conditions.   Officers
confirmed this was possible, and advised Members that a deposit was
taken which would be used to repair the Green, if
necessary. 
 
Members recalled that previously Beach’s
had been unable to move off the Green on time due to unsuitable
weather conditions, the damage caused had taken a long time to
recover.  Subsequently, Members had
received complaints from residents regarding the condition of the
Green. 
 
It was also noted that both in April and June
the turf was at its peak growing season.   Turf recovered better from damage in the
autumn or winter.  Any damage in April
would be visible throughout the summer period.
 
It was noted that the alternative dates in
June were not feasible due to cricket fixtures taking place on the
Green at that time.
 
Therefore, the Committee voted on the
application for the April dates only, the vote was
tied.   Therefore, the Chairman
used his casting vote; and it was
 
Resolved that:    The application from Beach’s
Funfair to hold their funfair on the
                            
Green be refused
topline: The Committee has decided to refuse Beach's Funfair application to hold their funfair on the Green.

content:
The Committee was updated on various issues
pertaining to the management and maintenance of Englefield
Green.
 
Car Parking
 
Officers advised the Committee that the Crown
had not given their approval for the introduction of a Council Car
Park, therefore the current arrangements would remain the
same. 
 
Tree Planting
 
The Committee was advised that the
Biodiversity and Conservation Manager at the Crown Estate had
verbally approved the tree planting plans for Englefield
Green.  Officers would, however, need
written approval before planting could commence.
 
 
Bollards
 
Officers advised the Committee that they were
still waiting for written permission from the Crown Estate for the
replacement of the bollards.  No further
work could be undertaken until written permission was
received. 
 
Sharing of best Practices with the Crown
Estate
 
A date was still yet to be agreed with the
Council’s Park and Greenspaces service to spend a day with
the Crown Estate to learn and share best practices in Estate
Management.  
 
Selection of Litter bin design
 
The Committee was advised that written consent
from the Crown Estates had still not been received for the
replacement of the 21 existing bins.   As previously requested by the Committee,
two options were detailed in the agenda papers for the Committee to
consider.   Once the Crown Estate
had given written approval the selected bin model would be
installed.    
 
The Committee considered the two
options.   The majority of the
Committee considered Option B to be their preferred
option. 
 
It was requested that signage on new bins
indicated it could also be used for the disposal of chewing
gum.
 
 
Wildflower planting funding
 
Members would recall that at the Englefield
Green Committee meeting on 3rd April 2025 the Englefield
Green CIC were given approval to plant wildflowers on the
Green.  This community led social
enterprise had submitted a further application for funding from the
Englefield Green earmarked reserves.   The sum of £920 was being requested in
order to plan native wildflower seeds, wildflower turf and native
bulbs. 
 
It was noted that the first planting had been
a huge success and the results had been spectacular with lots of
positive comments received from local residents.
 
The Committee were all fully supportive of the
use of funds for this purpose.
 
 
 
 
Resolved that:   Option B  was the
Committee’s choice of litter bin for use on
                           
Englefield Green
 
                           
£920 be released from the Englefield Green earmarked
reserves
                           
to fund further wildflower planting on St. Jude’s Road
verge
topline: The Committee has decided to choose Option B for litter bins in Englefield Green and allocate £920 for further wildflower planting on St. Jude's Road verge.

content:
There were seven recommendations received from
Committees of Council for consideration in public and these are set
out below:
 

a)   
Green Travel Strategy – recommendation from Corporate
Management Committee

Council received a
recommendation from the Corporate Management Committee which had
