content:
The Committee received a report which sought
approval to reduce Customer Services public opening hours by 90
minutes per day and delete the Customer Services Team Leader post,
delivering an estimated annual saving of £48,500.
 
Linda Norman (LN), Corporate head of Customer,
Digital and Collection Services presented the report drawing the
attention of members to the proposed benefits of the changes and
the mitigations proposed to reduce any negative impact on Runnymede
residents.
 
Councillor Robert King proposed the
recommendations within the report be adopted. The motion was
seconded by Councillor Linda Gillham.
 
In response to a question from a councillor,
LN confirmed that further interrogation of the data on service
users using customer services at the times proposed for closure had
not been undertaken, as mitigation in the form of ‘out of
hours’ call back requests would be introduced to ensure that
those few people who could not access the council in any other way,
or at any other time would not be excluded.
 
Further comments were received from
councillors, welcoming the proposals, recognising the benefit to
staff of dedicated time for administrative duties and seeking and
receiving confirmation that trade Unions had been consulted and
were supportive.
 
The recommendations were put to the vote.
 
For 11 Against 1 Abstentions 0
 
RESOLVED that:
 
i)              
a reduction of Customer Services public opening hours by 90 minutes
per day (proposed hours: 9:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m.), effective 1
February 2026 be APPROVED.
ii)             
the deletion of the Customer Services Team Leader post, with
associated structural changes as outlined in the report be
APPROVED.
iii)            
the estimated annual saving of £48,500 arising from these
changes be NOTED.
iv)            
the implementation of a comprehensive communication and marketing
plan to ensure residents are fully informed about the revised
opening hours, while emphasizing that appointments can still be
booked outside these times if preferred, along with other
alternative access options be ENDORSED
topline: The Council has decided to reduce Customer Services opening hours and delete the Team Leader post, saving £48,500 annually.

was being undertaken to encourage self-declarations from staff in
this regard.
 
The matter prompted discussion.  In response to questions raised and comments made

i.        
efforts were made to measure the impact of work undertaken in
relation to diversity and inclusion

    
ii.        
the council was keen to understand employee absence and that the
suggestions form the floor regarding benchmarking were noted,
particularly relating to reporting of absence as a % of a team
capacity in order to identify potential stress points in the
workforce

   
iii.        
workstation risk assessments were not carried out in people’s
homes where they undertook some or all of their work from home, but
there was an online self-assessment tool available to all staff,
and the option to work in the office remained available to all
staff
 
The report was received for information

content:
Council received a report of the Chief
Executive outlining the latest developments on Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR) following the decision from the Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 28 October
2025 to implement a two unitary model for Surrey.
 
The report set out the planning undertaken at
Runnymede and elsewhere in preparation for the LGR and sought
authority to establish a (voluntary) Joint Committee to further
this work.
 
Councillor D Whyte presented the report for
the benefit of Councillors and proposed Councillor R King as
representative of Runnymede BC at the Joint Committee should the
council agree to be a part of such arrangements
 
He referred Councillors to a late amendment to
the recommendation previously circulated as supplementary agenda
No1 which sought to appoint a named substitute and had been amended
to delegate authority instead to the monitoring officer to appoint
at such time as a substitute was required. 
 
Following questions from a councillors the Monitoring Officer;
 
i)              
explained that the delegation to appoint a substitute would provide
flexibility and certainty of representation over and above that
provided by a named substitute.  He also
reported that other authorities had taken this approach and it
was considered to be fully compliant
with the terms of procedure.
ii)             
confirmed that the meetings of the Joint Committee would be held in
public but that a determination on livestreaming had not been
made.  It was likely that the meeting
would utilise different venues across the West Surrey unitary
footprint and therefore the technology to livestream may not be
available at every venue.
 
Councillor D Whyte proposed the
recommendations in the report and the recommendation in the
supplementary agenda as amended, for approval.  Councillor Linda Gillham seconded and the matter
was put to the vote.
 
It was RESOLVED that:
 
i)              
LGR developments be NOTED.
ii)             
the establishment of a voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee as
detailed in the report and to the terms of reference attached at
Appendix 1 under the provisions of section 101(5) (arrangements for
discharge of functions by local authorities) of the Local
Government 1972 Act be AGREED;
iii)            
the appointment of Councillor R King as the Runnymede Borough
Council representative on the voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee
be AGREED;
iv)            
upon enactment of the proposed Surrey (Structural Changes) Order
2026 that the voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee shall become
the joint committee required to be established under the provisions
of that legislation and shall have the same terms of reference and
membership as the voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee and be
established under the provisions of section 101(5) (arrangements
for discharge of functions by local authorities) of the Local
Government 1972 Act and pursuant to the requirements of the
proposed Surrey (Structural Changes) Order 2026 be AGREED
v)             
that a delegation of authority to the Monitoring Officer to
nominate and appoint any substitute member to represent Runnymede
Borough Council on the voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee in
accordance with Part 6.1of the draft terms of procedure as attached
at appendix 1 be AGREED.
topline: The Council has decided to establish a voluntary West Surrey Joint Committee in preparation for Local Government Reorganisation following the decision to implement a two unitary model for Surrey.

Over the past year, parking services had
delivered a number of key improvements including the installation
of new pay-and-display machines across 19 car parks, the
introduction of a nominal recreational charge at open space car
parks and standardisation of charges. 
These changes aimed to improve fairness, accessibility and
operational efficiency whilst ensuring parking income contributed
to the cost of maintaining these assets.  Despite these improvements income from less than
half of our car parks currently covered all operational costs,
which highlighted the importance of these measures to achieve
financial sustainability.
 
Further actions identified in the Parking
Action Plan were scheduled to be delivered over the remainder of
the 2025/26 financial year and into 2026/27 which
included:  Installation of Camera
Assisted Enforcement (CAE) in four main car parks, EV Charger
installations, cycle racks and enhanced payments solutions.
 
Under the Traffic Management Act of 2004, the
Council was obliged to publish its annual parking report which
detailed parking activity and cost of service.
 
The Committee was advised that the newly
installed pay and display machines provided Officers with valuable
information i.e.  who was using our car parks, when they were
using it, how long they were using it for.  This information
could be used to ascertain the value/viability of car parks going
forward.
 
Some concerns were raised regarding the monies
sitting in surplus, which could only be used on maintaining car
parks and felt that surplus should not be used as a ‘savings
scheme’ and would be put to better use supporting car park
users.
 
The Committee was asked to note the contents
of the table at 4.4 of the agenda which detailed available balances
and committed expenditure.
 
The Chair advised the Committee that
£200,000 had been released to carry out maintenance on five
of the borough car parks which needed attention and further work
needed to be done to our other car parks.
topline: The Environment and Sustainability Committee has approved recommendations to improve the parking action plan for 2024/25.

content:
The Committee received a report which updated
them on the progress with installing electric vehicle (EV) charging
points in council-owned car parks.
 
Members would recall that in March 2025 this
Committee resolved that Officers be authorised to proceed with
detailed discussions with Surrey County Council (SCC) regarding the
terms and conditions of joining the SCC EV charging infrastructure
contract with the aim of facilitating the installation of EV
charging points in the following car parks:  Waspe Farm, Memorial Gardens and Runnymede
Pleasure Grounds.
 
Following feasibility work earlier this year,
RBC had entered into SCC’s contract with Connected Kerb,
which provided a cost-neutral delivery model and aligned with
county-wide sustainability goals.  
Technical assessments had confirmed seven viable sites in
Runnymede, namely, Waspe Farm, Addlestone One, Pooley Green,
Memorial Gardens, Gogmore Farm, Victoria Street and Coopers
Hill.  Each would host three dual-head
chargers and six bays per site.
 
The project required no capital funding from
the Council, parking fees and enforcement revenue would remain with
RBC.  The Committee was asked to
authorise a £30,000 underspend from electrical surveys to be
reallocated to this fund to cover any ancillary work such as
signage, integration with our payment machines and RingGo, making
good any repair not covered in the contract and any other project
work which RBC may need to cover.
 
Further work was currently being undertaken by
the Assets and Regeneration Team and Connected Kerb to implement
the framework approved, put in lease agreements for the individual
sites and to agree the specific installation timeliness to
implement the project. 
 
Some concerns were raised regarding
3rd parties undertaking the surveys as they might not
follow the same standards RBC would like them to
follow.  Officers advised the Committee
that Connected Kerb had worked very closely with RBC’s assets
team, and they felt given that Connected Kerb had deemed some
suggested sites unsuitable their surveys were reliable. 
 
It was noted that EV bays could only be used
whilst a vehicle was charging.   A
car left in an EV bay after charging would be subject to a PCN even
if payment of parking exceeded the time spent charging.
 
Concerns were also raised as to whether
Connected Kerb would be able to ‘cherry pick’ the bays
for EV charging, by using the most convenient and used
spaces.  Additionally, it was felt by
some members that dual use options would be beneficial, and
Officers were asked to pursue this option as part of
implementation.
 
Several members of the Committee felt more
clarification/flexibility was needed on the details of the contract
with Connected Kerb before Members could make a decision.
 
The Committee was advised that Officers could
go back to Connected Kerb prior to implementation to negotiate
following the points raised to get to the best position
possible. 
 
At the request of Cllr S Lewis a motion was
passed to defer consideration of the matter until the next ordinary
meeting of the Committee;
In accordance with Standing Order 39.2 and at
the request of Cllr Lewis a named vote was taken on the motion to
defer the item, and the voting was as follows: -
 
For: 3    Councillors Newman,
Saise-Marshall, Lewis
 
Against: 6 
Councillors Whyte, Ringham, Gahir, Gates, Kettle, Rowsell
 
This motion was lost.
 
 
 
 
In accordance with Standing Order 39.2 and at
the request of Cllr Lewis a named vote was taken on the motion
detailed in the report, and the voting was as follows: -
 
For:  5     Councillors Whyte, Ringham,
Gahir, Gates, Rowsell
 
Against:  
0
 
Abstain:  
4   Councillors Kettle, Newman,
Saise-Marshall, Lewis
 
 
This motion was carried.
 
 
Resolved that:
 

·      
The progress of EV charging implementation be noted
 

·      
Officers to be authorised to progress the implementation of EV
charging points in the following car parks:
 


Waspe Farm, Egham
Addlestone One Waitrose, Addlestone
(RBCI owned)
Pooley Green, Egham
Memorial Gardens, Virginia
Water
Gogmore Farm, Chertsey
Victoria Street, Englefield
Green
Coopers Hill, Englefield Green


 

 

 
·       
The Council’s Off-Street Parking Orders at each of the seven
car park locations be updated to support the effective management
and enforcement of electric vehicle (EV) charging
infrastructure
 
·      
The £30,000 underspend for electrical surveys be noted and
funds be reallocated to this fund to deliver this project.
.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the implementation of electric vehicle charging points in seven council-owned car parks.

content:
Members received an information report
relating to dealing with concerns relating to HMOs.
 
The report provided Members with an update and
outlined proposed new licensing conditions to be applied to new
licences and existing HMO licences at renewal.
 
The proposed new licence conditions related to
waste and anti-social behaviour.
 
It was anticipated that the existence of
conditions themselves would signal a shift change towards
responsible management of licensed HMOs.  The conditions placed positive requirements on
landlords when complaints were received with sanctions available
where there was non-compliance.
 
The new conditions would be added to new
licences and at licence renewal from January 2026.
 
It was noted that ASB evidence and complaints
did not currently meet the legal test for the introduction of an
additional licencing scheme.   This
was, however, possible when the legal test was met.
 
Officers were thanked for the report which was
welcomed and supported.
topline: The council has decided to implement new licensing conditions for HMOs to address concerns related to waste and anti-social behaviour.

content:
The Committee was pleased to note the interim
External Auditor’s Annual Report for 2024/25.
 
Officers advised that their focus for the
annual report was on financial sustainability, governance, and
improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness.  In respect of these for 2024/25 no significant
weaknesses in the Council’s arrangements had been
identified.  However, one improvement
recommendation had been made concerning data quality, specifically
on the benefits of having a Data Quality Policy.  Grant Thornton considered that such a policy would
reflect the Council’s commitment to robust data to support
decision making.  It was recommended
that the Council’s internal auditors, SIAP, conduct a test on
a sample of KPIs for accuracy and that the Council should conduct a
review of data quality, focussing on the effectiveness of data
collection, validation, and reporting processes across key service
areas.
 
Members were pleased to learn that no
statutory recommendations under schedule 7 of the Local Audit and
Accountability Act 2014 were being made, nor was there any cause
for Advisory Notices, judicial review or Public Interest
Reports.
 
Members noted the update with regard to two
key recommendations and findings from the 2023/24 report which had
been implemented in full.
 
Officers from Grant Thornton would bring the
external audit findings work on the Council’s Statement of
Accounts for 2024/25 to the next meeting of the Committee in
January 2026.
 
Officers from Grant Thornton were thanked for
their positive and open approach and the report was duly noted.
topline: The Council has approved recommendations from the External Auditor's Annual Report for 2024/25.

content:
The Committee noted data for complaints and
compliments for quarter 2 of 2025/26.
 
Officers reported a slight reduction in the
overall number of complaints which totalled 87 compared with 95 in
the previous quarter.  Officers
presented statistical information on complaint handling including
ward based data and were pleased to note
that there were only a handful of overdue complaints.
 
Officers highlighted a reduction in complaints
regarding waste and recycling which continued to be closely
monitored, with weekly meetings taking place at the Depot
specifically to deal with them at management and operational
level.  Members agreed that this
indicated the seriousness of how complaints were taken and were
encouraged by the involvement of front
line staff in making service improvements.  Officers agreed to bring an update to the meeting
in May 2026 on the operation of the trigger thresholds for refuse
and recycling as part of the annual LGO KPI report
 
Members were referred to the regular reports
to the Housing Committee where similar regular meetings took place
to actively address concerns raised by tenants.  The Chair of the Housing Committee asked that the
dedication of colleagues in Housing dealing with complaints be
included in the Minutes.
 
The system for complaints triaging was
explained in further detail; it being a rigorous process mainly
carried out by colleagues in Customer Services via the online
submissions.  The framework for
complaint handling was the guidance issued by the Local Government
and Social Care Ombudsman which was embedded in the Council’s
processes.
 
The Committee noted that the number of
compliments was slightly higher than in the previous quarter,
totalling 30, and details were set out in the exempt
appendix.  It was noted that Housing
colleagues also received a significant number of compliments.
 
The report was duly
noted.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve recommendations based on data for complaints and compliments for quarter 2 of 2025/26.

content:
The Committee reviewed the latest version of
the Council’s risk profile as at the end of Quarter 2
2025/26.
 
Members were advised that the Council
currently had 288 active riskscollated from generic risks that are
applicable across the organisation, service-specific risks ,
project risks and contract risks.
 
Officers confirmed that since the last report,
all risks had been reviewed by risk owners with the relevant
teams.  As a result, 8 new risks were
added, 6 risks archived as no longer relevant and 25 risk scores
amended either up or down.
 
Members recalled that corporately Officers
reviewed the post-mitigation score for the risk profile; the
probability and impact that a risk may happen after steps had been
taken to mitigate as this was the residual risk to which the
organisation was exposed to and carried.  Members noted the risk matrix and the thresholds
and reporting requirements.
 
It was noted that the highest scoring
categories remained Financial, Operations, and People.
 
Officers reported that the updated Corporate
Risk Register now contained 39 risks as agreed by CLT as having
corporate impact. These included: rising costs exceeding income in
the Housing Revenue Account, risk carried in Housing Services in
meeting new regulatory standards and the new inspection regime of
the Regulator of Social Housing, and the increased IT and cyber
security risk.
 
Officers confirmed that since March 2025 12
risks have increased, including housing compliance and private
rented sector availability and 13 risks had decreased, such as
Social Prescribing, which remained significant but reduced.
 
The Committee concurred that the risk profile
continued to reflect a maturing system with identification and
reporting now embedded in processes across the organisation.
 
Officers asserted that the whole risk profile
exercise had brought further consistency and transparency to risk
consideration, raising its profile and assisting the Internal
Auditors in their assessment of the Council’s
effectiveness.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to review and approve the latest version of the risk profile for Quarter 2 2025/26.

content:
The Committee noted an update on the outcome
of the Local Government Association’s (LGA) follow-up
Corporate Peer Challenge (CPC) visit, which took place in
September, which completed the process that began last year.
 
Officers considered that the follow-up report
provided strong external assurance that the Council had evidenced
its commitment to continuous improvement and in turn, met its
obligations under the Best value
duty.
 
Members were informed that through the
interviews with Officers and Members during the follow up visit,
the LGA were supplemented with an updated position statement and
documentation.  As a result, the peer
team confirmed that significant progress had been made on the
original recommendations of October 2024.
 
The Committee recalled that of the 20 actions
in the Council’s CPC action plan, eight were fully completed,
six embedded in day-to-day activity, and all of those that remained
in progress in September had now been delivered.
 
Officers highlighted that this was the first
time that the peer team had met with Officers and Members since the
outcome of the non-statutory Best value
Notice was communicated by MHCLG.  The
Council’s constructive and successful response was
highlighted as a major achievement.
 
The feedback letter appended to the
Officer’s report set out key observations with no formal
recommendations to be considered or actioned. Members were pleased
to note that Governance had improved, though some processes could
still be improved along with further streamlining to be considered
in light of Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR).  Officers advised
that Asset Management capacity had been strengthened and externally
validated, ensuring the Council would be well prepared for LGR. The
LGA recognised that Housing performance based on KPI results had
improved marginally, and the peer team noted that ongoing focus
would be needed to demonstrate continuous improvement to the
Regulator of Social Housing.
 
The Committee welcomed the view that on
workforce and culture, engagement was seen as strong. Furthermore,
leadership development and digitalisation were recognised as
driving cultural change and improving efficiency. It was agreed
that the Council had demonstrated investment in staff development,
delivered the pay and grading review, and enhanced internal
communications since the last visit.
 
Officers highlighted digital transformation as
a real success story, with new digital solutions for appraisals,
complaints, bookings, and procurement processes being developed
in-house through commitment to build versus buy, maximising return
on investment of existing systems.
 
The Committee agreed that the Council was also
playing a leading role in LGR preparations, including programme
management and set-up and support of the LGR hub website on behalf
of all Surrey’s district and borough councils.
 
Members noted that overall, the LGA CPC peer
team concluded that Runnymede was self-aware, focused on continuous
improvement, and committed to leaving a strong legacy for residents
ahead of reorganisation.
 
Officers were thanked for their considerable
efforts in achieving a positive outcome that reflected the hard
work across the organisation and provided ongoing independent
external assurance that the Council continued to operate to a high
level.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations following a positive Corporate Peer Challenge visit.

content:

re-approve the Council’s Statement of Accounts for
2019/20.
 
Officers advised that BDO, the
Council’s former external auditors, had finally resolved an
outstanding matter relating to a property acquisition made by the
Council in 2018 and the laws and regulations in the 2019/20
financial year. 
 
Members noted that no changes had
been made to the figures in the Statement of Accounts which were
approved by Corporate Management Committee in November
2021.  However, at the request of BDO,
Officers had made some minor changes to the Narrative Statement to
provide a further explanation of the Council’s Asset
Acquisition Strategy at that time and the process taken to address
the auditor’s challenge over the legality of the
Council’s final asset purchase thereunder. 
 
In addition, Officers had added
to note 4 of the accounts to reflect Local Government Re-organisation, and had also updated the associated
Annual Governance Statement (AGS) in respect of the property
issue. 
 
Members noted that making the
change as described would necessitate the AGS to be re-signed by
the current Co-Leadership and Chief Executive and the Section 151
Officer would also need to re-certify that the unaudited statement
of accounts for each year provided a true and fair view of the
Council’s financial standing during this period.  It was confirmed that this Officer felt confident
to do that as evidenced by the Council’s strong system of
governance.
 
Members also reviewed the
Management Letter of Representation and Audit Completion
Report.  Officers advised that the
letter of representation affirmed the accuracy of the information
provided to the external auditors and that all material information
had been disclosed.
 
Officers were pleased to have
completed this much awaited task and fulfil their statutory duty
accordingly.
 
Officers were thanked for their
significant efforts and asked to correct the minor typo on page 27
of supplementary Agenda No 3.

i)         
the Council’s Statement of Accounts for 2019/20 as set out in

re-approved;

Council and the Chief Executive and publication alongside the
Annual Statement of Accounts; and

Letter of Representation as set out in Appendix B of the
Officer’s report be approved

content:
The Committee was asked to note the 2019/20
Audit Completion Report presented by the Council’s former
auditors BDO.
 
Officers from BDO explained that the delay in
completion was originally attributable to a number of factors but
the most significant issue was the work BDO had undertaken to
address their concerns regarding the lawfulness of transactions
relating to the acquisition of commercial property.  BDO had concluded that one acquisition outside of
the borough was unlawful, the Council disagreed, having taken legal
advice both ahead of the acquisition and following BDO’s
challenge.  As a result, BDO had issued
an adverse opinion on the Value for Money audit alongside a
disclaimed opinion on the Statement of Accounts due to the
inability to complete all work within the required deadlines.
 
BDO confirmed that no further action would be
taken, other than the issuing of the recommendations as set out in
their report, and that it was not in the public interest to do
so.  The Council had made no further
purchases, and there were no repercussions.
 
The Committee was asked to note the management
letter of representation contained within the auditor’s
report and the proposed fees. 
BDO’s planned audit fee for 2019/20 was the Public Sector
Audit Appointments LTD (PSAA) published scale fee of
£34,754.  In addition, they would
be seeking a variation to the scale fee to reflect the
Council’s significant investment in commercial property in
recent years, and changes to the audit scope linked to the current
audit requirements for property assets, pension liabilities, and
group accounts.  This was £80,000,
plus a further £19,750 for reporting on government
grants.  The total fee being sought for
2019/20 was £134,504.
 
Officers were asked to confirm progress with
the formal complaint to BDO when available as Members considered it
was still warranted.
 
Resolved that -
 
the 2019/20 Audit
completion report be referred to full Council on 18 December 2025
for information
topline: The Council has decided to approve the 2019/20 Audit Completion Report despite contentious issues with the auditors regarding the lawfulness of property acquisitions.

content:
The Committee was asked to note additional
background to the recommendations made in BDO’s annual audit
letter and audit completion report for 2019/20 and the Management
Responses thereto.
 
Members were well versed in the reasons for
the delay in producing the completion report for 2019/20, which had
been documented nationally and locally in previous reports.
 
The Committee was reminded that in order to
clear the backlog of historical accounts and ‘reset’
the system, the Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024
required local bodies to publish audited financial statements for
all outstanding years up to and including 2022/23 by 13 December
2024 (‘the backstop date’). 
Members were informed that for the financial year 2019/20, the
auditor planned to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the financial
statements as it had not been possible to perform all necessary
audit procedures by the backstop date.
 
BDO had been unable to issue their opinion by
the backstop date due to further investigation into the lawfulness
of the Council’s decision to borrow to invest in commercial
property. The outcome of this work was that the auditor has issued
an adverse conclusion on the Council’s arrangements for
securing economy efficiency and effectiveness (known as
“value for money” arrangements), as they considered the
Council’s decision to acquire commercial property using
borrowed funds to be unlawful.
 
Members heard that the Council had sought its
own legal advice from Kings Counsel which continued to support the
actions taken by the Council in relation to the property
acquisition undertaken in 2019/20, which were considered
lawful.
 
The auditor’s report covering 2019/20,
recognised that this issue was limited to that year as no further
commercial acquisition had been undertaken, and set out two
recommendations. Members noted the steps already taken in the
intervening years that set out how the Council was already
delivering against these recommendations.
 
Three recommendations were also made by the
auditor in respect of the financial statements, and Members noted
the draft responses provided by Officers.
 
Resolved that
–
 
this
report (Response to External Audit Recommendations 2019/20), and
BDO’s audit reports for the years 2019/20 to 2022/23 be
referred to Full Council on 18 December 2025, for
information
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations in response to external audit findings on the lawfulness of borrowing for commercial property investment.

content:
The Committee noted an update on the outcome
of the Government consultation on strengthening the Standards and
Conduct framework for local authorities in England.
 
Members recalled completing a comprehensive
consultation comprising 40 questions in January 2025.  This was arranged under the following headings:
strengthening the standards and conduct framework, and Introducing
the power of suspension with related safeguards.
 
The Council, had, as required by the Localism
Act 2011, adopted a code of conduct consistent with the 7 Nolan
principles of standards in public life and set out in the
Constitution rules on requiring elected Members and Co-opted
Members to register and disclose pecuniary and non-pecuniary
interests.  The Council also had
arrangements for dealing with allegations of breaches of the code
of conduct and to consult one independent person in the process
before coming to decisions.
 
Members were aware that currently there was no
provision in current legislation for a sanction to suspend a
councillor found to have breached the code of conduct, nor to
withhold allowances.  This meant that
Councils had no effective way of dealing with serious
misconduct.
 
Officers advised that here were 2,092
respondents to the consultation. This clearly indicated a
widespread appetite for a whole system reform and the steers the
Government received from respondents had shaped their decisions on
the policy proposals, as set out below:
 
“• the introduction of a mandatory
code of conduct, which will include a behavioural code, for all
local authority types and tiers
• a requirement that all principal
authorities convene formal standards committees, to include
provisions on the constitution of standards committees to ensure
objectivity, accountability and transparency
• the requirement that all principal
authorities offer individual support during any investigation into
code of conduct allegations to both the complainant and the
councillor subject to the allegation
• the introduction at the authority level
of a ‘right for review’ for both complainant and the
subject elected member to have the case reassessed on grounds that
will be set out in legislation
• powers for authorities to suspend
elected members for a maximum of 6 months for serious code of
conduct breaches, with the option to withhold allowances during
suspension for the most serious breaches and introduce premises and
facilities bans either in addition or as standalone sanctions
• in response to the most serious
allegations involving police investigation, or where sentencing is
pending, the introduction of powers to suspend elected members on
an interim basis for an initial period of 3 months which, if
extended, will require regular review
• a new disqualification criterion for
any elected member subject to the maximum period of suspension more
than once within 5 years
• the creation of a new national appeals
function, to consider appeals from elected members to decisions to
suspend them and/or withhold allowances, and for complainants if
they consider their complaint was mishandled. Any appeal submitted
will only be permitted after complainant or elected member has
invoked their ‘right for review’ of the local standards
committee decision has been invoked and that process is
completed.”
 
It was unlikely that these would come into
force before Runnymede became part of the new unitary authority of
West Surrey.  Nevertheless, the
Committee welcomed the reform and were pleased to have taken a
pro-active part in the consultation.
 
The report was duly noted.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for strengthening the Standards and Conduct framework for local authorities in England.

content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine an
application from Surrey Police to review the premises licence in
respect of ‘The Carlton’ (trading as Carlton
Newsagents), 77 Station Road, Addlestone, Surrey, KT15 2AR.
 
The Sub-Committee noted the Senior Licensing
Officer’s report, the papers supplied by Surrey Police, and a
supplementary agenda containing submissions made by the Premises
Licence Holder (PLH) and named Designated Premises Supervisor (DPS)
and their representative.
 
Members were advised that Surrey Police had
made an application to review the premises licence under section 52
of the Licensing Act 2003, for the licensable activity of the sale
of alcohol (off sales only).
 
The application related to all four of the
Licensing Objectives and made reference to the Police’s view
that all four had been undermined as evidenced by witness
statements, and a series of photographs taken at the licensed
premises, copies of which were made available to Members and those
attending the meeting.
 
Members noted detailed information supplied by
Surrey Police setting out the sequence of events.  Members noted that the PLH had also failed to
notify the relevant licensing authority of a change of
address.  This had subsequently been
advised.
 
Members noted interactions between Surrey
Police and the PLH and DPS, whom the Police considered had failed
to uphold the licensing objectives by allegedly allowing criminal
activity, as described at the meeting, to take place on the
premises.  The Police were represented
by Counsel, who stated that the Police took the case very seriously
and that it was not sufficient to claim unawareness of the
situation.  Counsel went on to say that
as a key person, the DPS should have day to day control of the
premises, but that by effectively being ‘an absentee
DPS’ they were unable to fulfil that function.
 
The Sub-Committee’s attention was drawn
to the relevant guidance and the options available when reviewing
the Licence.  The applicants considered
that the proportionate option was to revoke the licence in respect
of the sale of alcohol.
 
There being no questions for the applicant,
the representative of the PLH and DPS was invited to state their
case.
 
The PLH/DPS maintained that they were unaware
of what was taking place at the premises, and had, on discovery of
it, taken pro-active steps to remove the staff allegedly involved
and were considering an application for a new DPS to be
appointed.  This demonstrated that the
PLH had not been complicit with the alleged activities, nor had
they participated therein or been tolerant of it.
 
It was stressed that the alleged activity was
confined to one employee and that the PLH/DPS should not be
adversely impacted, although they readily accepted their
responsibility for the day to day running of the premises which had
been lacking.  However, actions had been
decisive and systems put in place to remedy the situation including
log books, details of training, and CCTV.
 
The Sub-Committee’s attention was drawn
to the suggested modifications to the conditions as presented in
the applicant’s submission, with which they were happy to
comply, and had in fact implemented, or were in the process of
doing so.  The PLH’s
representative stated that it would be disproportionate to revoke
the premises licence.
 
The PLH and DPS and the other person present
were asked a series of questions by the Committee and Counsel to
clarify actions of individuals concerned and future arrangements,
including frequency of visits to the licensed premises and what
checks and balances and level of scrutiny were undertaken to ensure
the licensing objectives were upheld.
 
The requirements for a DPS were also
noted.  A brief adjournment allowed the
PLH/DPS to confirm their intentions.
 
In their closing submission, the Police gave
their view on the impact of the alleged activities on the wider
community and re-stated that revocation of the licence was their
desired outcome.  Counsel re-iterated
points made previously with regard to the alleged and perceived
failure to uphold the licensing objectives, and the likelihood of
being able to do so going forward.
 
In their closing submission the
PLH/DPS’s representative sought to emphasise how apologetic
they were but urged the Sub-Committee to look forward and be
assured that the causes of the events had been satisfactorily
rectified and that proper checks would be made in
future.  The good standing of the
PLH/DPS was also considered pertinent to future arrangements.
 
The meeting adjourned at 15:30 for the
Sub-Committee to determine the matter in private session.
 
The meeting reconvened at 16:20.
 
Based on the evidence submitted, the
Sub-Committee decided to exercise its powers under section 52(4)(e)
of the Licensing Act 2003 to revoke the Premises Licence for the
premises known as The Carlton Newsagents, 77 Station Road,
Addlestone, KT15 2AR, which permits the licensable activity of the
sale by retail of alcohol (off sales only).
 
In arriving at its decision, the Sub-Committee
had regard to the Revised Guidance issued under section 182 of the
Licensing Act 2003 dated February 2025 and The Runnymede Borough
Council Statement of Licensing Policy (2021-2026).
 
By virtue of the evidence given the
Sub-Committee reached the conclusion that the Designated Premises
Supervisor was not in day-to-day control of the premises and the
Premises Licence Holder was not upholding the requirements under
the Licensing Act 2003 to prevent crime taking place at the
licensed premises.
 
The Sub-Committee considered that the action
taken was an appropriate and proportionate response to address the
causes of concern that instigated the review.
 
The parties present were advised that a formal
decision notice would be issued within 7 working days of the
meeting and also advised of the right to appeal the decision and
that revocation, would, subject to appeal take effect, within 21
days thereafter.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the Premises Licence
in respect of The Carlton (trading as Carlton Newsagents) 77
Station Road, Addlestone, Surrey, KT15 2AR, be revoked, for the
reasons set out in the decision notice to be issued within 7
working days of the meeting.
topline: The Licensing Sub Committee has decided to revoke the premises licence for The Carlton Newsagents following concerns about crime prevention and lack of day-to-day control by the Designated Premises Supervisor.

content:
The Committee was asked to approve the final
version of the revised Statement of Licensing Policy for
2026-2031.  This followed a public
consultation exercise lasting 6 weeks, which had been extensively
promoted to all interested parties. 
Officers confirmed that the only amendment post consultation was to
update the contact details for the Home Office Immigration
Enforcement Service.
 
Officers reported that the Government had
recently concluded a fast track review of the Licensing Act 2003,
to which Officers had responded.  Any
changes arising from the review would be considered at a later date
and incorporated in the Council’s local policy.  Officers listed the areas likely to have an
impact.  These included:
 

·        
Establishment of a national framework for the harmonisation of
licensing practices across local authorities whilst preserving
local discretion.  This could also
include a 5th licensing objective of ‘promoting
economic growth.’

·        
Introduce an amnesty process to allow removal of outdated or
disproportionate licence conditions.

·        
Ending the requirement to publish alcohol licence notices in
printed local newspapers.

·        
Simplify and extend pavement licence durations, remove outdated
COVID-related conditions, and clarify licensing rules for outdoor
alcohol sales, and promote best practice guidance to support
seasonal flexibility and economic activity.

·        
Permanently increase the number of TENs allowed per year for
licensed premises to support community events. Consider retaining
safeguards such as the 24-hour gap between events and transferring
licence conditions to TENs.

·        
Introduce requirements for regular review or sunset clauses for
blanket licensing policies, such as core opening hours, to ensure
they remain proportionate and evidence based.

·        
Develop a national protocol to standardise providential
requirements, promote early mediation and clarify objection
procedures. Consider giving licensing officers greater influence in
decision-making, similar to planning officers.

·        
Enable longer-term or perpetual licences for recurring festivals
and events to support investment, planning and stability in the
sector.

·        
Strengthen the application of the Agent of Change principle in
licensing decisions to protect existing venues from complaints
arising due to new residential developments nearby.

·        
Explore the use of designated zones to preserve and manage vibrant
night-time economies. Encourage local consultation and use of
licensing and planning mechanisms to support economic and cultural
activity.
 
Members were advised that the call for
evidence additionally sought to assess the potential impacts of the
proposed reforms on public safety, crime, public health and
equality, as well as identifying the reforms that may place burdens
on licensing authorities and any potential mitigation measures.
 
Officers confirmed that with forthcoming local
government re-organisation, initial discussions for the alignment
of policies across the new West Surrey cluster were taking
place.
 
The Committee was pleased with the work
undertaken to review and update the Policy, and content to
recommend its adoption by full Council on 18 December 2026, for
implementation in early January 2026.
 
Recommend that
–
 
the revised
Statement of Licensing Policy 2026 - 2031, as attached at Appendix
A of the Officer’s report, be approved for adoption by the
full Council on 18 December 2025
topline: The Council has decided to approve the revised Statement of Licensing Policy for 2026-2031, impacting various stakeholders and potential changes to licensing practices.

content:
The Officer gave an introduction on
Awaab’s Law as outlined in the report.
Awaab’s Law, introduced under the Social
Housing (Regulation) Act 2023, came into force on 27 October 2025.
It mandates strict timeframes for social landlords to investigate
and resolve health hazards, particularly damp and mould, in
tenants’ homes
 
To ensure compliance with Awaab’s Law,
social landlords must meet a series of strict statutory
requirements designed to protect tenants from health hazards such
as damp and mould. These requirements are divided into two
categories, emergency hazards and significant hazards, and set
clear expectations for response times, communication and
accountability.
 
 The Officer listed
the key requirements under Awaab’s law as outlined in the
report.
Next Year Awaab’s Law will be extended
to cover additional hazard.
 
NEC System Integration
2.5 of the report shows the dedicated CRM
contact category for damp and mould, which has been created,
ensuring that all related tenant communities are accurately
recorded and tracked.
 
Staff Training
 
All staff have received significant awareness
training around the implications and processes required.and
Customer Services included.
 
In September, the Council appointed the
services of contractors Bell Group. who are a specialist contractor
who offer services in damp and mould remediation for social
housing. Preventing damp and treating mould.
 
The Officer reported that KPIs are being
developed to provide oversight, assurance and accountability.
Managers will get an overview of damp and
mould cases; this will give the Housing Committee an oversight too
on progression.
 
Officers have engaged with residents, and the
website has been updated to include Awaab’s Law and the
implications.
 
The Committee were reminded that in September
20 Go Mobile app was approved and licences purchased.  The app allows Officers in real time in
people’s houses to complete forms and update orders. It is
integrated with the housing IT solution.
As the expansion of Awaab Law gets underway,
IT systems will be monitored to see that it is fit for services.
Members attentions were brought to additional staffing and
resources needed to comply with the legislation.
 
Members were drawn to the legal implications
as outlined in the report for non-compliance including reputational
damage, and health and safety. Safeguarding residents that are
living in Council properties.
 
 
 
Chair thanked Officers for their comprehensive
work and members agreed that it was important and appreciated the
work put in behind the scenes.
 
Members asked about the additional staffing
capacity and if there were any resources available, which was not
covered in the current budget.
The decent home standards, are they attached
to Housing Association properties. Also, will the same standard
applies to private properties. Is it just Local Authority. How will
the resource be covered and managed.
 
The Officer responded that there is a report
on resourcing which is going through the budget process and new
requirements on Awaab’s law which is going to the Leadership
Committee.  Everything pertaining
Awaab’s Law will not be covered with current
structures.  Additional staffing is
needed to cover cases. This will not be possible within the
existing work frame. Other local authorities have lots of cases
too
 
In response to Members question on decent
homes; The Officer said, It does feed into decent homes standard.
i.e. elements like the building structure and key elements such as
kitchens and bathrooms. There is the HSS Anything that is
identified in Awaab’s Law will mean it has failed the decent
homes standards.
 
The Officer said that it was only applicable
to Social Housing at the moment and will be rolled out to Private
sector.
 
Members asked if advice was provided to
residents relating to ventilation and mould avoidance.
 
The Corporate Head of Law and Governance,
confirmed that part of the guidance is given to internal
managements tenants would be advised on how to manage mould and
ventilation by Officers if asked to respond to complaints arising
from such matters.
 
 
For Information.
topline: The Housing Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the implementation of Awaab's Law to address health hazards like damp and mould in social housing.

content:
The Officer outlined the Corporate Debt
Policy.
Members were reminded of the actions on
housing. The Corporate Debt & Financial Inclusion Policy which
was approved at June Housing Committee.
 
 
Key things were outlined to Members as
included in the report.
 
The Housing response to that, is to provide
tailored support primarily by a tenant sustainability Officer to
tenants. They will work directly with tenants and provide advice on
benefits and discretionary payment. Thy help identify other debts
such as council tax and fuel arrears.
           
Tailored support is provided to residents and
those who may be vulnerable through the Council’s Tenancy
Sustainment Officers (TSOs).
 

-       
Officers will also guide residents in terms of any court
actions.

-       
Officers will provide breathing space for tenants, whereby they
will not be pursued for debt on rent arrears. 

-       
There are other initiatives like debt orders.
 
The Officer gave a summary of risk
implications to the Council, in terms of revenue loss, which
impacts on housing repairs due to delays in rent arrears
 
Information on Low-income family tracker, the
data analytics will be brought back to the Committee. Data is
currently being collected, and Officers will provide feedback to
Committee members at the next meeting.
 
Members appreciated the value in terms of
residents and asked if the Council achieved any savings.
 
In response to the Committee the Officers are
currently collating data on support for tenants and how that
affects the Council. Things like getting funds from Universal
Credit  through back payments would be a
significant gain.
 
Officers reported that evictions and court
actions arising from arrears are very rare.  There is joint working, which will ensure that
tenants are not affected by rent arrears, that will not allow them
to pay for other Council services. Only those that have not been
able to come to an arrangement.
 
Members commented that some residents
complained that they go into arrears, although short
term.  This is caused by Universal
Credit not being paid on time. Members wanted to know if there were
anything the Council could do. Some of the residents do get
stressed about the situation.
 
The Officer responded to questions, that
automated letters are sent to tenants alerting them of rent
arrears. The housing department would not know until four weeks
later of any issues relating to arrears.  Rent is paid in advance, this would elevate any
arrears if residents became unemployed or Universal Credit delays
in paying rent. Whilst this is difficult for tenants, the
Department would contact them.  The
housing should endeavour not to send letters to tenants, but if
this is not carried out, then tenants would not know that benefits
have been stopped.
 
In respect of Para 2.7 in relation to debt
relief orders (DRO), how does this work operationally in terms of
rent arrear.  Members wanted to know if
debts are consolidated into one debt.
 
In response to Members questions. The Officer
said that the Housing Department is contacted and presented with
the DRO and ask if the debt can be written off. These do not occur
often and the debts are with various creditors.  The order notification states that the debt would
be written off and not attainable by a specific period. DRO
normally are from people who are on low income.
 
Member asked what feeds into the platform of
arrears and do other authorities or organisation feed data and do
they identify risk.
 
The Officer provided data on rent and work
closely with the housing team and inclusion Officer.  Daniel Lloyd will feed back data to the Housing
Committee.
 
For Information.

towards more sustainable discretionary services, and reduced
service subsidies, where the minimum increases were proposed to
ensure the subsidy did not grow.  Taking

Committee in mind, when setting the 2025/2026 fees and charges,
where Members were keen to see small incremental increases in
charges as opposed to gaps where charges were not increased
followed by larger percentage increases.

content:
The Committee noted progress with the Service

Officers reported that they continued to
monitor 37 objectives, with 6 completed, 19 in progress, and a
small number paused or not yet started, mainly owing to capacity or
resourcing issues.  This reflected both
the ambition of the plan and the reality of delivering
transformation alongside business-as-usual.
 
The Committee was pleased to learn that the
Meadow Management Policy had been delivered under budget and to
specification, with positive feedback from stakeholders.
 
In addition, the digitisation of telecare
services was now almost complete, with final outreach underway, as
highlighted in the Officer’s report.
 
Officers confirmed that following their
approval at the last meeting of the Committee
the Voluntary Sector Grant Policy was being
rolled out and Officers had updated both the Safeguarding Policy
and Prevent Strategy.
 
Members noted that a number of reviews and
strategic projects were progressing well, including the Community
Buildings Review, and the SANG Infrastructure Plan. New initiatives
such as the Banking Hubs Engagement Process and the Whole Systems
Approach to Gambling, were being supported, where Runnymede was
acting as a pilot borough, working with the County
Council.  In this regard Officers agreed
to seek confirmation of whether there was a corporate policy on
advertising standards for the borough’s bus stops, because
Members were keen that appropriate advertising which did not for
example promote gambling should be used.
 
Members sought progress with the new skatepark
at Heathervale.  Officers confirmed that planning permission had
been given.  However, discussions were
taking place with Surrey Cricket with regard to the proximity of
the outfield to the proposed location of the skatepark, as it was
not a ‘like for like’ footprint.  If there were any issues Officers would bring an
update to the Committee.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.

content:
The Committee received the CCTV Annual report
for 2025 produced by Safer Runnymede.
 
The report presented detailed information on
the CCTV policy, principles and objectives, as well as a series of
statistics pertaining to CCTV operations and related services,
including Freedom of Information requests, subject access requests,
and privacy, and data impact assessments. 
 
Officers were pleased to report positive
feedback for the team and that no complaints had been recorded
about Safer Runnymede CCTV since 2022. 
Members also praised the commitment and professionalism of the team
in Safer Runnymede, who continued to work closely with the Police
and other partner agencies.
 
It was noted that the total number of CCTV
incidents recorded was 6499 in 2025. 
These were broken down by type across a range of issues; such as
explosives, shoplifting, begging, vehicle crime, and knife
crime.
 
Officers were asked to update the
Council’s website with the most recent CCTV statistics.
 
Officers agreed to update the Committee
with regard to an issue related to
vandalism in Victory Park, and CCTV sightlines following conclusion
of discussions with colleagues in Environmental Services.
 
Members were asked to note that whilst
feedback was welcome, the provision of additional CCTV had to be
evidence led, with finite resources available to review current and
potential locations and/or relocation assessments in the longer
term.
 
The report was duly
noted.

content:
The Committee’s approval was sought to
make a recommendation to Corporate Management Committee regarding
the outcome of a review of Chertsey Museum and how this related to
the museum’s resourcing in terms of staff and other
operational arrangements.
 
The report sought approval for the proposed
re-structure and to enter into
consultation with affected staff and Unison.
 
The report also provided an update on storage
and asset risks, which Officers were continuing to progress with
colleagues in Assets and Regeneration.
 
Officers explained that the re-structure, if
approved, would improve service delivery, increase resilience,
especially for Saturday openings, and ensure staff were supported
and fairly recognised.
 
Officers outlined the proposed structure, the
full details of which were contained in the consultation document
which would be issued to staff subject to approval by Corporate
Management Committee.  This also set out
the implications for responsibilities and working patterns, and how
this might be achieved in a cost neutral way.
 
Members agreed that Chertsey Museum remained a
cultural cornerstone for the borough, staff were praised for their
commitment and the wish to support them was expressed.  It was also stated that the museum continued to
demonstrate strong community and educational engagement and an
international audience, with over 17,000 users in 2024/25.
 
The recent partnership work with St
Peter’s Hospital was also highlighted, as reported at the
last meeting of the Committee in September 2025.
 
A question was raised about how the proposals
might be implemented, subject to consultation.  In response, Members were assured that should
there be any challenges to the proposed re-structure, changes would
not be imposed on staff; the employer would look to make changes
when circumstances allowed.
 
The intention of the restructure was to add
resilience, address any anomalies, and relieve pressure on existing
staff, whose workload was currently unbalanced.
 
Members were content to approve the
recommendation accordingly.
 
Recommend to
Corporate Management Committee that –
 
the proposed
restructure of Chertsey Museum staff be approved, and to enter
consultation with affected employees and Unison on the proposals
outlined in the Officer’s report to Community Services
Committee.
topline: The Community Services Committee has decided to restructure Chertsey Museum staff and enter into consultation with affected employees and Unison.

content:
The Committee reviewed the Quarter 2 updates
for the 2025/26 Community Services key performance indicators.
 
Members recalled that some KPIs were purely
statistical, without targets, but remained vital in demonstrating
service impact.
 
A full breakdown of KPIs, including officer
commentary and RAG ratings was set out in the appendix to the
Officer’s report.  It was
highlighted that in Quarter 2 20 KPIs rated Green, 6 Amber, and 5
Red, with continued strong performance across several areas.
 
The Committee was pleased to note that Digital
Alarm Transition had reached completion. In addition, the Community
Development Team also turned around performance on funded spaces
for its activities and events programme, moving from Red in Quarter
1 to Green in Quarter 2.  Members agreed
this demonstrated the value of the work put in to ensure that such
services provided by the Council, in partnership with others, were
reaching those most in need.
 
Officers reported that Chertsey Museum visitor
numbers, remained slightly below target due to ongoing school
travel cost constraints, and Meals at Home in Runnymede, was within
2.2% of target, showing a modest improvement from Quarter 1.
 
Officers were concerned by Social Prescribing
referrals in Runnymede which remained significantly below target
due to funding reductions and staffing constraints, as well as the
changing structure to service delivery, as outlined in a report to
the previous meeting of the Committee. 
Officers agreed to review the relevant KPI target for Social
Prescribing in light of service changes.
 
Members were further advised that some of the
amber and red KPIs related to services delivered in Surrey Heath
Borough, under the partnership arrangements between the two
Councils, and reported to both authorities accordingly.
 
Officers agreed it would be helpful to include
narrative on the Quarter 3 update where targets showing amber or
red including steps to improve the rating.
 
Officers were thanked for their report which
was duly noted.

Proposal: erection
of seven dwellings with associated garages/car parking, access and
landscaping following demolition of existing dwelling.
 
The Committee noted the Officer’s report
and presentation as well as information contained within the
addendum, updating the recommendation with regard to the proposed
pedestrian crossing facility and pedestrian access to the
site. 
 
Members also noted updated information which
confirmed Surrey Wildlife Trust’s queries regarding the
baseline biodiversity had been satisfactorily resolved.
 
Officers advised that the proposed development
was considered appropriate development in the Green Belt and would
have an acceptable impact on the character of the area and
neighbouring amenity. 
 
In addition, subject to conditions, there
would be no material highway impacts, and subject to securing the
legal agreement for SAMM and SANG, no harm to ecology.  Officers also considered that a suitable drainage
strategy for the site could be secured via condition.
 
Members noted the previous appeal decision,
and welcomed the provision of 6 (net) additional dwellings,
commenting that single storey dwellings were welcomed in the
location and provided a valuable mix.
 
Officers confirmed that the width of the road
appeared to provide suitable access for emergency vehicles with
reference to the site plan(s).
 
The Committee was content that the application
be referred back to the Head of Planning to approve, subject to the
completion of a S106 agreement which secured the SPA mitigation and
subject to the conditions as set out in the Officer’s report
and accompanying addendum.
 
Resolved that
–
 
The
Head of Planning be authorised to

 

i)         
grant consent, subject to the completion of a S106 legal agreement
to secure mitigation against the impacts of the development on the
Thames Basin Heath Special Protection Area and the conditions set
out in section 11 of the report, and the updated condition 8 set
out in the Addendum to the agenda; and

 

ii)         refuse
planning permission at his discretion should the S106 not progress
to his satisfaction

content:
Proposal: Change of use of public house and guest accommodation
(Sui Generis) into 6 residential units (C3) with extensions and
alterations to existing building and roof and associated cycle
storage, hard and soft landscaping following demolition of lean-to
structure and chimney
 
The Committee noted the
Officer’s report and presentation as well as information
contained within the addendum including an additional condition
regarding the northern side of the elevation in the development to
comply with Policy EE1 of the Runnymede 2030 Local Plan and
guidance within the NPPF.
 
Officers informed the Committee
that the presumption in favour of sustainable development applied
for the development and a material consideration was the provision
of housing to meet the Council’s need, and supporting
development of underutilised land in urban locations.  Officers had attributed substantial weight to
using suitable brownfield sites for homes.
 
The Committee noted that the
development had been assessed against the relevant Development Plan
policies, the 2030 Runnymede Local Plan, the policies of the NPPF,
guidance in the PPG and other material considerations, including
third party representations.
 
Some Members expressed concerns
with regard to the perceived loss of a well
established public house, and one Member queried whether the
proposals demonstrated Suitable Residential
Environment.  Officers were satisfied
that the proposal was sustainable and acceptable in accordance with
the relevant policies as set out in the report and met the SPD
objectives.
 
Some Members also echoed the
concerns outlined in residents’ representations with regard
to car parking.  However, Officers
advised that although there was only a minimum of one car parking
space provided, this was considered appropriate, given the
sustainable location.  Furthermore,
Officers advised that the Highways Authority had raised no
objections, but had recommended conditions with regard to parking,
cycle parking and EV charging, all of which would be taken into
consideration.  The provision of parking
spaces and the need for the Developer to apply for and be granted a
Stopping Up Order, prior to the commencement of any work on the
land was noted.
 
Officers addressed each of these
points raised by Members and it was acknowledged that several of
the proposed units would have a limited outlook.  However, it was confirmed that in the
Officers’ view there were insufficient harms to justify
refusing the application, given the other positives of the scheme
and the modest harm.
 
 
Some Members felt the price asked
was too high for the pub building. 
However, it was noted that there was significant alternative pub
provision within close range of the pub.  No application to register the premises as an
Asset of Community Value had been made.
 
Members agreed that the demise of
the public house was regrettable, but the need for more housing
outweighed these concerns and that applying the concept of
‘tilted balance’ led to the conclusion that the
application should be granted, subject to the conditions as set
down in the Officer’s report and the accompanying
addendum.
 
Resolved that –
 
The
Head of Planning be authorised to grant planning permission subject
to the conditions set out in section 11 of the report, and the
additional condition set out in the Addendum to the
agenda
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve the change of use of a public house and guest accommodation into residential units, despite concerns raised by some Members and residents.

content:
The Committee was updated on issues pertaining
to the management and maintenance of the Green and Members were
asked to approve various works being  carried out from
the Englefield Green Earmarked reserves. 
 
Officers advised the Committee that the Parks
and Green Spaces Manager and the Senior Green Spaces Officer had
met with representatives from the Crown Estates office at Windsor
Great Park on the 24th
September.   The intention of the
meeting was that both parties reached an agreement on which grounds
maintenance activities the Crown Estate would approve in
generality.
 
During the meeting a verbal agreement was
reached on a number of issues including replacement of litter bins
and bollards.  Officers had subsequently
written to the Crown Estates office seeking written confirmation of
the consented works agreed.
 
The written confirmation and details of all
agreements would be incorporated into the Englefield Green
Management Plan.
 
Bollards
 
The Committee was asked to consider the
Officers proposal to install 9 composite bollards which were
already purchased and in stock.  
Additionally, the Committee was asked to approve the installation
of a replacement metal dropped bollard.   This bollard would facilitate entrance onto
the Green for event organisers.  The
Committee supported this proposal.
 
Litter bins
 
The Committee was asked to consider a proposal
for replacement and removal of 16 litter and dog waste bins on the
Green to the specification detailed in Appendix A of the
report.  The Committee felt the proposed
bins were too corporate for the Green and a more rural type of bin
would be more fitting for the aesthetic of the Green. 
The Committee voted against the Officers
specification for replacement bins.
 
 
Replacement of cricket pavilion clock
 
The Committee was advised that the clock on
the front of the pavilion was broken. 
The existing clock was over 25 years old and beyond economic
repair.  Members were asked to approve
the replacement of the clock at a cost of £2,515 which
included installation.  The Committee
supported this proposal. 
 
 
Englefield Green Management Plan
 
Members were advised that the ongoing tree
audit had left limited Officer capacity to draft the Englefield
Green Management Plan for this Committee. 
 
 
Tree Audit
 
The trees at Englefield Green had been
inspected during August as part of the Council’s tree
audit.  The audit had identified that
there were approximately 22,662 trees on Englefield
Green.   The audit identified that
99.8% of trees were in good or fair condition.  Any dead trees would be felled.
 
 
 
Tree planting
 
The Committee considered the proposed tree
planting programme detailed in the report along with the location
plan.   The work could commence
once the Crown Estates office had confirmed their consent to the
planting and approved the choice and specimen and
location.  
 
The Committee discussed the location plan at
some length, agreeing that establishing where the trees would be
planted was key to enabling the Committee to make a
decision.   It was agreed that any
tree planting should take place at the southern end of the Green.
The Committee agreed on an option for planting locations subject to
the Crown Estates consent.
 
 
Resolved that:
 
The transfer of up
to £15,955 Englefield Green earmarked reserves be approved to
pay for the works listed and costed as below:
 
a. Installation of
the 9 composite permanent bollards already purchased and
    held in store.
Installation costs £700
 
b. Installation of a
replacement metal dropped bollard used to facilitate
    entrance onto the green
for event organisers. Purchase cost £150, removal
    and installation cost
£100
 
c.  The Committee voted against the Officers proposal
for the replacement and
      removal of 16
litter and dog waste bins on Englefield Green as per the
      specification
and map at Appendix A.
 
d. Planting and
3-year maintenance of up to 10 trees to be planted. The final
    planting location to be
confirmed with one option laid out in Appendix A.
    Cost will be circa
£2,000

e. Replacement of
the cricket pavilion clock, the cost of clock and
installation
    being £2,515
topline: The Committee has decided to approve installation of bollards, replacement of cricket pavilion clock, and tree planting program at Englefield Green, while rejecting the proposal for replacement of litter bins.

content:
The Sub-Committee was asked to determine an
application for a new Premises Licence in respect of 10 Woodham
Lane, New Haw, Addlestone, Surrey. KT15 3NA.
 
The application was as set out in the agenda
papers, including a change to the proposed hours of operation for
the sale of alcohol from 09:00 to 22:00, instead of 08:00 to 23:00
hours as originally applied for.
 
Members noted that the premises had formerly
been a hairdressers’ salon, and this application was for an
off licence within a convenience store. 
The only licensable activity applied for was for the sale by retail
of alcohol (off the premises only).  It
was proposed to call the business ‘Vape and Wine.’
 
Officers confirmed that 21 valid
representations had been received in respect of the
application.  These were summarised in
the report and attached in full for the Sub-Committee to
consider.  Members’ attention was
drawn to the potential impact on nearby residential properties,
including one that physically adjoined the premises.  Other representations referenced potential noise
issues, litter, risk to public safety, anti-social behaviour, and
the potential of harm to children and the community.
 
It was noted that none of the Responsible
Authorities had made representations.
 
The applicant’s representative was
invited to state their case.
 
Members were advised that the applicant had
previous experience of retail, as part of a family run business,
aware of the requirements with regard to compliance and community
safety.  The applicant had been a
delivery driver for Ocado for approximately 18 months and was
familiar with the local area.  He had
recently become a Personal Licence Holder and had attained level 2
BIIAB accreditation.  A 999 year lease
had been secured for the premises, thus longevity and
sustainability of the business was a priority.  Notices had been prepared to advise customers to
leave the premises quietly and to avoid disturbance to
residents.  The applicant was keen to
promote public safety and planned to install CCTV, as set out in
the application.  He assured the
Sub-Committee that they would not start trading without it being in
place, including coverage of the front door of the
premises.  With regard to promoting the
licensing objectives; the premises would have a refusals book and
incident book; staff would be trained, and their training would be
logged.  The applicant endeavoured to
work with the community and stated that the business would be
operated by himself, his partner and his brother.  It was stressed that younger family members would
not be involved in the sale of alcohol and that a strict challenge
25 policy would be in place.
 
The Sub-Committee was asked to note that there
were no cumulative impact zones in Runnymede and that each
application should be treated on its merits.  It was stressed that none of the Responsible
Authorities had made representations. 
 
The applicant confirmed that it was estimated
to have the shop fitted out and ready to open in approximately 2
– 3 weeks if the licence was granted.
 
One of the 21 residents that had made
representations attended the meeting to speak, expressing their
disappointment that other residents had not attended the
meeting.  The resident spoke of the
potential impact on them, and their quality of life if the
application was granted.  They had
significant concerns about noise, anti-social behaviour, vandalism,
litter, and the constant pedestrian traffic in and around the
premises on a daily basis, which they felt would have a detrimental
effect on their privacy, health and wellbeing.  The Sub-Committee expressed their sympathy with
the resident, also highlighting potential concerns about public
safety, and the potential for anti-social behaviour, which would
need to be well managed by the applicant, if the application were
granted.
 
The applicant sought to re-assure the resident
that there would be no music in the shop and would ensure their
customers behaved properly and quietly. 
There would be no vaping or consumption of alcohol on the premises,
and customers would be encouraged to move away from the area having
made their purchases.  The applicant
offered to let the resident have their mobile phone number; this
offer was declined.  The applicant also
undertook to ensure the area was kept clean and tidy.
 
All parties were given an equal opportunity to
speak and ask questions, and the meeting was adjourned at 15:18 pm
with the press and public excluded while the Sub-Committee
determined the application.
 
The meeting reconvened at 16:10.
 
The Sub-Committee unaminously agreed that the
premises licence should be granted. 
However, they added three additional conditions to the licence
which it was hoped would alleviate the situation for local
residents.  Members were also keen to
stress that any failure to abide by the licensing objectives could
result in the premises licence being subject to a review at any
time.
 
Resolved that
–
 
the application for
a premises licence in respect of 10 Woodham Lane, New Haw,
Addlestone, Surrey. KT15 3NA, be granted, subject to the Mandatory
Conditions, Conditions consistent with the operating schedule, and
with the following additional conditions:
 

i)         
all staff must be trained in responsible alcohol
retailing.  Details of such training
shall be kept on the premises and available for inspection by any
Authorised Officer on request;
 

ii)         no
deliveries to the premises shall take place between 21:00 hours and
09:00 hours on the following day; and
 

iii)        staff will
undertake routine litter picks to a distance of 5 metres around the
main entrance to the premises, including the private forecourt and
public highway
topline: The Sub-Committee has decided to grant a new Premises Licence for a convenience store to sell alcohol off the premises
